lessons.title: General Group Trends of Representative Elements
lessons.notes_html:
The representative elements are the s-block and p-block elements of groups IA to VIIIA. Their properties change in regular trends down a group and across a period, and these trends can be explained from atomic size, shielding and effective nuclear charge.

Atomic Radii

Atomic radii of the alkali metals increase regularly from Li to Cs, because a new electron shell is added at each step and shielding increases. A famous exception in group IIIA is gallium: gallium has a smaller atomic radius than aluminium although it lies below it, because gallium comes after the first transition series and its ten 3d electrons shield the nuclear charge poorly. The increased effective nuclear charge pulls the outer electrons closer (d-block contraction), so gallium is slightly smaller than aluminium.

Ionization Energy

Ionization energy decreases from top to bottom in the s-block elements. Down the group a new shell is added at each step, so the valence electron is farther from the nucleus and is better shielded by the inner electrons. The effective nuclear attraction on it therefore decreases, and less energy is needed to remove it. In group IIIA the trend is irregular: ionization energy falls from B to Al, then rises slightly at Ga, falls at In and rises again at Tl. The rises at Ga and Tl are due to the poor shielding of the filled d and f electrons (d-block and f-block contractions), which increases the effective nuclear charge. The overall trend is a decrease with irregular increases at gallium and thallium.

Electronegativity

Electronegativities of the alkali metals decrease from Li to Cs (Li 1.0 to Cs 0.7). Down the group the atomic size increases and the valence electron is held less tightly because of greater distance and shielding, so the atom attracts a shared pair of electrons less strongly. As a result, metallic and electropositive character, and chemical reactivity, increase down the group.

Melting and Boiling Points

Melting and boiling points regularly decrease down group IA: in the alkali metals the metallic bonding weakens regularly as atomic size increases down the group, so the points decrease steadily from Li to Cs. In the other groups the trend is irregular because of changes in structure and bonding type. Boiling points of the halogens, on the other hand, increase down the group: the halogen molecules become larger and their electron clouds more easily polarised, so the van der Waals forces between the molecules become stronger and more heat is needed to separate them.

Electrical Conductivity

Alkali metals are good conductors of electricity. They have one loosely held valence electron per atom in a sea of delocalised electrons within the metallic lattice. These free electrons move readily under an applied potential, so the metals conduct electricity and heat very well.

mcqs.why: Outside group IA the trend is irregular because structure and bonding type change from element to element in those groups.

lessons.title: Reactions of Representative Elements
lessons.notes_html:
The representative elements show their characteristic chemistry in reactions with air, water, nitrogen and acids. The balanced equations below are the standard examples from the book.

Reaction with Air and Nitrogen

Sodium in excess air: sodium burns in excess air to form mainly sodium peroxide, a pale yellow solid: 2Na + O2 -> Na2O2. With a limited supply of air the normal oxide is formed instead: 4Na + O2 -> 2Na2O. Potassium is still more reactive and forms the superoxide KO2 on burning in excess air, while lithium forms only the normal oxide Li2O.

Magnesium with nitrogen: hot magnesium combines directly with nitrogen to form magnesium nitride, a greenish-yellow solid: 3Mg + N2 -> Mg3N2. The nitride is hydrolysed by warm water to give ammonia: Mg3N2 + 6H2O -> 3Mg(OH)2 + 2NH3. The general formula of the nitrides of the alkaline earth metals is M3N2, because the metal forms M2+ ions and nitrogen forms N3- ions, so three M2+ ions balance two N3- ions, as in Mg3N2 and Ca3N2.

Reactions with Alcohols and Alkalis

Potassium with ethyl alcohol: potassium reacts with ethanol to form potassium ethoxide with the evolution of hydrogen gas, more vigorously than sodium does: 2K + 2C2H5OH -> 2C2H5OK + H2. This shows the weakly acidic character of the -OH group of alcohols.

Ferric chloride with caustic soda: a brown precipitate of ferric hydroxide is formed in this double decomposition reaction: FeCl3 + 3NaOH -> Fe(OH)3 + 3NaCl. The reddish-brown Fe(OH)3 precipitate is a characteristic test for Fe3+ ions.

Reaction of Aluminium with Sulphuric Acid

Aluminium is oxidised by hot concentrated sulphuric acid, which itself is reduced to sulphur dioxide: 2Al + 6H2SO4 -> Al2(SO4)3 + 3SO2 + 6H2O. This shows that concentrated H2SO4 acts as a strong oxidising agent towards metals.

lessons.title: Flame Test of s-Block Elements
lessons.notes_html:
The Flame Test

In a flame test a small amount of a metal salt on a clean platinum or nichrome wire is held in a Bunsen flame, and the metal imparts a characteristic colour to the flame. The heat of the flame excites the metal atoms, and they emit light of a characteristic colour on returning to the ground state. The test is used to identify alkali metal ions in a sample.

Flame Colours of Alkali Metals

  • Lithium: crimson red
  • Sodium: golden yellow
  • Potassium: lilac
  • Rubidium: red-violet
  • Caesium: blue-violet

Sodium is the alkali metal that gives the yellow colour in a flame test; the golden yellow flame is so intense that it can mask the colours of other metals present.

mcqs.why: A flame test uses a clean platinum or nichrome wire to hold the salt in the Bunsen flame without adding its own colour.

mcqs.why: Lithium gives a crimson red flame, one of the characteristic alkali metal flame colours listed in the book.

mcqs.why: Sodium gives the golden yellow flame; it is so intense that it can mask the colours of other metals present.

mcqs.q: Potassium gives which flame colour?
mcqs.why: Potassium gives a lilac flame, whereas rubidium gives red-violet and caesium gives blue-violet.

mcqs.q: Rubidium gives which colour in a flame test?
mcqs.why: Rubidium gives a red-violet flame, distinct from potassium lilac and caesium blue-violet.

mcqs.q: Caesium gives which colour in a flame test?
mcqs.why: Caesium gives a blue-violet flame in the flame test for alkali metal ions.

Burns the metal to a coloured oxide

mcqs.why: The flame excites metal atoms, and they emit light of a characteristic colour when they return to the ground state.

The melting point of a metal
mcqs.why: The flame test is used to identify alkali metal ions because each one imparts a characteristic colour to the flame.

mcqs.why: Sodium can mask other colours because its golden yellow flame is so intense compared with the other flame colours.

options: Li golden yellow, Na lilac, K crimson red

Li crimson red, Na golden yellow, K lilac
mcqs.why: The correct set is lithium crimson red, sodium golden yellow and potassium lilac, as given for the alkali metal flame test.

lessons.title: Chemistry of Important Compounds of s-Block Elements
lessons.notes_html:
Caustic Soda by the Castner-Kellner Cell

Caustic soda (NaOH) is obtained by the electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride in the Castner-Kellner cell. The cell has a flowing mercury cathode at the bottom and titanium anode blocks in brine compartments separated by partitions, with a central compartment containing water or dilute NaOH. At the anode, chloride ions are discharged: 2Cl- -> Cl2 + 2e-, and chlorine gas is collected. At the mercury cathode, sodium ions are discharged into the mercury: Na+ + e- -> Na (amalgam). The sodium amalgam flows to the central compartment where it reacts with water: 2Na(Hg) + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2 + Hg, and the mercury is recycled, so pure caustic soda free from NaCl is obtained. The cathode in the Castner-Kellner cell is mercury.

Bleaching Powder

Bleaching powder is calcium oxychloride, Ca(OCl)Cl, a yellowish-white powder used as a bleaching and disinfecting agent. It is prepared by passing chlorine gas over dry slaked lime at about 40 C: Ca(OH)2 + Cl2 -> Ca(OCl)Cl + H2O. With water it gives nascent oxygen which does the bleaching; in the presence of moisture and CO2 it slowly releases chlorine, and with dilute hydrochloric acid it liberates chlorine rapidly: Ca(OCl)Cl + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + Cl2 + H2O.

Potassium Nitrate and Fireworks

The chemical commonly used in fireworks is potassium nitrate (saltpetre). It is the oxidising agent in gunpowder-type firework mixtures and supplies oxygen for rapid burning. Metal salts present with it produce the characteristic colours of fireworks.

lessons.title: Reactions of p-Block Elements
lessons.notes_html:
The p-block elements include the non-metals and metalloids of groups IIIA to VIIIA. Their reactions below show the oxidising power of their compounds and the special behaviour of elements such as gallium.

Gallium and the d-Block Contraction

Gallium has a smaller atomic radius than aluminium despite being below aluminium in group IIIA. Gallium comes after the first transition series, and its ten 3d electrons shield the nuclear charge poorly. The increased effective nuclear charge pulls the outer electrons closer, a contraction called the d-block contraction, so gallium is slightly smaller than aluminium. For the same reason the ionization energy of group IIIA rises slightly at gallium instead of falling regularly.

Aluminium with Concentrated Sulphuric Acid

When a piece of aluminium is dipped into hot concentrated sulphuric acid, the acid oxidises the metal and is itself reduced to sulphur dioxide: 2Al + 6H2SO4 -> Al2(SO4)3 + 3SO2 + 6H2O. Concentrated sulphuric acid therefore acts as a strong oxidising agent towards p-block metals.

Double Decomposition: Ferric Chloride and Caustic Soda

When ferric chloride is mixed with an aqueous solution of caustic soda, a reddish-brown precipitate of ferric hydroxide separates: FeCl3 + 3NaOH -> Fe(OH)3 + 3NaCl. This precipitate is a characteristic test for Fe3+ ions.

mcqs.q: Gallium is slightly smaller than aluminium mainly because:
options: It has fewer protons than aluminium
Its ten 3d electrons shield the nuclear charge poorly
It lies in an earlier period than aluminium
Its outer electrons are in a lower shell
mcqs.why: Gallium comes after the first transition series; its 3d electrons shield poorly, so increased effective nuclear charge pulls its outer electrons closer.

mcqs.q: The contraction responsible for the small size of gallium is called:
mcqs.why: The effect is called the d-block contraction, caused by the poor shielding of the ten 3d electrons in gallium.

mcqs.q: Because of the same poor shielding, the ionization energy of group IIIA at gallium:
options: Rises slightly instead of falling regularly
Falls much more sharply than expected
Becomes equal to that of boron
mcqs.why: For the same reason as its small radius, the ionization energy of group IIIA rises slightly at gallium instead of falling regularly.

mcqs.why: 2Al + 6H2SO4 -> Al2(SO4)3 + 3SO2 + 6H2O, so the salt formed is aluminium sulphate.

mcqs.why: The acid is reduced to sulphur dioxide, SO2, which is the gas evolved in this reaction with aluminium.

mcqs.q: In that reaction, concentrated sulphuric acid is itself:
mcqs.why: Concentrated H2SO4 oxidises aluminium and is itself reduced to SO2, showing its strong oxidising action towards p-block metals.

mcqs.q: Ferric chloride with aqueous caustic soda is an example of:
mcqs.why: FeCl3 + 3NaOH -> Fe(OH)3 + 3NaCl is a double decomposition reaction forming a ferric hydroxide precipitate.

mcqs.q: The precipitate formed from FeCl3 and NaOH has the colour:
mcqs.why: The Fe(OH)3 precipitate formed is reddish-brown, which is why it is used as a characteristic test.

mcqs.why: The reddish-brown Fe(OH)3 precipitate is a characteristic test for Fe3+ ions in a sample.

mcqs.q: The p-block elements discussed in this lesson belong to groups:
options: IA to VIIIA including the s-block
mcqs.why: The p-block elements are the non-metals and metalloids of groups IIIA to VIIIA, as stated in the lesson.

lessons.title: Chemical Behaviour of Halogens
lessons.notes_html:
Trends in the Halogen Group

Boiling point of the halogens increases down the group. The molecules become larger and their electron clouds more easily polarised, so the van der Waals forces between them become stronger, more heat is needed to separate them, and boiling point increases from F2 to I2.

Acidity of the Hydrogen Halides

The acidity of the hydrogen halides increases from HF to HI. Down the group the H-X bond becomes longer and weaker as the halogen atom becomes larger, so the bond breaks more easily to release H+ ions. Bond strength, and not electronegativity, controls the acidity here, so the order is HI > HBr > HCl > HF.

Fluorine: the Strongest Oxidising Agent

Fluorine is the smallest and most electronegative halogen, the F-F bond is weak and the hydration energy of the small F- ion is very high. It therefore gains electrons most readily and oxidises other substances most powerfully, making F2 the strongest oxidising agent. Oxidising power decreases down the group in the order F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.

Disproportionation of Chlorine

In some reactions chlorine is oxidised and reduced at the same time, a process called disproportionation (auto oxidation-reduction), so it acts as its own oxidising and reducing agent. With cold dilute NaOH it gives chloride and hypochlorite: Cl2 + 2NaOH -> NaCl + NaOCl + H2O, in which chlorine goes from 0 to -1 and to +1. With hot concentrated NaOH it forms chloride and chlorate: 3Cl2 + 6NaOH -> 5NaCl + NaClO3 + 3H2O.

mcqs.why: Halogen boiling points increase from F2 to I2 because the molecules become larger and their van der Waals forces stronger.

mcqs.q: Acidity of the hydrogen halides increases in the order:
mcqs.why: Acidity increases from HF to HI, giving the order HI > HBr > HCl > HF, because the H-X bond weakens down the group.

mcqs.why: Bond strength, not electronegativity, controls acidity here: the longer, weaker H-X bond breaks more easily to release H+ ions.

mcqs.why: F2 is the strongest oxidising agent because fluorine is the smallest and most electronegative halogen and gains electrons most readily.

mcqs.why: Oxidising power decreases down the group in the order F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2, with fluorine the most powerful.

The F- ion is the largest halide ion

mcqs.why: Fluorine is the strongest oxidising agent because the F-F bond is weak and hydration energy of the small F- ion is very high.

mcqs.why: Cl2 + 2NaOH -> NaCl + NaOCl + H2O with cold dilute NaOH, giving chloride and hypochlorite.

mcqs.why: With hot concentrated NaOH, 3Cl2 + 6NaOH -> 5NaCl + NaClO3 + 3H2O, so chlorate is formed instead of hypochlorite.

mcqs.why: Chlorine goes from 0 to -1 in NaCl (reduction) and to +1 in NaOCl (oxidation), which is disproportionation.

lessons.title: Chemistry of Sulphuric Acid
lessons.notes_html:
Sulphuric acid is called the king of chemicals; its old name is oil of vitriol, because concentrated sulphuric acid is an oily, dense liquid obtained historically from vitriol minerals. It is manufactured by the Contact process.

The Contact Process

The flow of the process is: sulphur (or iron pyrites) burner -> SO2 gas -> purification unit -> converter containing V2O5 at about 450 C -> SO3 gas -> absorption tower with concentrated H2SO4 -> oleum -> dilution with water -> concentrated H2SO4.

  • Step 1, burning: S + O2 -> SO2
  • Step 2, catalytic oxidation: 2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3 in the presence of the catalyst vanadium pentoxide, V2O5, at about 450 C. This is the key step of the process.
  • Step 3, absorption: SO3 + H2SO4 -> H2S2O7 (oleum), followed by H2S2O7 + H2O -> 2H2SO4. SO3 is not absorbed directly in water, because that produces a dense mist which is difficult to condense.

mcqs.why: Concentrated sulphuric acid was historically called oil of vitriol because it is an oily, dense liquid obtained from vitriol minerals.

mcqs.why: Sulphuric acid is manufactured by the Contact process, whose key step uses a V2O5 catalyst at about 450 C.

mcqs.why: H2S2O7 + H2O -> 2H2SO4, so each oleum molecule gives two molecules of concentrated sulphuric acid on dilution.

mcqs.why: After the converter, SO3 goes to the absorption tower with concentrated H2SO4, forming oleum which is then diluted.

lessons.title: Diagonal Relationship of Representative Elements
lessons.notes_html:
What is a Diagonal Relationship?

A diagonal relationship is the similarity in properties between an element and the element lying diagonally below it in the next group, caused by a balance of increasing size down the group and increasing charge across the period. Three such pairs among the representative elements are: lithium and magnesium, beryllium and aluminium, and boron and silicon.

Beryllium and Aluminium

The diagonal member of beryllium is aluminium. Beryllium lies diagonally next to aluminium in the periodic table and resembles it closely: both form amphoteric oxides and hydroxides that dissolve in acids as well as alkalis, and both form largely covalent chlorides. Beryllium also shows unique behaviour within its own group IIA: its oxide and hydroxide are amphoteric, unlike the basic oxides of the others; its compounds are largely covalent and it never shows a coordination number greater than four; and it does not react with water even on heating, whereas magnesium and the heavier metals react readily.

mcqs.q: A diagonal relationship is the similarity between an element and the element:
options: Directly below it in the same group
Directly next to it in the same period
In the same group two rows below it
Lying diagonally below it in the next group
mcqs.why: A diagonal relationship is similarity with the element lying diagonally below in the next group, from a balance of size increase down and charge increase across.

mcqs.q: Which pair shows a diagonal relationship?
mcqs.why: Lithium and magnesium are one of the three diagonal pairs named in the book, along with Be-Al and B-Si.

mcqs.q: Which of the following pairs does NOT show a diagonal relationship?
mcqs.why: Sodium and calcium is not a diagonal pair. The diagonal pairs among the representative elements are lithium-magnesium, beryllium-aluminium and boron-silicon, where the lower element of the next group resembles the upper one.

mcqs.q: The diagonal member of beryllium is:
mcqs.why: Beryllium lies diagonally next to aluminium and resembles it closely, so aluminium is its diagonal member.

mcqs.why: Both elements form largely covalent chlorides, another similarity arising from their diagonal relationship.

mcqs.why: Beryllium compounds are largely covalent and beryllium never shows a coordination number greater than four, unlike the heavier group IIA metals.

lessons.title: General Features of Outer Transition Elements
lessons.notes_html:
The d-block elements are called transition elements because their properties are intermediate between those of the highly reactive s-block metals and the p-block elements, and they form a bridge between them in the periodic table. They are called outer transition elements because their differentiating electron enters the outer (n-1)d subshell, in contrast to the inner transition (f-block) elements. Their atoms or ions have partially filled d orbitals, which gives them their characteristic properties. The 5d series lies in the sixth period and runs from lanthanum (La) to mercury (Hg); Sc to Zn is the 3d series, Y to Cd the 4d series and Ac to Cn the 6d series.

Variable Oxidation States

Transition elements show variable oxidation states because the (n-1)d and ns orbitals have very similar energies, so a variable number of electrons from both can take part in bonding. In the 3d series the common state is +2 (loss of 4s electrons), and the maximum oxidation state rises from Sc (+3) to Mn (+7), equal to the total number of 4s and 3d electrons. After manganese the maximum falls (Fe +6, Co +5, Ni +4, Cu +2, Zn +2) because the d electrons become held more tightly. Chromium (3d5 4s1) can use all six valence electrons in bonding, so its highest oxidation state is +6, shown in compounds such as K2Cr2O7 and CrO3, where chromium is a powerful oxidising agent.

Special Electronic Configurations

Chromium exists in the 4s1 3d5 configuration and not in 4s2 3d4, because a half-filled d subshell (3d5) has extra stability due to symmetrical electron distribution and maximum exchange energy. One electron therefore shifts from 4s to 3d to make the d subshell exactly half-filled, which makes 4s1 3d5 lower in energy and more stable.

Paramagnetic Behaviour

Paramagnetism is caused by unpaired electrons, and its strength increases with their number. Across the 3d series the number of unpaired electrons rises from Sc (1) to a maximum in the Mn/Fe region (Mn2+ and Fe3+ have 5) and then falls as pairing begins, reaching zero at Zn (3d10). Hence paramagnetism first increases, becomes maximum in the middle of the series, and then decreases; Zn2+ and Sc3+ are diamagnetic. Fe3+ (3d5) is the most strongly paramagnetic of the common ions Fe2+, Fe3+, Co2+ and Cr3+.

Colour Formation

Most transition metal compounds are coloured because their ions have partially filled d orbitals which split into two sets (t2g and eg) in the presence of ligands. Electrons absorb visible light of a definite colour to jump between these sets (d-d transition), and the compound shows the complementary colour. Cu2+ (3d9) has one unpaired electron that can undergo d-d transition, so its compounds are blue. Zn2+ has the configuration 3d10 with all electrons paired, so no d-d transition is possible; it absorbs no visible light and its compounds are white or colourless. Ions with d0 (Sc3+, Ti4+) or d10 (Zn2+, Cu+) configurations are likewise colourless.

Melting Points and Binding Energy

Binding energy (cohesive energy) is the energy required to break one mole of a metal into isolated gaseous atoms; it measures the strength of metallic bonding. Melting point and binding energy depend on the number of unpaired d electrons taking part in bonding: both increase from Sc to a maximum around the middle of the series (Cr, Mo, W group; binding energy maximum around V-Cr-Mn) and then decrease as electron pairing begins. Binding energy is least for zinc, whose completely filled 3d10 configuration contributes no unpaired electrons to metallic bonding, so its melting point and hardness are also the lowest in the 3d series.

Alloy Formation

Transition elements form alloys readily because their atomic sizes are very similar, differing only slightly across a series, so atoms of one metal can easily replace atoms of another in the lattice without distorting it much. They therefore mix readily in the molten state and form solid solutions called alloys, such as brass, bronze and stainless steel.

Catalytic Properties

Transition elements and their compounds act as catalysts in many reactions because they can show several oxidation states, accept and donate electrons easily, and provide a suitable surface on which reactants are adsorbed. Reactants form temporary bonds with the metal surface or the metal ion, which lowers the activation energy. Examples are Fe in the Haber process for ammonia, V2O5 in the Contact process, Ni in the hydrogenation of oils and Pt in catalytic converters.

Electroplating

Zinc, tin and chromium are commonly deposited by electroplating to protect or decorate metal surfaces. Manganese is too reactive and difficult to deposit from aqueous solution, so it is not used for electroplating. When manganese is oxidised in air it forms the mixed oxide Mn3O4 (a mixture of MnO and Mn2O3): 3Mn + 2O2 -> Mn3O4.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Coordination Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Coordination Complexes and Ligands

A coordination complex is a compound in which a central metal atom or ion is bonded to a fixed number of surrounding ions or molecules (ligands) by coordinate bonds, for example [Cu(NH3)4]2+. The number of coordinate bonds formed by the ligands with the metal is the coordination number: in Na4[Co(C2O4)3] the coordination number of cobalt is 6, because oxalate is a bidentate ligand donating two electron pairs per ligand, and three oxalate ligands form six coordinate bonds.

A chelating ligand is a polydentate ligand that binds through two or more donor atoms at the same time and forms a ring structure with the metal; the resulting complex is called a chelate, for example oxalate and EDTA complexes. Ligands are classified by the number of donor atoms: monodentate ligands donate through one atom (NH3, Cl-, CN-), bidentate ligands through two atoms (oxalate C2O4 2-, ethylenediamine), and polydentate ligands through many atoms (EDTA is hexadentate). Ligands may also be neutral (NH3, H2O, CO) or negatively charged (Cl-, CN-, C2O4 2-). Oxalate, C2O4 2-, is a bidentate ligand because it has two oxygen donor atoms through which it binds at two positions; OH-, Cl- and CN- are monodentate.

IUPAC Names of Complexes

  • Na2[Pt(OH)4]: sodium tetrahydroxoplatinate(II). The complex anion contains Pt with four hydroxo ligands; charge balance with two Na+ ions shows Pt is in the +2 oxidation state. The name of an anionic complex ends in -ate and the oxidation state is shown in Roman numerals.
  • K2[Fe(CN)5NO]: potassium pentacyanonitrosylferrate(II). This is the nitroprusside ion, containing five cyano ligands and one nitrosyl (NO) ligand around iron(II). The ligands are named alphabetically and the anionic complex of iron takes the name ferrate.
  • [Zn(NH3)4]2+: tetraamminezinc(II) ion. The cation contains four ammine (NH3) ligands around zinc(II); the complex is cationic, so the metal keeps its ordinary name. Zinc shows only the +2 oxidation state in its complexes.
  • [Ni(SCN)4]2-: tetrathiocyanatonickelate(II) ion. The anion contains four thiocyanato ligands around nickel(II), and an anionic complex of nickel is named as a nickelate.

mcqs.why: Oxalate is bidentate, donating two electron pairs per ligand; three oxalates form six coordinate bonds, so the coordination number of cobalt is 6.

lessons.title: Chemistry of Some Important Transition Elements
lessons.notes_html:
Important Reactions

  • Copper with concentrated nitric acid: Cu + 4HNO3 -> Cu(NO3)2 + 2NO2 + 2H2O. The acid oxidises copper and is itself reduced to nitrogen dioxide; brown fumes of NO2 are evolved and a blue solution of copper nitrate is formed.
  • Copper with hot concentrated sulphuric acid: Cu + 2H2SO4 -> CuSO4 + SO2 + 2H2O. Copper does not react with dilute sulphuric acid because it lies below hydrogen in the reactivity series.
  • Permanganate with oxalic acid: 2KMnO4 + 5H2C2O4 + 3H2SO4 -> K2SO4 + 2MnSO4 + 10CO2 + 8H2O. The purple colour of KMnO4 is discharged, which is used in volumetric analysis.
  • Dichromate with ferrous sulphate: K2Cr2O7 + 6FeSO4 + 7H2SO4 -> K2SO4 + Cr2(SO4)3 + 3Fe2(SO4)3 + 7H2O. The orange colour of dichromate changes to green.
  • Manganese with dilute sulphuric acid: Mn + H2SO4 -> MnSO4 + H2. Manganese lies above hydrogen in the reactivity series; a pale pink solution of manganese sulphate is obtained.
  • Iron with chlorine: 2Fe + 3Cl2 -> 2FeCl3. Chlorine is a strong oxidising agent and takes iron to its higher oxidation state; brown fumes of FeCl3 are produced.

Chromate-Dichromate Equilibrium and pH

In aqueous solution chromate and dichromate exist in equilibrium: 2CrO4 2- (yellow) + 2H+ <-> Cr2O7 2- (orange) + H2O. Adding acid (lowering pH) shifts the equilibrium to the right and the solution turns orange due to dichromate. Adding alkali (raising pH) removes H+ ions, shifts the equilibrium to the left, and the solution becomes yellow due to chromate.

Extraction and Refining of Copper

Chalcopyrite, CuFeS2, is first concentrated by froth flotation, the step in which the gangue (earthy impurities) is eliminated. The concentrate is roasted in a reverberatory furnace: 2CuFeS2 + O2 -> Cu2S + 2FeS + SO2, and the roasted ore is smelted with silica so that FeO is removed as slag (FeO + SiO2 -> FeSiO3), leaving copper matte (Cu2S + FeS). In the Bessemer converter, air is blown through the matte: 2Cu2S + 3O2 -> 2Cu2O + 2SO2 and Cu2S + 2Cu2O -> 6Cu + SO2, giving blister copper of about 98% purity. Finally it is refined electrolytically using thick plates of blister copper as anode and thin sheets of pure copper as cathode in acidified CuSO4 solution; pure copper (99.99%) deposits on the cathode while impurities collect as anode mud.

Important Alloys

  • Stainless steel: about 74% iron, 18% chromium and 8% nickel. It resists rusting, does not react with food and is easy to clean, so it is used for cutlery, surgical instruments, fry pans and chemical plant.
  • Brass: about 70% copper and 30% zinc; used for utensils, taps, locks and musical instruments.
  • Bronze: about 90% copper and 10% tin; hard and corrosion-resistant, used for statues, coins, bells and bearings.

lessons.title: Sources
lessons.notes_html:
Organic Chemistry and the Vital Force Theory

Organic chemistry is the branch of chemistry that deals with carbon compounds, mainly hydrocarbons and their derivatives. The vital force theory stated that organic compounds could only be produced inside living organisms with the help of a mysterious vital force, and could never be prepared in the laboratory. It was disproved in 1828 when Friedrich Wohler prepared urea, a typical organic compound, by heating the inorganic salt ammonium cyanate: NH4CNO -> CO(NH2)2. After this, many organic compounds were synthesised in the laboratory, so the theory was abandoned.

Natural Sources of Organic Compounds

The main natural sources are fossil remains, plants and animals. Coal, petroleum and natural gas were formed from the remains of plants and animals buried millions of years ago under high temperature and pressure, and they supply most hydrocarbons and fuels. Natural gas consists mainly of methane, usually about 85-90%, with small amounts of ethane, propane and butane, so methane is its chief constituent and the main source of its fuel value.

Plants and Animals as Sources

Natural product chemistry deals with the isolation, structure and synthesis of organic compounds produced by living organisms. Plants are a rich source: they give carbohydrates, vegetable oils, essential oils, alkaloids such as quinine and morphine, natural rubber, and vitamins. Animals provide fats and oils, proteins, hormones such as insulin, enzymes, wool and silk. Many important medicines were first obtained from these natural sources and are now also made in the laboratory.

Total and Partial Synthesis

In total synthesis an organic compound is built up in the laboratory starting from the elements themselves or from very simple inorganic materials, passing through all the steps in the laboratory. In partial synthesis the starting material is a natural organic compound obtained from plants or animals, which is then converted into the desired product by a few chemical steps. Total synthesis proves the structure of a compound completely, while partial synthesis is shorter and is often used commercially.

lessons.title: Coal as a Source of Organic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Destructive Distillation of Coal

Destructive distillation is the heating of coal strongly in the absence of air, so that it decomposes instead of burning. The products are: coke, the solid residue used as a fuel and reducing agent in metallurgy; coal tar, a thick black liquid from which benzene, toluene, phenol, naphthalene and many dyes and drugs are obtained; coal gas, a mixture of hydrogen, methane and carbon monoxide used as a fuel; and ammonia liquor (ammoniacal liquor), an aqueous solution containing ammonia formed from the nitrogen present in coal, used to make fertilisers such as ammonium sulphate. The process is carried out industrially in coke ovens and gas works.

Types of Coal

Coal is classified by rank, that is, by increasing carbon content and calorific value, into peat, lignite, bituminous coal and anthracite.

  • Peat: the first stage, soft and brown, with the least carbon (about 30-40% in dry form) and much moisture.
  • Lignite (brown coal): contains more carbon and less moisture than peat.
  • Bituminous coal: black, contains about 70-85% carbon and is the most widely used coal for industry and power generation.
  • Anthracite: the highest-rank coal, hard and shiny, with about 90% or more carbon, the highest calorific value and a clean, almost smokeless flame.

lessons.title: Characteristics of Organic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Unique Characteristics

Organic compounds have several unique features. Carbon shows catenation and forms chains, branches and rings, and it forms strong covalent bonds with H, O, N, S and halogens, giving millions of compounds. They show isomerism, are generally covalent with low melting and boiling points, and are mostly insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents. Their reactions are usually slow and molecular rather than ionic, and most of them are combustible.

Catenation

Catenation is the property of an element, especially carbon, to form long chains and rings by joining with atoms of the same element through covalent bonds. Carbon shows catenation to the maximum extent because the C-C bond is strong and carbon is small and tetravalent. This property is a main reason for the existence of millions of organic compounds.

Isomerism

Isomerism is the phenomenon in which two or more compounds have the same molecular formula but different structures and therefore different properties; such compounds are called isomers. For example, n-butane and isobutane both have the formula C4H10 but different arrangements of carbon atoms: CH3-CH2-CH2-CH3 and CH3-CH(CH3)-CH3 are a pair of structural isomers. Isomerism may be structural, based on different connectivity, or stereo, based on different spatial arrangement. Pairs with different molecular formulas, such as C2H5-OH and C3H7-OH, are homologues, not isomers.

lessons.title: Uses of Organic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Importance in Everyday Life

Organic compounds are essential in daily life: fuels such as petrol, LPG and natural gas, medicines such as aspirin and antibiotics, plastics, synthetic fibres like nylon, soaps, detergents, dyes, perfumes and food items are all organic. Common uses include fuels (petrol, diesel, natural gas, coal), medicines (aspirin, paracetamol, antibiotics), polymers (polythene, PVC, nylon, polyester) for plastics and fibres, and solvents, paints, dyes, perfumes, soaps, detergents, pesticides and fertilisers such as urea. Almost every industry from agriculture to medicine depends on organic compounds.

Reforming of Petrol

Reforming is the process in which straight-chain alkanes of low-grade petrol are converted into branched-chain alkanes and aromatic hydrocarbons by heating with a catalyst such as platinum. It is useful because branched and aromatic hydrocarbons have a high octane number and burn smoothly without knocking, the damaging metallic sound produced by uneven combustion in the engine. Reforming therefore improves the quality of petrol for modern high-compression engines.

Products of Biotechnology

Biotechnology produces useful materials using living organisms or enzymes. Examples include insulin for diabetic patients, antibiotics such as penicillin, vaccines, interferons and growth hormones. It is also used to produce ethanol fuel, enzymes for detergents, and improved seeds and crops in agriculture.

lessons.title: New Allotrope of Carbon: Bucky Ball
lessons.notes_html:
Buckminsterfullerene, C60

Bucky ball is the common name of buckminsterfullerene, C60, an allotrope of carbon discovered in 1985. Its 60 carbon atoms form a hollow cage shaped like a football, made of exactly 12 pentagonal (five-membered) rings and 20 hexagonal (six-membered) rings, with each carbon sp2 hybridised and part of a delocalised pi system.

Properties and Uses

It is a black solid, insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents such as benzene, and it can accept electrons to form salts. Fullerenes are used in research on superconductors, lubricants, drug delivery and new materials.

lessons.title: Functional Groups and Homologous Series
lessons.notes_html:
Functional Groups

A functional group is an atom or a group of atoms in a molecule which is responsible for the characteristic chemical properties of that compound. The amide group -CONH2 is the functional group that contains a nitrogen atom bonded to a carbonyl carbon; alcohol (-OH), ketone (C=O) and ester (-COO-) groups contain only carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. Three oxygen-containing functional groups are: hydroxyl group -OH (alcohol, R-OH); carbonyl group C=O, in aldehydes as -CHO (R-CHO) and in ketones as R-CO-R; and carboxyl group -COOH (carboxylic acid, R-COOH). The ester group -COO- (R-COO-R) is another common oxygen-containing group.

Homologous Series

A homologous series is a family of organic compounds having the same functional group and similar chemical properties, in which successive members differ by a -CH2- group, for example the alkanes CH4, C2H6, C3H8 and so on. Its main properties are: all members can be represented by one general formula, such as CnH2n+2 for alkanes and CnH2n+1OH (or R-OH) for alcohols, examples being CH3OH (methanol) and C2H5OH (ethanol); all members show similar chemical properties because they have the same functional group; physical properties such as boiling point change gradually with increasing molecular mass; and all members can be prepared by similar general methods. C2H4 (ethene) belongs to the alkene family because it fits the alkene general formula CnH2n and has a carbon-carbon double bond, while CH4, C2H6 and C3H8 are alkanes of formula CnH2n+2.

lessons.title: Introduction of Hydrocarbons and their Derivatives
lessons.notes_html:
Organic compounds exhibit great diversity, with millions of known compounds and an infinite number of possible isomers. They can possess distinct functional groups, different types of substituents, and variable lengths, branches and cyclic structures of carbon chains, leading to a wide range of structural possibilities. It was a big challenge for organic chemists to establish a systematic and simplified method for naming this vast number of compounds in a consistent and uniform manner.

Hydrocarbons and their Derivatives

Organic compounds are mainly made up of carbon and hydrogen; certain other elements such as oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur and halogens may also be present in their structures. A wide range of organic compounds are derivatives of hydrocarbons, formed by substituting one or more hydrogen atoms with a hetero atom or group of atoms. These derivatives are distinguished by their unique structures and properties and are categorised into families or groups of organic compounds. Each family is characterised by a specific functional group, which imparts distinct chemical and physical properties to the compounds within that family. Functional groups are specific groups of atoms that are responsible for the characteristic chemical reactions and properties of organic compounds.

Five Organic Families

  • Alcohols: functional group -OH (hydroxyl); suffix -ol; for example ethanol.
  • Aldehydes: functional group -CHO; suffix -al; for example ethanal.
  • Ketones: functional group C=O (carbonyl) within the chain; suffix -one; for example propanone.
  • Carboxylic acids: functional group -COOH; suffix -oic acid; for example ethanoic acid.
  • Amines: functional group -NH2; suffix -amine; for example methylamine.

Root Words for the Carbon Chain

The prefix (root word) shows the number of carbon atoms in the chain: 1 Meth-, 2 Eth-, 3 Prop-, 4 But-, 5 Pent-, 6 Hex-, 7 Hept-, 8 Oct-, 9 Non-, 10 Dec-, 11 Undec-, 12 Dodec-. With the primary suffixes these give methane, ethane, propane and so on for alkanes; ethene, propene, butene for alkenes; and ethyne, propyne, butyne for alkynes.

lessons.title: History of Nomenclature
lessons.notes_html:
Common (Trivial) Names

Initially the names of organic compounds were assigned on the basis of their origin or the person who discovered them. These specific designations are referred to as common names or trivial names. With the rapid growth of organic chemistry the number of compounds increased tremendously, and it became impossible to assign a common name to such an extensive range of compounds; scientists felt the need for a structural or systematic name that would accurately reflect the molecular structure of the compound. The common system gives names based on source or history, so one compound may have several names and the name tells nothing about its structure.

Geneva Conference and IUPAC

An attempt was made at the Geneva conference (1892) to create a unique nomenclature in which only one official name would be assigned to each compound. In 1958 a new commission on nomenclature was appointed by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC) for further work on the nomenclature, and the system has set rules for naming organic molecules on the basis of their structures. The latest updates to the IUPAC rules were recommended in 2013.

Iso and Neo Prefixes of the Common System

In the common system, the prefix iso- is used when one methyl group is attached to the second carbon of the chain, that is, the chain ends in a -CH(CH3)2 group; for example, (CH3)2CH-CH3 is isobutane and (CH3)2CH-CH2-OH is isobutyl alcohol. The prefix neo- is used when two methyl groups are attached to the second carbon, that is, the chain contains a -C(CH3)3 end group; for example, (CH3)4C is neopentane. These prefixes describe branching without using numbers.

lessons.title: IUPAC System
lessons.notes_html:
The systematic or scientific system for the naming of organic compounds is the IUPAC method. This system provides distinct names for over fifteen million reported organic compounds and can be devised for the millions of compounds yet to be synthesised. The IUPAC method considers the arrangement of carbon atoms, the types and positions of functional groups and other distinctive features of the compound to generate a standard name. An IUPAC name is built from a prefix (substituents), a root word (length of the carbon chain), a primary suffix (nature of the carbon chain: -ane, -ene, -yne) and a secondary suffix (functional group).

General Rules

  • Identify the longest unbroken (continuous) carbon chain within the molecule which will act as the parent chain, selecting the chain that contains the functional group.
  • Allocate numerical designations (locants) to the carbon atoms of the parent chain, numbering from the terminal side to which the functional group is nearer, so that the functional group and then the substituents get the lowest possible locants.
  • Identify substituents and name them using prefixes such as methyl, ethyl, methoxy, chloro, bromo, etc., mentioning their position in the longest carbon chain. Substituent prefixes are written in alphabetical order, using di-, tri- for repeats.
  • If any functional group is present in the molecule, name it by using the appropriate suffix, such as -one for ketone, -al for aldehyde and -ol for alcohol, etc.
  • If more than one functional group is present, write the name on the priority basis set by the priority rules: (-COOH) > (-CHO) > (C=O) > (-OH) > (-NH2) > (-O-) > (=) > (triple bond). The highest-priority group becomes the suffix and the others are named as prefixes.

Locants are separated by commas and are joined to the name by hyphens. For example, CH3-CH(CH3)-CH2-OH is 2-methylpropan-1-ol. The IUPAC system is preferred over the common system because it is systematic and universal: each compound gets one unique name from its structure, and from the name the correct structure can be drawn anywhere in the world.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Alkane
lessons.notes_html:
Common System

In the common system of naming alkanes, all the carbon atoms present in the structure are included in the name, regardless of whether they are attached to each other in a straight chain or in a branched form; the prefixes iso- and neo- are used for branched chains (see History of Nomenclature). In the IUPAC system the longest continuous chain is selected as the parent and branches are named as alkyl prefixes with locants.

Cycloalkanes

An open-chain saturated hydrocarbon must fit the formula CnH2n+2, as butane is C4H10. A saturated hydrocarbon with the formula C4H8 can only be saturated if it is cyclic, because forming the ring removes two hydrogen atoms; C4H8 as a saturated compound is therefore cyclobutane. Ring compounds are named by adding the prefix cyclo- to the name of the corresponding open-chain alkane.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Alkene
lessons.notes_html:
Alkenes are named by replacing the suffix -ane of the parent alkane with -ene, and the position of the double bond is shown by the locant of its first carbon. The structure of 1,3-pentadiene is CH2=CH-CH=CH-CH3: the two double bonds start at carbons 1 and 3 of the five-carbon chain. (CH2=CH-CH2-CH=CH2 would be 1,4-pentadiene.)

Chains with Both Double and Triple Bonds

If an organic compound contains both a double and a triple bond in the main carbon chain, the chain is numbered so that the multiple bonds together get the lowest possible locants; if there is still a choice, the double bond is given the lower locant. In the suffix, -ene is written before -yne, and the final -e of -ene is dropped, giving endings like -en-yne with both locants stated. For example, HC triple bond C-CH=CH2 is but-3-en-1-yne, and CH3-CH=CH-C triple bond CH is pent-3-en-1-yne: in the latter, the chain of five carbons is numbered from the end nearer the triple bond, giving the triple bond position 1 and the double bond position 3.

Worked Example

HC triple bond C-CH(CH3)-CH=CH2: the longest chain has five carbons and contains both a triple bond and a double bond, with a methyl branch on carbon 3. Numbering from the triple-bond end gives the triple bond position 1 and the double bond position 4. Its IUPAC name is 3-methylpent-4-en-1-yne.

lessons.notes_html: Alkynes are named by replacing the suffix -ane of the parent alkane with -yne, with a locant for the triple bond where needed. A hydrocarbon with the molecular formula C7H12 fits the alkyne general formula CnH2n-2 (for n = 7, 2n - 2 = 12), so it is heptyne with one triple bond; heptane is C7H16 and heptene is C7H14, so they do not fit this formula. When a chain contains both a double and a triple bond, the name ends in -en-yne and the numbering rules of the alkene lesson apply, for example pent-3-en-1-yne and 3-methylpent-4-en-1-yne.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Alkyl Halide
lessons.notes_html:
Alkyl halides are the derivatives of alkanes in which one or more hydrogen atoms are replaced by a halogen atom.

Common System

The common name of an alkyl halide is formed by naming the alkyl group first, followed by the term "halide": CH3-Cl is methyl chloride, CH3-CH2-Br is ethyl bromide and CH3-CH2-CH2-I is propyl iodide. The terms secondary (sec.) and tertiary (tert.) are used as prefixes if the carbon atom bonded to halogen is further attached to two and three other carbon atoms respectively, for example sec-propyl chloride, CH3-CH(Cl)-CH3, and tert-butyl bromide, (CH3)3C-Br. The terms iso and neo are also used as prefixes when the penultimate carbon is further attached to two or three other carbon atoms respectively, for example isobutyl bromide and neopentyl iodide.

IUPAC System

In the IUPAC system alkyl halides are named as haloalkanes, where halo is chloro, bromo, iodo, etc. The rules are: (i) determine the longest carbon chain that contains the carbon atom directly bonded to halogen; (ii) number the carbon atoms in the chain from the end closest to the halogen atom; (iii) when a double or triple bond is present in the halogenated chain, number from the end nearest to the double or triple bond; (iv) prefixes di-, tri-, tetra, etc. indicate the number of halogen atoms attached to the main chain; (v) when two different halogens are attached at the same position from opposite ends, the halogen names are written in alphabetical order. Examples: CH3-CH2-Br is bromoethane; CH3-CH(Cl)-CH3 is 2-chloropropane; (CH3)3C-Br is 2-bromo-2-methylpropane; and a five-carbon chain with Br at position 2 and Cl at position 4 is 2-bromo-4-chloropentane. Dichlorodifluoromethane (CCl2F2) has been used as a refrigerant gas; it is now being replaced by more environmentally friendly alternatives.

mcqs.why: Alkyl halides are alkanes in which one or more hydrogen atoms are replaced by a halogen atom.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Amines
lessons.notes_html:
Amines are organic compounds that contain a nitrogen atom bonded to one or more alkyl or aryl groups. A primary amine contains one alkyl group bonded to the nitrogen atom, while secondary and tertiary amines are identified by the direct attachment of two and three alkyl groups to the nitrogen atom respectively. In the IUPAC system the suffix for the amine family is -amine, added to the name of the parent chain, for example methylamine and ethylamine from the -NH2 functional group.

Worked Example: 3-Chlorobenzamide

Benzamide is a benzene ring attached to a -CONH2 group, which is taken as position 1; in 3-chlorobenzamide chlorine is placed at position 3 (meta). Its structure is written as Cl-C6H4-CONH2 with Cl meta to the amide group. Amides are the nitrogen derivatives of carboxylic acids.

options: One or more alkyl or aryl groups
mcqs.why: Amines contain a nitrogen atom bonded to one or more alkyl or aryl groups, as defined in the lesson.

mcqs.why: A primary amine contains one alkyl group bonded to the nitrogen atom; secondary has two and tertiary has three.

mcqs.why: Tertiary amines are identified by direct attachment of three alkyl groups to the nitrogen atom.

mcqs.why: The suffix for the amine family is -amine, added to the name of the parent chain, for example methylamine and ethylamine.

mcqs.why: Methylamine and ethylamine come from the -NH2 functional group, the amine functional group.

mcqs.why: Benzamide is a benzene ring attached to a -CONH2 group, which is taken as position 1 in 3-chlorobenzamide.

mcqs.why: Secondary amines are identified by direct attachment of two alkyl groups to the nitrogen atom.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Alcohol
lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols are named by replacing the final -e of the parent alkane with the suffix -ol, with a locant for the -OH group where needed. The IUPAC name of isopropyl alcohol is 2-propanol (propan-2-ol): isopropyl alcohol is (CH3)2CH-OH, in which the -OH group is attached to the middle carbon of a three-carbon chain, so numbering gives the -OH group position 2.

Worked Example: Glycerol

CH2(OH)-CH(OH)-CH2(OH) has a three-carbon chain with one hydroxyl group on every carbon. Its IUPAC name is propane-1,2,3-triol. Its common name is glycerol (glycerine), obtained from fats and used in medicines, cosmetics and food.

mcqs.q: What suffix is used to name an alcohol in the IUPAC system?
mcqs.why: The suffix -ol is correct because alcohols are named by replacing the final -e of the parent alkane with -ol for the -OH group.

mcqs.q: What is the IUPAC name of isopropyl alcohol?
mcqs.why: Propan-2-ol is correct because isopropyl alcohol is (CH3)2CH-OH, with the -OH group on the middle carbon, carbon 2, of a three-carbon chain.

mcqs.q: What is the structure of isopropyl alcohol?
mcqs.why: (CH3)2CH-OH is correct because the -OH group is attached to the central carbon of the three-carbon isopropyl group.

mcqs.why: Propane-1,2,3-triol is correct because the three-carbon chain carries one hydroxyl group on each of carbons 1, 2 and 3.

mcqs.q: How many hydroxyl groups are present in one molecule of glycerol?
mcqs.why: Three is correct because glycerol has the structure CH2(OH)-CH(OH)-CH2(OH), with an -OH group on every carbon.

mcqs.q: From which natural source is glycerol obtained, according to the lesson?
mcqs.why: Fats is correct because the lesson states that glycerol, also called glycerine, is obtained from fats.

mcqs.why: Carbon 2 is correct because propan-2-ol has the -OH group on the middle carbon of the three-carbon propane chain.

mcqs.why: In medicines, cosmetics and food is correct because the lesson lists these as the uses of glycerol obtained from fats.

mcqs.why: The final -e is replaced by -ol is correct because this is the stated IUPAC rule for naming alcohols, with a locant for the -OH group where needed.

options: Three carbon atoms in a ring
mcqs.why: Three hydroxyl groups is correct because triol means three -ol groups, at positions 1, 2 and 3 in glycerol.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Phenol
lessons.notes_html:
Phenol is the parent name for a benzene ring carrying an -OH group, and the ring is numbered from the carbon bearing the -OH group. Resorcinol is a phenol containing two -OH groups at positions 1 and 3: it is benzene-1,3-diol, with the two -OH groups in meta positions to each other. The 1,2-diol is catechol and the 1,4-diol is hydroquinone (quinol). 1,2,3-Benzenetriol is a ring carrying three -OH groups on three consecutive carbons; its common name is pyrogallol, used in photography and hair dyes.

Worked Examples

4-Ethylphenol: a benzene ring with -OH at the top and -C2H5 at the bottom (para positions). The -OH group makes the parent compound phenol, and the ethyl group is opposite to it, at position 4, so the name is 4-ethylphenol.

Picric acid: picric acid is 2,4,6-trinitrophenol: a phenol ring carrying three -NO2 groups at positions 2, 4 and 6 around the -OH group, C6H2(NO2)3-OH. The three electron-withdrawing nitro groups make it a strong acid for a phenol, and it is also an explosive and a yellow dye.

mcqs.q: How is the benzene ring numbered in phenols?
options: From the carbon bearing the -OH group
From the carbon bearing the largest substituent
mcqs.why: From the carbon bearing the -OH group is correct because phenol is the parent name and numbering starts at the carbon carrying the -OH group.

mcqs.q: Resorcinol is correctly named as:
mcqs.why: Benzene-1,3-diol is correct because resorcinol is a phenol containing two -OH groups at positions 1 and 3.

mcqs.q: Catechol is which dihydroxybenzene?
mcqs.why: Benzene-1,2-diol is correct because the lesson states that the 1,2-diol is catechol, while the 1,3-diol is resorcinol.

mcqs.q: Hydroquinone, also called quinol, has its two -OH groups at positions:
mcqs.why: 1 and 4 is correct because the lesson states that the 1,4-diol is hydroquinone (quinol), with the -OH groups para to each other.

mcqs.why: Meta to each other is correct because positions 1 and 3 on the benzene ring are meta positions.

mcqs.q: What is the common name of 1,2,3-benzenetriol?
mcqs.why: Pyrogallol is correct because 1,2,3-benzenetriol, with three -OH groups on three consecutive carbons, has the common name pyrogallol.

mcqs.q: Pyrogallol is used in:
mcqs.why: Photography and hair dyes is correct because the lesson gives these as the uses of pyrogallol, the common name of 1,2,3-benzenetriol.

mcqs.q: In 4-ethylphenol, where is the ethyl group relative to the -OH group?
mcqs.why: At position 4, para, is correct because the -OH group defines position 1 as phenol and the ethyl group is opposite to it at position 4.

mcqs.q: Picric acid is correctly identified as:
mcqs.why: 2,4,6-trinitrophenol is correct because picric acid is a phenol ring carrying three -NO2 groups at positions 2, 4 and 6 around the -OH group.

mcqs.q: Why is picric acid a strong acid for a phenol?
