mcqs.why: Its three electron-withdrawing nitro groups is correct because the lesson states that these nitro groups make picric acid a strong acid for a phenol, as well as an explosive and a yellow dye.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Ether
lessons.notes_html:
Ethers contain an oxygen atom joining two alkyl or aryl groups, R-O-R. They are named either as alkoxyalkanes in the substitutive system or by naming the two groups followed by the word ether in the common functional-class system.

Worked Examples

CH3-CH2-O-C(CH3)2-C2H5: oxygen joins an ethyl group and a C(CH3)2(C2H5) group. Treating it as a substituted butane, the longest chain is four carbons with an ethoxy group and a methyl group on carbon 2. Its IUPAC name is 2-ethoxy-2-methylbutane, also named ethyl (2-methylbutan-2-yl) ether in the functional-class system.

Ethyl neopentyl ether: neopentyl is the group (CH3)3C-CH2- and ethyl is CH3CH2-, joined through an oxygen atom: CH3CH2-O-CH2-C(CH3)3. It is an unsymmetrical ether because the two alkyl groups on oxygen are different.

mcqs.q: What is the general form of an ether?
mcqs.why: R-O-R is correct because an ether contains an oxygen atom joining two alkyl or aryl groups, written as R-O-R.

mcqs.q: What is the IUPAC substitutive name of CH3-CH2-O-C(CH3)2-C2H5?
mcqs.why: 2-ethoxy-2-methylbutane is correct because the longest chain is four carbons with an ethoxy group and a methyl group both on carbon 2.

mcqs.q: In naming CH3-CH2-O-C(CH3)2-C2H5 as a substituted butane, the longest chain has how many carbons?
mcqs.why: Four carbons is correct because treating the ether as a substituted butane gives a four-carbon parent chain carrying ethoxy and methyl groups on carbon 2.

mcqs.q: Which groups are present on carbon 2 in 2-ethoxy-2-methylbutane?
options: A chloro and a methyl group
An ethoxy group and a methyl group
A hydroxyl and an ethyl group
mcqs.why: An ethoxy group and a methyl group is correct because this is how the structure CH3-CH2-O-C(CH3)2-C2H5 is described in the worked example.

mcqs.q: What is the functional-class name of CH3-CH2-O-C(CH3)2-C2H5?
mcqs.why: Ethyl (2-methylbutan-2-yl) ether is correct because in the functional-class system the two groups on oxygen are named followed by the word ether.

mcqs.q: Ethyl neopentyl ether has which structure?
mcqs.why: CH3CH2-O-CH2-C(CH3)3 is correct because ethyl is CH3CH2- and neopentyl is (CH3)3C-CH2-, joined through an oxygen atom.

mcqs.q: The neopentyl group has which formula?
mcqs.why: (CH3)3C-CH2- is correct because the lesson defines the neopentyl group in ethyl neopentyl ether as (CH3)3C-CH2-.

mcqs.q: Why is ethyl neopentyl ether called an unsymmetrical ether?
options: The two alkyl groups on oxygen are different
mcqs.why: The two alkyl groups on oxygen are different is correct because ethyl and neopentyl are different groups, making the ether unsymmetrical.

mcqs.q: Ethers can be named in which two ways given in the lesson?
options: As alkyl alkanoates and as haloalkanes
As alkoxyalkanes and by naming the two groups followed by ether
mcqs.why: As alkoxyalkanes and by naming the two groups followed by ether is correct because these are the substitutive and functional-class systems described for ethers.

mcqs.q: In the substitutive naming of an ether, the -O-alkyl part is named as:
options: An alkoxy group, such as ethoxy
mcqs.why: An alkoxy group, such as ethoxy, is correct because 2-ethoxy-2-methylbutane is named as an alkoxyalkane with an ethoxy substituent.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Aldehyde and Ketone
lessons.notes_html:
Aldehydes are named with the suffix -al, the aldehyde carbon always being position 1. For ketones the final -e of the main carbon chain is replaced by the suffix -one, as in propanone and butan-2-one. (The suffix -ol is used for alcohols and -al for aldehydes.)

Worked Examples: Naming Structures

  • (CH3)2CH-C(=O)-CH(Cl)-CH3: the longest chain containing the carbonyl group has five carbons, with C=O at carbon 3, a methyl group at carbon 2 and a chlorine at carbon 4: 4-chloro-2-methylpentan-3-one. Substituent prefixes are written in alphabetical order (chloro before methyl) with their locants.
  • (CH3)2CBr-CHO: the -CHO group is carbon 1 of a three-carbon chain, and carbon 2 carries both a bromine atom and a methyl group: 2-bromo-2-methylpropanal.
  • CH3-C(=O)-CH=CH-CH3: five carbons with the ketone group at carbon 2 and a double bond between carbons 3 and 4; numbering gives the carbonyl group the lower locant: pent-3-en-2-one.
  • Benzene ring with -COCH3 and -Cl in meta positions: the -COCH3 (acetyl) group is taken as position 1 and the chlorine is at position 3 (meta). The name is 1-(3-chlorophenyl)ethan-1-one, commonly called 3-chloroacetophenone; acetophenone itself is named systematically as 1-phenylethan-1-one.
  • 1-Bromo-3-methylhexan-2-one: a six-carbon chain with a ketone group at carbon 2, bromine at carbon 1 and a methyl branch at carbon 3: BrCH2-C(=O)-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH2-CH3.

Worked Examples: Structures from Names

  • Butyraldehyde: the common name of the four-carbon aldehyde with a straight chain ending in -CHO: CH3-CH2-CH2-CHO. Its IUPAC name is butanal.
  • Ethyl isopropyl ketone: in the common ketone naming system the two groups on the carbonyl carbon are ethyl (CH3CH2-) and isopropyl ((CH3)2CH-): CH3-CH2-C(=O)-CH(CH3)2. Its IUPAC name is 2-methylpentan-3-one.
  • alpha-Methyl butyraldehyde: butyraldehyde is CH3-CH2-CH2-CHO; the alpha carbon is the one next to the -CHO group and it carries a methyl group: CH3-CH2-CH(CH3)-CHO, IUPAC name 2-methylbutanal.

mcqs.q: In an aldehyde name, the -CHO carbon is always given which position?
mcqs.why: Position 1 is correct because aldehydes take the suffix -al and the aldehyde carbon is always position 1 in the chain.

mcqs.q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH3)2CH-C(=O)-CH(Cl)-CH3?
mcqs.why: 4-chloro-2-methylpentan-3-one is correct because the five-carbon chain has C=O at carbon 3, a methyl group at carbon 2 and chlorine at carbon 4.

mcqs.q: In the name 4-chloro-2-methylpentan-3-one, why is chloro written before methyl?
options: Substituent prefixes are written in alphabetical order
Chloro always has the higher locant
Methyl is written last in all names
mcqs.why: Substituent prefixes are written in alphabetical order is correct because the lesson states chloro comes before methyl alphabetically, each with its locant.

mcqs.q: What is the IUPAC name of (CH3)2CBr-CHO?
mcqs.why: 2-bromo-2-methylpropanal is correct because the -CHO group is carbon 1 of a three-carbon chain and carbon 2 carries both bromine and a methyl group.

mcqs.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH3-C(=O)-CH=CH-CH3?
mcqs.why: Pent-3-en-2-one is correct because the five-carbon chain has the ketone group at carbon 2 and a double bond between carbons 3 and 4, with the carbonyl given the lower locant.

mcqs.q: A benzene ring with -COCH3 and -Cl in meta positions is commonly called:
mcqs.why: 3-chloroacetophenone is correct because the acetyl group is taken as position 1 and chlorine at position 3 is meta to it.

mcqs.q: Acetophenone itself is named systematically as:
mcqs.why: 1-phenylethan-1-one is correct because the lesson gives this as the systematic name of acetophenone, whose acetyl group is -COCH3.

mcqs.q: 1-Bromo-3-methylhexan-2-one contains a ketone group at which position?
mcqs.why: Position 2 is correct because the six-carbon chain in BrCH2-C(=O)-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH2-CH3 has its carbonyl group at carbon 2.

mcqs.q: Butyraldehyde, CH3-CH2-CH2-CHO, has which IUPAC name?
mcqs.why: Butanal is correct because butyraldehyde is the common name of the straight-chain four-carbon aldehyde ending in -CHO.

mcqs.q: Ethyl isopropyl ketone, CH3-CH2-C(=O)-CH(CH3)2, has which IUPAC name?
mcqs.why: 2-methylpentan-3-one is correct because the carbonyl carbon joins ethyl and isopropyl groups, giving a five-carbon chain with a methyl branch at carbon 2 and C=O at carbon 3.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Carboxylic Acid
lessons.notes_html:
Carboxylic acids are named by replacing the final -e of the parent alkane with -oic acid, the -COOH carbon being carbon 1. In the common system the straight-chain six-carbon acid CH3-(CH2)4-COOH is called caproic acid (IUPAC name hexanoic acid).

Common Names of the First Five Acids

  • HCOOH: formic acid (1 carbon) - IUPAC methanoic acid
  • CH3COOH: acetic acid (2 carbons) - IUPAC ethanoic acid
  • CH3CH2COOH: propionic acid (3 carbons) - IUPAC propanoic acid
  • CH3CH2CH2COOH: butyric acid (4 carbons) - IUPAC butanoic acid
  • CH3(CH2)3COOH: valeric acid (5 carbons) - IUPAC pentanoic acid

The common names come from natural sources: formic acid from ants, acetic acid from vinegar, and caproic acid is the six-carbon acid (propionic has three carbons, valeric five and stearic eighteen).

Worked Examples

  • CH2=C(CH3)-COOH: the parent chain has three carbons including the -COOH carbon, which is carbon 1, with a double bond between carbons 2 and 3 and a methyl group on carbon 2: 2-methylprop-2-enoic acid. Its common name is methacrylic acid, an important monomer for plastics.
  • alpha,beta-Dimethyl butyric acid: butyric acid is a four-carbon acid; the carbon next to -COOH is alpha and the next is beta, and each carries one methyl group: CH3-CH(CH3)-CH(CH3)-COOH, in IUPAC terms 2,3-dimethylbutanoic acid.
  • alpha-Chloro-beta-methyl valeric acid: valeric acid is a five-carbon acid; chlorine is on the alpha carbon (position 2) and a methyl group on the beta carbon (position 3): CH3-CH2-CH(CH3)-CH(Cl)-COOH, in IUPAC terms 2-chloro-3-methylpentanoic acid.

mcqs.q: Carboxylic acids are named by replacing the final -e of the parent alkane with:
mcqs.why: -oic acid is correct because this is the stated rule for carboxylic acids, with the -COOH carbon counted as carbon 1.

mcqs.q: In a carboxylic acid, the -COOH carbon is counted as:
options: It is not counted in the chain
mcqs.why: Carbon 1 is correct because the parent chain includes the -COOH carbon and numbering starts from it.

mcqs.q: HCOOH, the one-carbon acid, has the common name:
mcqs.why: Formic acid is correct because HCOOH is the first acid, with IUPAC name methanoic acid, and its common name comes from ants.

mcqs.q: CH3COOH has which common name and carbon count?
mcqs.why: Acetic acid, 2 carbons, is correct because CH3COOH is ethanoic acid in IUPAC naming and acetic acid from vinegar in the common system.

mcqs.q: The common name of the straight-chain six-carbon acid CH3-(CH2)4-COOH is:
mcqs.why: Caproic acid is correct because the six-carbon straight-chain acid is caproic acid, with IUPAC name hexanoic acid; valeric has five carbons and propionic three.

mcqs.q: Valeric acid contains how many carbon atoms?
mcqs.why: Five is correct because valeric acid is CH3(CH2)3COOH, the five-carbon acid with IUPAC name pentanoic acid.

mcqs.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH2=C(CH3)-COOH?
mcqs.why: 2-methylprop-2-enoic acid is correct because the three-carbon chain has the -COOH carbon as carbon 1, a double bond between carbons 2 and 3 and a methyl group on carbon 2.

mcqs.q: Methacrylic acid, 2-methylprop-2-enoic acid, is important as:
mcqs.why: A monomer for plastics is correct because the lesson states that methacrylic acid is an important monomer for plastics.

mcqs.q: Alpha,beta-dimethyl butyric acid is, in IUPAC terms:
mcqs.why: 2,3-dimethylbutanoic acid is correct because alpha is position 2 and beta is position 3, and each carries one methyl group in CH3-CH(CH3)-CH(CH3)-COOH.

mcqs.q: Alpha-chloro-beta-methyl valeric acid is, in IUPAC terms:
mcqs.why: 2-chloro-3-methylpentanoic acid is correct because chlorine is on the alpha carbon, position 2, and the methyl group is on the beta carbon, position 3, of the five-carbon valeric acid chain.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Ester
lessons.notes_html:
An ester is named as alkyl alkanoate: the alkyl part from the alcohol is written first, followed by the name of the acid part with -oate ending. CH3COOCH(CH3)2 is therefore isopropyl ethanoate: the acid part CH3COO- comes from ethanoic acid and the alcohol part -CH(CH3)2 is the isopropyl group. Isopropyl acetate is only its common name, since acetate is the common name of ethanoate.

Worked Examples

  • CH3-C(=O)-O-CH(CH3)2: an ester formed from ethanoic acid and propan-2-ol, because the -O-CH(CH3)2 part is the isopropyl (propan-2-yl) group: isopropyl ethanoate (propan-2-yl ethanoate).
  • Isopropyl butanoate: formed from butanoic acid and propan-2-ol, so the acid part is CH3-CH2-CH2-COO- and the alcohol part is -CH(CH3)2: CH3-CH2-CH2-C(=O)-O-CH(CH3)2. Like other low-molecular esters it has a fruity smell.

mcqs.q: An ester is named in the IUPAC system as:
mcqs.why: Alkyl alkanoate is correct because the alkyl part from the alcohol is written first, followed by the acid part with the -oate ending.

mcqs.q: In an ester name, which part is written first?
options: The alkyl part from the alcohol
mcqs.why: The alkyl part from the alcohol is correct because an ester is named alkyl alkanoate, with the alcohol-derived alkyl group first.

mcqs.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH3COOCH(CH3)2?
mcqs.why: Isopropyl ethanoate is correct because the acid part CH3COO- comes from ethanoic acid and the alcohol part -CH(CH3)2 is the isopropyl group.

mcqs.q: Why is isopropyl acetate not the IUPAC name of CH3COOCH(CH3)2?
options: Acetate is only the common name of ethanoate
mcqs.why: Acetate is only the common name of ethanoate is correct because the systematic acid part must be named ethanoate, making the IUPAC name isopropyl ethanoate.

mcqs.q: The ester CH3-C(=O)-O-CH(CH3)2 is formed from which acid and alcohol?
mcqs.why: Ethanoic acid and propan-2-ol is correct because the -O-CH(CH3)2 part is the isopropyl, or propan-2-yl, group from propan-2-ol and the acid part is ethanoate.

mcqs.q: Isopropyl butanoate is formed from:
mcqs.why: Butanoic acid and propan-2-ol is correct because its acid part is CH3-CH2-CH2-COO- and its alcohol part is -CH(CH3)2.

mcqs.q: What is the structure of isopropyl butanoate?
mcqs.why: CH3-CH2-CH2-C(=O)-O-CH(CH3)2 is correct because it combines the butanoate acid part with the isopropyl alcohol part.

mcqs.q: Low-molecular-mass esters such as isopropyl butanoate are noted for having:
mcqs.why: A fruity smell is correct because the lesson states that, like other low-molecular esters, isopropyl butanoate has a fruity smell.

mcqs.q: In the ester name propan-2-yl ethanoate, the group propan-2-yl comes from:
mcqs.why: The alcohol, propan-2-ol, is correct because the alkyl part of an ester name, here propan-2-yl, is derived from the alcohol.

mcqs.q: The acid part of an ester name ends in:
mcqs.why: -oate is correct because the acid part of an alkyl alkanoate name carries the -oate ending, as in ethanoate and butanoate.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Amide
lessons.notes_html: Amides are the nitrogen derivatives of carboxylic acids, in which the -OH of the -COOH group is replaced by -NH2; they are named from the parent acid by changing -oic acid to -amide. The worked example of this family is 3-chlorobenzamide: benzamide is a benzene ring attached to a -CONH2 group, taken as position 1, with chlorine at position 3 (meta) - Cl-C6H4-CONH2 with Cl meta to the amide group.

mcqs.q: Amides are described in the lesson as:
mcqs.why: Nitrogen derivatives of carboxylic acids is correct because amides are formed from carboxylic acids by replacing the -OH of -COOH with -NH2.

mcqs.q: In forming an amide from a carboxylic acid, the -OH of the -COOH group is replaced by:
mcqs.why: -NH2 is correct because this replacement gives the -CONH2 amide group from the -COOH group of the parent acid.

mcqs.q: Amides are named from the parent acid by changing -oic acid to:
mcqs.why: -amide is correct because the stated rule changes the -oic acid ending of the parent acid to -amide.

mcqs.q: Benzamide consists of a benzene ring attached to which group?
mcqs.why: -CONH2 is correct because benzamide is a benzene ring attached to a -CONH2 group, which is taken as position 1.

mcqs.q: In 3-chlorobenzamide, the chlorine atom is at which position?
mcqs.why: Position 3 is correct because in 3-chlorobenzamide chlorine is placed at position 3 relative to the -CONH2 group taken as position 1.

mcqs.q: Position 3 in 3-chlorobenzamide is described as which position relative to the amide group?
mcqs.why: Meta is correct because position 3 on the ring relative to the group at position 1 is the meta position, as stated for 3-chlorobenzamide.

mcqs.q: In benzamide, which group is taken as position 1 for numbering?
mcqs.why: The -CONH2 group is correct because benzamide is numbered from the carbon bearing the amide group, taken as position 1.

mcqs.q: The structure of 3-chlorobenzamide is written as:
options: Cl-C6H4-CONH2 with Cl meta to the amide group
mcqs.why: Cl-C6H4-CONH2 with Cl meta to the amide group is correct because this is the structure given for 3-chlorobenzamide in the worked example.

mcqs.q: Applying the amide naming rule, ethanoic acid would give an amide named:
mcqs.why: Ethanamide is correct because the rule changes -oic acid to -amide, so ethanoic acid gives ethanamide.

mcqs.q: The functional group characteristic of an amide such as benzamide is:
mcqs.why: -CONH2 is correct because benzamide carries the -CONH2 group, formed when the -OH of a carboxylic acid is replaced by -NH2.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Acyl Halides
lessons.notes_html:
The acyl group is R-CO-, and in R-CO-X it is attached to a halogen atom, forming an acyl halide, the typical acyl compound. (R-CO-R is a ketone, R-COO-CH3 is an ester, and in an amide the acyl group is present as part of the -CONH2 group.) Acyl halides are named from the parent acid by changing -oic acid to -oyl halide.

Worked Example: Butanoyl Iodide

Butanoyl iodide is the acyl halide of butanoic acid, with the -OH of the acid replaced by iodine: CH3-CH2-CH2-C(=O)-I. Acyl halides are highly reactive and fume in moist air.

mcqs.q: The acyl group is represented as:
mcqs.why: R-CO- is correct because the lesson defines the acyl group as R-CO-, which is attached to a halogen in an acyl halide.

mcqs.q: Which formula represents an acyl halide?
mcqs.why: R-CO-X is correct because in an acyl halide the acyl group R-CO- is attached to a halogen atom X.

mcqs.q: Acyl halides are named from the parent acid by changing -oic acid to:
mcqs.why: -oyl halide is correct because this is the stated naming change, as in butanoic acid giving butanoyl iodide.

mcqs.q: Butanoyl iodide is the acyl halide of which acid?
mcqs.why: Butanoic acid is correct because butanoyl iodide is formed from butanoic acid with the -OH replaced by iodine.

mcqs.q: What is the structure of butanoyl iodide?
mcqs.why: CH3-CH2-CH2-C(=O)-I is correct because butanoyl iodide has a four-carbon chain ending in the -C(=O)-I acyl iodide group.

mcqs.q: In forming butanoyl iodide from butanoic acid, the -OH group is replaced by:
mcqs.why: Iodine is correct because butanoyl iodide is the acyl halide of butanoic acid with the acid -OH replaced by iodine.

mcqs.q: Acyl halides are described in the lesson as:
options: Highly reactive and fuming in moist air
mcqs.why: Highly reactive and fuming in moist air is correct because the lesson gives this as the characteristic behaviour of acyl halides such as butanoyl iodide.

mcqs.q: The compound R-CO-R is classified as:
mcqs.why: A ketone is correct because the lesson distinguishes R-CO-R as a ketone, while R-CO-X is the acyl halide.

mcqs.q: The compound R-COO-CH3 is classified as:
mcqs.why: An ester is correct because the lesson identifies R-COO-CH3 as an ester, distinct from the acyl halide R-CO-X.

mcqs.q: In an amide, the acyl group is present as part of which group?
mcqs.why: -CONH2 is correct because the solved exercise notes that in an amide the acyl group is present as part of the -CONH2 group.

lessons.title: Types of Hydrocarbons
lessons.notes_html:
Aliphatic and Aromatic Hydrocarbons

  • Aliphatic hydrocarbons have open-chain or non-aromatic ring structures, while aromatic hydrocarbons contain a benzene ring with delocalised pi electrons.
  • Aliphatic unsaturated compounds mainly give addition reactions, while aromatic compounds prefer electrophilic substitution reactions that preserve the ring.
  • Aromatic hydrocarbons have a much higher carbon percentage and burn with a smoky flame, whereas most aliphatic hydrocarbons burn with a comparatively clean flame.

Reactivity: Ethane, Ethene and Ethyne Compared

Reactivity increases with the number of pi bonds, because pi electrons are loosely held, exposed and easily attacked by electrophiles, whereas the sigma bonds of ethane are strong and non-polar. Ethane has no pi bond and reacts only by slow free-radical substitution. Ethene has one pi bond and readily gives addition reactions, while ethyne has two pi bonds and an even greater density of exposed pi electrons, so it is the most reactive of the three towards addition: ethyne > ethene > ethane.

mcqs.q: Aliphatic hydrocarbons have which type of structure?
mcqs.why: Open-chain or non-aromatic ring structures is correct because this is how aliphatic hydrocarbons are distinguished from aromatic hydrocarbons containing a benzene ring.

mcqs.q: Aromatic hydrocarbons are characterised by:
options: An open chain with a triple bond
A benzene ring with delocalised pi electrons
mcqs.why: A benzene ring with delocalised pi electrons is correct because aromatic hydrocarbons contain this ring system, unlike open-chain aliphatic hydrocarbons.

mcqs.q: Aliphatic unsaturated compounds mainly give which type of reaction?
mcqs.why: Addition reactions is correct because aliphatic unsaturated compounds mainly give addition, while aromatic compounds prefer electrophilic substitution that preserves the ring.

mcqs.q: Aromatic compounds prefer electrophilic substitution because it:
options: Adds atoms across a double bond
mcqs.why: Preserves the benzene ring is correct because aromatic compounds undergo electrophilic substitution reactions that preserve the ring instead of addition.

mcqs.q: Which hydrocarbons burn with a smoky flame due to high carbon percentage?
mcqs.why: Aromatic hydrocarbons is correct because they have a much higher carbon percentage and burn with a smoky flame, whereas most aliphatic hydrocarbons burn with a comparatively clean flame.

mcqs.q: The correct order of reactivity towards addition is:
mcqs.why: Ethyne > ethene > ethane is correct because reactivity increases with the number of pi bonds, and ethyne has two, ethene one and ethane none.

mcqs.q: Why are pi electrons easily attacked by electrophiles?
options: They are tightly held inside sigma bonds
They form very strong non-polar bonds
They are loosely held and exposed
They are absent in unsaturated compounds
mcqs.why: They are loosely held and exposed is correct because the lesson explains that pi electrons are loosely held, exposed and easily attacked by electrophiles.

mcqs.q: Ethane reacts only by which slow reaction type?
mcqs.why: Free-radical substitution is correct because ethane has no pi bond and its strong non-polar sigma bonds react only by slow free-radical substitution.

mcqs.q: How many pi bonds are present in ethene?
mcqs.why: One pi bond is correct because ethene has one pi bond and readily gives addition reactions, while ethyne has two pi bonds.

mcqs.q: Ethyne is the most reactive of ethane, ethene and ethyne towards addition because it has:
options: The greatest density of exposed pi electrons
mcqs.why: The greatest density of exposed pi electrons is correct because ethyne has two pi bonds, giving an even greater density of exposed pi electrons than ethene.

lessons.title: Alkanes and Cycloalkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Why Alkanes are Called Paraffins

The word paraffin means little affinity, and alkanes are unreactive because all their bonds are strong, non-polar C-C and C-H sigma bonds. They have no pi bonds, lone pairs or polar sites for reagents to attack, and their bond energies are high. They therefore do not react with acids, alkalis, oxidising agents or electrophiles under ordinary conditions, and react mainly by free-radical substitution in sunlight.

Orbital Structure of Ethane

In ethane each carbon is sp3 hybridised and tetrahedral, with bond angles of about 109.5 degrees. The C-C bond is formed by head-on overlap of two sp3 orbitals (a sigma bond), and each C-H bond is formed by overlap of an sp3 orbital of carbon with the 1s orbital of hydrogen. The structure CH3-CH3 therefore contains seven sigma bonds, and free rotation is possible about the C-C bond.

Cycloalkanes

A saturated hydrocarbon with the formula C3H6 cannot be propane (C3H8) or propene (C3H6 is unsaturated) or propyne (C3H4); a saturated compound of this formula is only possible as a ring, cyclopropane, because ring formation removes two hydrogen atoms. Cycloalkanes fit the general formula CnH2n.

mcqs.q: The word paraffin, used for alkanes, means:
mcqs.why: Little affinity is correct because paraffin means little affinity, reflecting that alkanes are unreactive towards most reagents.

mcqs.q: Alkanes are unreactive mainly because their bonds are:
options: Strong, non-polar C-C and C-H sigma bonds
mcqs.why: Strong, non-polar C-C and C-H sigma bonds is correct because alkanes have no pi bonds, lone pairs or polar sites for reagents to attack.

mcqs.q: Under ordinary conditions, alkanes do NOT react with:
options: Acids, alkalis, oxidising agents or electrophiles
mcqs.why: Acids, alkalis, oxidising agents or electrophiles is correct because the lesson states alkanes do not react with these under ordinary conditions and react mainly by free-radical substitution in sunlight.

mcqs.q: In ethane, each carbon atom is hybridised as:
mcqs.why: sp3 is correct because in ethane each carbon is sp3 hybridised and tetrahedral, with bond angles of about 109.5 degrees.

mcqs.q: The bond angle in ethane is about:
mcqs.why: 109.5 degrees is correct because ethane has tetrahedral sp3 carbons with bond angles of about 109.5 degrees.

mcqs.q: The C-C bond in ethane is formed by:
options: Head-on overlap of two sp3 orbitals
Overlap of sp and s orbitals
mcqs.why: Head-on overlap of two sp3 orbitals is correct because this forms the C-C sigma bond in ethane, while each C-H bond is sp3-s overlap.

mcqs.q: How many sigma bonds are present in total in CH3-CH3?
mcqs.why: Seven is correct because ethane contains one C-C sigma bond and six C-H sigma bonds, giving seven sigma bonds in total.

mcqs.q: Cycloalkanes fit which general formula?
mcqs.why: CnH2n is correct because cycloalkanes fit the general formula CnH2n, having two fewer hydrogens than open-chain alkanes due to ring formation.

mcqs.q: A saturated hydrocarbon with formula C3H6 must be:
mcqs.why: Cyclopropane is correct because propane is C3H8 and propene is unsaturated, so a saturated C3H6 compound is only possible as the ring compound cyclopropane.

mcqs.q: Free rotation in ethane is possible about which bond?
mcqs.why: The C-C bond is correct because the lesson states that free rotation is possible about the C-C sigma bond in ethane.

lessons.title: Radical Substitution Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
Free Radical Chlorination of Methane

The reaction of methane with chlorine in sunlight occurs in three stages.

  • Initiation: sunlight splits a chlorine molecule into two free radicals: Cl2 -> 2Cl. (in the presence of hv).
  • Propagation: Cl. + CH4 -> CH3. + HCl, and then CH3. + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + Cl., so the chain continues and more chlorine can be substituted to give CH2Cl2, CHCl3 and CCl4.
  • Termination: two radicals combine and end the chain, for example Cl. + Cl. -> Cl2 and CH3. + CH3. -> C2H6.

mcqs.q: The chlorination of methane with chlorine takes place in the presence of:
mcqs.why: Sunlight is correct because free radical chlorination of methane occurs in sunlight, which splits chlorine molecules in the initiation stage.

mcqs.q: In the initiation stage, sunlight causes:
options: Cl2 to split into two chlorine free radicals
mcqs.why: Cl2 to split into two chlorine free radicals is correct because initiation is Cl2 -> 2Cl. in the presence of hv (sunlight).

mcqs.q: Which equation belongs to the propagation stage?
mcqs.why: Cl. + CH4 -> CH3. + HCl is correct because in propagation a chlorine radical attacks methane to give a methyl radical and HCl, continuing the chain.

mcqs.q: In the second propagation step, the methyl radical reacts with Cl2 to give:
options: CH3Cl and a new Cl. radical
mcqs.why: CH3Cl and a new Cl. radical is correct because CH3. + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + Cl., so the chain continues.

mcqs.q: Further substitution of methane with chlorine can eventually give:
mcqs.why: CH2Cl2, CHCl3 and CCl4 is correct because continued propagation substitutes more hydrogens of methane by chlorine in successive steps.

mcqs.q: The termination stage of the methane chlorination involves:
options: Two radicals combining to end the chain
mcqs.why: Two radicals combining to end the chain is correct because termination occurs when radicals combine, for example Cl. + Cl. -> Cl2.

mcqs.q: Which equation is an example of termination?
mcqs.why: CH3. + CH3. -> C2H6 is correct because two methyl radicals combining to form ethane ends the chain, which is termination.

mcqs.q: The correct order of the three stages of free radical chlorination is:
mcqs.why: Initiation, propagation, termination is correct because the chain starts with radical formation, continues through propagation steps and ends when radicals combine.

mcqs.q: The role of the Cl. radical regenerated in propagation is to:
options: Attack another methane molecule and continue the chain
mcqs.why: Attack another methane molecule and continue the chain is correct because the regenerated Cl. repeats the propagation step Cl. + CH4 -> CH3. + HCl.

mcqs.q: Free radical chlorination of methane is an example of which reaction type?
mcqs.why: Free-radical substitution is correct because chlorine radicals substitute hydrogens of methane step by step through initiation, propagation and termination.

lessons.title: Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
Orbital Structure of Ethylene

In ethylene (ethene) each carbon is sp2 hybridised and the molecule is planar with bond angles of about 120 degrees. The C-C sigma bond is formed by overlap of sp2 orbitals, the four C-H bonds by sp2-s overlap, and the second C-C bond is a pi bond formed by sideways overlap of the unhybridised p orbitals above and below the plane. Ethene thus has one sigma and one pi bond between the carbons, CH2=CH2, and rotation about the double bond is restricted.

Important Reactions of Alkenes

  • Dehydration of ethanol: C2H5OH -> CH2=CH2 + H2O (conc. H2SO4, 170 C). Ethanol is dehydrated by concentrated sulphuric acid, -OH being removed from one carbon and H from the adjacent carbon (elimination); the major product is ethene.
  • Dehydrohalogenation: C2H5Br + KOH (alcoholic, heat) -> CH2=CH2 + KBr + H2O. With alcoholic KOH ethyl bromide loses HBr to give ethene; aqueous KOH would instead give ethanol by substitution.
  • Addition of HBr (Markownikov rule): CH3-CH=CH2 + HBr -> CH3-CHBr-CH3. The hydrogen goes to the carbon already having more hydrogens and bromine attaches to the middle carbon; the major product is 2-bromopropane.
  • Ozonolysis: CH2=CH2 + O3 -> (ethene ozonide) -> 2HCHO (with Zn/H2O). The ozonide on decomposition with Zn and water cleaves the double bond and gives carbonyl compounds; aldehydes are formed from =CH- groups, so ethene gives formaldehyde (methanal).

Polymerisation and Epoxidation

On heating under high pressure with a peroxide catalyst, ethene molecules join together to form the polymer polythene: n(CH2=CH2) -> -(CH2-CH2)n-. This is addition polymerisation, and polythene is used for bags, bottles and insulation. In the presence of peracetic acid, ethene is oxidised (epoxidised) to ethylene oxide, a three-membered cyclic ether: CH2=CH2 + CH3COOOH -> C2H4O (ethylene oxide) + CH3COOH. Ethylene oxide is an important industrial chemical used to make ethylene glycol and detergents.

mcqs.q: In ethylene (ethene), each carbon is hybridised as:
mcqs.why: sp2 is correct because in ethene each carbon is sp2 hybridised and the molecule is planar with bond angles of about 120 degrees.

mcqs.q: The pi bond in ethene is formed by:
options: Sideways overlap of unhybridised p orbitals
mcqs.why: Sideways overlap of unhybridised p orbitals is correct because the pi bond forms above and below the plane by sideways overlap, while the sigma bond is sp2-sp2 overlap.

mcqs.q: Rotation about the C=C double bond in ethene is:
mcqs.why: Restricted is correct because the pi bond in ethene locks the carbons, so rotation about the double bond is restricted, unlike the free rotation in ethane.

mcqs.q: Dehydration of ethanol with conc. H2SO4 at 170 C gives:
mcqs.why: Ethene is correct because C2H5OH -> CH2=CH2 + H2O by elimination of -OH from one carbon and H from the adjacent carbon.

mcqs.q: Ethyl bromide with alcoholic KOH on heating gives ethene by:
mcqs.why: Dehydrohalogenation, loss of HBr, is correct because C2H5Br + KOH (alcoholic, heat) -> CH2=CH2 + KBr + H2O; aqueous KOH would instead give ethanol.

mcqs.q: Addition of HBr to propene, CH3-CH=CH2, gives as major product:
mcqs.why: 2-bromopropane is correct because by Markownikov rule the hydrogen goes to the carbon already having more hydrogens and bromine attaches to the middle carbon.

mcqs.q: Ozonolysis of ethene with O3 followed by Zn/H2O gives:
mcqs.why: Formaldehyde (methanal) is correct because the ozonide decomposes with Zn and water to give 2HCHO, since aldehydes are formed from =CH- groups.

mcqs.q: On heating under high pressure with a peroxide catalyst, ethene forms:
mcqs.why: Polythene by addition polymerisation is correct because n(CH2=CH2) -> -(CH2-CH2)n-, and polythene is used for bags, bottles and insulation.

mcqs.q: Ethene with peracetic acid gives ethylene oxide by:
mcqs.why: Epoxidation is correct because CH2=CH2 + CH3COOOH -> C2H4O (ethylene oxide) + CH3COOH, forming a three-membered cyclic ether.

mcqs.q: Ethylene oxide is an important industrial chemical used to make:
mcqs.why: Ethylene glycol and detergents is correct because the lesson states ethylene oxide is used to make ethylene glycol and detergents.

lessons.title: Alkynes
lessons.notes_html:
Orbital Structure of Acetylene

In acetylene (ethyne) each carbon is sp hybridised and the molecule is linear with a bond angle of 180 degrees. The C-C sigma bond comes from sp-sp overlap, the two C-H bonds from sp-s overlap, and two pi bonds are formed by sideways overlap of the two pairs of unhybridised p orbitals. Ethyne, HC triple bond CH, therefore contains one sigma and two pi bonds between the carbon atoms. Acetylene burns in oxygen with an extremely hot flame of about 3000 C, called the oxy-acetylene flame, which is hot enough to melt and join metals, so acetylene is the welding gas.

Addition Reactions

  • Addition of HBr: ethyne adds two molecules of HBr in two steps, and both additions follow Markownikov rule, so both bromine atoms go to the same carbon. The final product is CH3-CHBr2, 1,1-dibromoethane; bromoethene is only the intermediate of the first step.
  • Addition of chlorine: HC triple bond CH + Cl2 -> CHCl=CHCl (1,2-dichloroethene), and CHCl=CHCl + Cl2 -> CHCl2-CHCl2. The final product, 1,1,2,2-tetrachloroethane, is a heavy liquid formerly used as a solvent.

Preparations

Ethyne from ethyl chloride: ethyl chloride is treated with alcoholic KOH to give ethene (CH3CH2Cl -> CH2=CH2), brominated to 1,2-dibromoethane (CH2Br-CH2Br), and then heated with strong alcoholic KOH (or NaNH2), which removes 2HBr: CH2Br-CH2Br -> HC triple bond CH + 2HBr. In the same way, 1,2-dibromobutane with 2KOH (alc., heat) gives but-1-yne: CH3-CH2-CHBr-CH2Br -> CH3-CH2-C triple bond CH + 2KBr + 2H2O. Heating 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane with zinc powder removes bromine (debromination) and forms the triple bond: CHBr2-CHBr2 + 2Zn -> HC triple bond CH + 2ZnBr2.

Acidic Nature of Terminal Alkynes

In ethyne the carbon is sp hybridised and has 50% s-character, so it is strongly electronegative and holds the C-H electrons close, allowing the hydrogen to leave as H+ and leaving a stable acetylide ion. Two reactions show this acidity: (1) with sodium metal: 2HC triple bond CH + 2Na -> 2HC triple bond CNa (sodium acetylide) + H2; (2) with ammoniacal silver nitrate it gives a white precipitate of silver acetylide: HC triple bond CH + 2[Ag(NH3)2]OH -> AgC triple bond CAg + 4NH3 + 2H2O. This test distinguishes ethyne from ethene, which gives no such precipitate, although both gases decolourise bromine water and KMnO4 solution. Internal alkynes and alkenes do not show these reactions.

mcqs.q: What is the hybridisation and shape of each carbon in ethyne?
mcqs.why: Ethyne carbon is sp hybridised and linear, because sp-sp overlap gives a 180 degree bond angle with two pi bonds.

mcqs.q: How many sigma and pi bonds are there between the two carbons in ethyne?
options: Two sigma and one pi bond
One sigma and two pi bonds
One sigma and one pi bond
mcqs.why: Ethyne has one sigma and two pi bonds between the carbons, the pi bonds coming from sideways overlap of two pairs of p orbitals.

mcqs.q: Why is acetylene used as a welding gas?
options: It forms an explosive mixture with air at room temperature
It burns in oxygen with an oxy-acetylene flame of about 3000 C
mcqs.why: Acetylene burns in oxygen with an oxy-acetylene flame of about 3000 C, hot enough to melt and join metals, so it is the welding gas.

mcqs.q: What is the final product when ethyne adds two molecules of HBr?
mcqs.why: 1,1-dibromoethane is correct because both HBr additions follow Markownikov rule, so both bromine atoms go to the same carbon, giving CH3-CHBr2.

mcqs.q: What is the final product of addition of chlorine to ethyne?
mcqs.why: 1,1,2,2-tetrachloroethane is formed in two steps via 1,2-dichloroethene, and it is a heavy liquid formerly used as a solvent.

mcqs.q: In the preparation of ethyne from ethyl chloride, what is the intermediate after bromination of ethene?
mcqs.why: Ethene is brominated to 1,2-dibromoethane, CH2Br-CH2Br, which then loses 2HBr with strong alcoholic KOH to give ethyne.

mcqs.q: What does heating 1,2-dibromobutane with 2KOH (alcoholic, heat) give?
mcqs.why: But-1-yne is correct because double dehydrohalogenation removes 2HBr from CH3-CH2-CHBr-CH2Br to form the terminal triple bond.

mcqs.q: What happens when 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane is heated with zinc powder?
mcqs.why: Ethyne is formed because zinc removes bromine (debromination) from CHBr2-CHBr2, giving HC triple bond CH and 2ZnBr2.

mcqs.q: Why is the terminal hydrogen of ethyne acidic?
options: The carbon is sp3 with 25% s-character
Ethyne contains a polar O-H bond
The hydrogen is attached to nitrogen
The carbon is sp with 50% s-character and is strongly electronegative
mcqs.why: The sp carbon has 50% s-character, is strongly electronegative and holds C-H electrons close, so H can leave as H+ leaving a stable acetylide ion.

mcqs.q: Which reagent distinguishes ethyne from ethene?
mcqs.why: Ammoniacal silver nitrate gives a white precipitate of silver acetylide with ethyne only; ethene gives no precipitate though both decolourise bromine water.

lessons.title: Isomerism
lessons.notes_html:
Isomerism is the existence of compounds with the same molecular formula but different structures and properties.

Types of Structural Isomerism

  • Chain isomerism: due to different carbon skeletons, for example n-butane and isobutane (C4H10).
  • Position isomerism: due to different positions of a functional group or multiple bond, for example 1-butene and 2-butene.
  • Functional group isomerism: due to different functional groups, for example ethanol and dimethyl ether (both C2H6O; ethanol has the -OH alcohol group and dimethyl ether the -O- ether group).
  • Metamerism: due to different alkyl groups on either side of a polyvalent functional group, for example diethyl ether and methyl propyl ether (C4H10O).

Chiral Carbon and Optical Isomerism

A chiral carbon is a carbon atom attached to four different atoms or groups, so that its molecule has no plane of symmetry and exists as non-superimposable mirror images (optical isomers). An example is the central carbon of lactic acid, CH3-CH(OH)-COOH, which is bonded to -H, -OH, -CH3 and -COOH, four different groups. Optical isomers (enantiomers) have identical physical and chemical properties except that they rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions; lactic acid exists as (+) and (-) forms, and 2-butanol is another example pair. Such a compound shows optical activity.

Geometrical Isomerism

Geometrical (cis-trans) isomers are stereoisomers arising from restricted rotation about a double bond, in which the groups attached to the double-bonded carbons are arranged differently in space. In cis-2-butene both -CH3 groups are on the same side of the double bond, while in trans-2-butene they are on opposite sides. The two isomers have different melting points, boiling points and dipole moments.

Elements with the same atomic number

Two CH3 groups, OH and H

Rotate plane-polarised light in opposite directions

On opposite sides of the double bond
Free to rotate about the double bond

lessons.title: Benzene and its Derivatives
lessons.notes_html:
Molecular Orbital Structure of Benzene

In benzene all six carbons are sp2 hybridised and form a planar hexagonal ring with bond angles of 120 degrees; the C-C sigma framework is made from sp2-sp2 overlaps and each C-H bond from sp2-s overlap. Each carbon has one unhybridised p orbital perpendicular to the ring, and the six p orbitals overlap sideways all around the ring to form a continuous delocalised pi cloud above and below the ring plane. This delocalisation makes all C-C bonds equal in length (between single and double bond values) and gives benzene its extra stability (resonance energy about 150 kJ/mol) and substitution rather than addition reactions. Benzene, C6H6, contains about 92% carbon, and there is not enough air in an ordinary flame to burn all of it completely; the unburnt carbon particles glow and escape as soot, so benzene burns with a smoky flame.

Reactions of Benzene

  • Hydrogenation: C6H6 + 3H2 -> C6H12 (Ni catalyst, about 150-200 C, pressure). All three pi bonds of the ring are reduced to give cyclohexane.
  • Acylation (Friedel-Crafts): C6H6 + CH3COCl -> C6H5COCH3 + HCl (anhydrous AlCl3). The product is acetophenone, an aromatic ketone. Reaction with CH3Cl under similar conditions (alkylation) would give toluene.
  • Nitration: C6H6 + HNO3 -> C6H5NO2 + H2O (conc. H2SO4, 50-60 C). Nitrobenzene is a pale yellow oily liquid smelling of bitter almonds.
  • Sulphonation: C6H6 + H2SO4 -> C6H5SO3H + H2O (conc./fuming H2SO4, heat). The reaction is reversible and is an electrophilic substitution by the SO3 electrophile.

Mechanism of Electrophilic Substitution

Nitration: (1) conc. HNO3 + conc. H2SO4 generate the nitronium ion, NO2+, the attacking electrophile (HNO3 + 2H2SO4 -> NO2+ + H3O+ + 2HSO4-). (2) The pi electrons of benzene attack NO2+ to form a resonance-stabilised carbocation (arenium ion) intermediate, in which aromaticity is temporarily lost. (3) HSO4- removes the proton from the carbon bearing the NO2 group, the pi system is restored and nitrobenzene is formed.

Acylation: (1) acetyl chloride reacts with anhydrous AlCl3 to form the acylium ion electrophile, CH3CO+ (CH3COCl + AlCl3 -> CH3CO+ + AlCl4-). (2) The benzene pi cloud attacks the acylium ion to give a resonance-stabilised arenium ion. (3) AlCl4- removes the ring proton, aromaticity is restored and acetophenone is formed, with AlCl3 regenerated on aqueous work-up.

Chlorination: (1) chlorine reacts with the Lewis acid catalyst FeCl3 (or AlCl3) to generate the electrophile Cl+ (Cl2 + FeCl3 -> Cl+ + FeCl4-). (2) Benzene pi electrons attack Cl+ to form a resonance-stabilised arenium ion. (3) FeCl4- removes the proton from the same carbon, the aromatic pi system is restored, and chlorobenzene plus HCl are formed with the catalyst regenerated.

Directing Groups

Positions 2 and 6 relative to a substituent are ortho, 3 and 5 are meta, and 4 is para. Activating groups with lone pairs or electron-donating effect, such as -OH, -NH2 and -CH3, increase electron density at the ortho and para positions, so they direct the incoming electrophile there and speed up substitution (o/p directors). Deactivating electron-withdrawing groups, such as -NO2, -COOH and -CHO, remove electron density most from the ortho and para positions, leaving the meta position relatively richer, so substitution occurs at meta and more slowly (meta directors). Halogens are a special case: deactivating but still o/p directing. Thus -COOH and -NO2 are meta directors, while -Cl, -CH3 and -OH are ortho/para directors.

Conversions

Toluene to o- and p-nitrobenzoic acid: toluene is nitrated with conc. HNO3/conc. H2SO4 to give a mixture of o-nitrotoluene and p-nitrotoluene, which is then oxidised with alkaline KMnO4 (or acidified K2Cr2O7) on heating, converting -CH3 into -COOH: O2N-C6H4-CH3 -> O2N-C6H4-COOH.

Benzene to m-nitrotoluene: the -NO2 (meta director) must be introduced before the -CH3 group. Step 1, nitration: C6H6 -> C6H5NO2. Step 2, Friedel-Crafts alkylation: C6H5NO2 + CH3Cl/anhydrous AlCl3 -> m-CH3-C6H4-NO2 + HCl, because the nitro group directs the incoming methyl group to the meta position.

mcqs.q: In benzene, all six carbons are:
options: sp2 hybridised in a planar hexagonal ring
mcqs.why: All six carbons in benzene are sp2 hybridised in a planar hexagonal ring with 120 degree angles, each leaving one p orbital for the pi cloud.

mcqs.q: The delocalised pi cloud in benzene results in:
options: Alternate long and short C-C bonds
All C-C bonds equal in length between single and double bond values
mcqs.why: Delocalisation makes all C-C bonds equal in length between single and double values and gives benzene extra stability and substitution reactions.

mcqs.q: The resonance energy of benzene is about:
mcqs.why: Benzene has resonance energy about 150 kJ/mol, which is the extra stability arising from delocalisation of its six pi electrons.

options: It contains about 92% carbon and unburnt carbon escapes as soot
mcqs.why: Benzene is about 92% carbon, so ordinary air cannot burn it completely and glowing unburnt carbon particles escape as soot, giving a smoky flame.

mcqs.q: Hydrogenation of benzene with Ni catalyst at 150-200 C under pressure gives:
mcqs.why: Cyclohexane, C6H12, is formed because all three pi bonds of benzene are reduced by 3H2 over a nickel catalyst under pressure.

mcqs.q: Friedel-Crafts acylation of benzene with CH3COCl and anhydrous AlCl3 gives:
mcqs.why: Acetophenone, C6H5COCH3, is the aromatic ketone formed in acylation, whereas CH3Cl under similar conditions would give toluene by alkylation.

mcqs.q: Nitration of benzene at 50-60 C with conc. HNO3 and conc. H2SO4 gives:
options: Nitrobenzene, a pale yellow oily liquid smelling of bitter almonds
mcqs.why: Nitrobenzene is formed under these conditions; it is a pale yellow oily liquid smelling of bitter almonds, as stated in the lesson.

mcqs.q: Sulphonation of benzene is described as:
options: A reversible electrophilic substitution by SO3
mcqs.why: Sulphonation is a reversible electrophilic substitution in which SO3 is the electrophile, giving benzene sulphonic acid, C6H5SO3H.

mcqs.q: In nitration of benzene, the attacking electrophile is:
mcqs.why: The nitronium ion NO2+ is the electrophile, generated by HNO3 + 2H2SO4 giving NO2+ + H3O+ + 2HSO4-, and it is attacked by benzene pi electrons.

mcqs.q: The intermediate formed when benzene pi electrons attack an electrophile is:
mcqs.why: A resonance-stabilised carbocation called the arenium ion is formed, in which aromaticity is temporarily lost before the proton is removed.

mcqs.q: In Friedel-Crafts acylation, the electrophile formed from CH3COCl and AlCl3 is:
mcqs.why: The acylium ion CH3CO+ is formed by CH3COCl + AlCl3 giving CH3CO+ + AlCl4-, and this ion is attacked by the benzene pi cloud.

mcqs.q: In chlorination of benzene, Cl+ is generated using which catalyst system?
options: Cl2 with FeCl3 (or AlCl3) as Lewis acid
mcqs.why: Cl2 reacts with FeCl3 to give Cl+ + FeCl4-; benzene then attacks Cl+ and FeCl4- removes the proton to give chlorobenzene.

mcqs.q: Positions 2 and 6 relative to a substituent on benzene are called:
mcqs.why: Positions 2 and 6 are ortho, positions 3 and 5 are meta, and position 4 is para relative to the existing substituent.

mcqs.q: Which set correctly identifies directing groups given in the lesson?
options: -COOH and -NO2 are meta directors; -Cl, -CH3 and -OH are ortho/para directors
mcqs.why: -COOH and -NO2 are deactivating meta directors, while -Cl, -CH3 and -OH are ortho/para directors, with halogens deactivating but still o/p directing.

mcqs.q: To convert benzene to m-nitrotoluene, the correct order is:
mcqs.why: Nitration must come first because -NO2 is a meta director; subsequent alkylation of nitrobenzene then places -CH3 at the meta position.

lessons.title: Alkyl Halides
lessons.notes_html:
Alkyl halides (haloalkanes) are organic compounds in which one or more hydrogen atoms of an alkane have been replaced by halogen atoms, general formula CnH2n+1X, for example C2H5Br. They are classified by the carbon atom carrying the halogen: in a primary (1 degree) alkyl halide the halogen-bearing carbon is attached to only one other carbon (composition RCH2X), for example 1-bromopropane; in a secondary (2 degree) alkyl halide it is attached to two other carbons (R2CHX); and in a tertiary (3 degree) alkyl halide it is attached to three other carbons (R3CX). CH3X is a methyl halide.

Orbital Structure of Methyl Iodide

In methyl iodide, CH3I, the carbon atom is sp3 hybridised: its one 2s and three 2p orbitals mix to form four sp3 hybrid orbitals arranged tetrahedrally with angles of about 109.5 degrees. Three sp3 orbitals overlap with the 1s orbitals of the three hydrogens to form three C-H sigma bonds. The fourth sp3 orbital overlaps with a p orbital of iodine to form the polar C-I sigma bond, which is longer and weaker than a C-H bond. The molecule is therefore tetrahedral, and the polarity of the C-I bond makes CH3I highly reactive in nucleophilic substitution.

Preparation from Alcohols

  • With HX: R-OH + HX -> R-X + H2O, for example C2H5OH + HBr -> C2H5Br + H2O (ZnCl2 is used as catalyst with HCl). The reactivity order of the acids is HI > HBr > HCl, and tertiary alcohols react fastest.
  • With PX3: 3R-OH + PX3 -> 3R-X + H3PO3, for example 3C2H5OH + PBr3 -> 3C2H5Br + H3PO3. This method gives good yields, especially for bromides and iodides prepared in situ from red phosphorus and the halogen.
  • With SOCl2: R-OH + SOCl2 -> R-Cl + SO2 + HCl, for example C2H5OH + SOCl2 -> C2H5Cl + SO2 + HCl. The by-products are gaseous, so the halide is obtained pure; a little pyridine is often added to absorb the HCl formed.

Why Alkyl Halides are Insoluble in Water

Alkyl halides are polar molecules, but they cannot form hydrogen bonds with water because they have no hydrogen attached to a strongly electronegative atom. The energy released when halide molecules are surrounded by water is not enough to break the strong hydrogen bonds already present between water molecules. They therefore remain almost insoluble in water, although they dissolve readily in organic solvents of similar nature.

Nucleophiles

A nucleophile is an electron-pair donor, a species with a lone pair or negative charge that attacks an electron-deficient carbon centre and forms a new covalent bond. Four examples with their typical reagents are: hydroxide ion OH- (aqueous KOH or NaOH), cyanide ion CN- (KCN in alcohol), ammonia NH3 (alcoholic ammonia), and alkoxide ion RO- (sodium alkoxide, RONa). Halide ions such as I- (KI) are also common nucleophiles.

SN1 and SN2 Mechanisms

A nucleophilic substitution is a reaction in which a nucleophile replaces an atom or group (the leaving group) attached to a saturated carbon, for example R-X + OH- -> R-OH + X-. In the SN1 mechanism the reaction occurs in two steps: the halide slowly ionises to a planar carbocation and X-, and the nucleophile then attacks the carbocation rapidly from either side, giving a racemic product; the rate depends only on the concentration of the substrate, rate = k[RX], and tertiary halides react fastest. In the SN2 mechanism the nucleophile attacks the carbon from the back side at the same time as the leaving group departs, passing through a single transition state in which the carbon is partially bonded to both groups; because bond-making and bond-breaking are simultaneous and no carbocation intermediate is formed, the whole substitution is completed in one concerted step. The product shows complete inversion of configuration (Walden inversion), the rate depends on both [RX] and [Nu-], and the reaction is fastest when there is least steric hindrance: methyl iodide undergoes SN2 most easily, in the order methyl > primary > secondary.

Elimination Reactions: E1 and E2

Beta-elimination is the removal of a hydrogen atom from the beta-carbon (the carbon adjacent to the one bearing the leaving group) together with the leaving group itself, forming a double bond; dehydrohalogenation of alkyl halides with alcoholic KOH is the common example. Methyl bromide, CH3Br, has only one carbon and no beta-carbon at all, so it cannot form an alkene with alcoholic KOH. In the E1 mechanism the halide first ionises slowly to a carbocation, and a base then removes a beta-proton to give the alkene, so the rate depends only on [RX]. In the E2 mechanism a strong base removes the beta-proton at the same time as the halide leaves, in a single concerted step, so the rate depends on both [RX] and [base]. In both cases the more substituted alkene (Saytzeff product) usually predominates.

Substitution versus Elimination

In substitution a nucleophile replaces the halogen and the carbon remains saturated, for example C2H5Br + KOH (aq.) -> C2H5OH + KBr, while in elimination the halogen and a beta-hydrogen are removed and an unsaturated product is formed, C2H5Br + KOH (alc.) -> C2H4 + KBr + H2O. Substitution is favoured by aqueous alkali, lower temperature and a good nucleophile that is a weak base, whereas elimination is favoured by alcoholic alkali, higher temperature and a strong bulky base. Both reactions compete for the same substrate, substitution dominating for primary halides and elimination becoming more important for secondary and tertiary halides under basic conditions. Mechanistically, SN1 competes with E1 through a common carbocation, and SN2 competes with E2 as concerted pathways.

mcqs.why: Alkyl halides have general formula CnH2n+1X, for example C2H5Br, formed by replacing hydrogen atoms of an alkane with halogen.

mcqs.q: The C-I bond in methyl iodide compared with a C-H bond is:
mcqs.why: The C-I bond is longer, weaker and polar compared with C-H, which makes CH3I highly reactive in nucleophilic substitution.

mcqs.q: The reactivity order of hydrogen halides with alcohols is:
mcqs.why: The order is HI > HBr > HCl, and tertiary alcohols react fastest; ZnCl2 is used as catalyst when HCl is the reagent.

options: By-products SO2 and HCl are gaseous, so the halide is obtained pure

Concentration of substrate only, rate = k[RX]

The nucleophile attacks only from the back side

The leaving group leaves slowly first

mcqs.why: Methyl iodide undergoes SN2 most easily because it has least steric hindrance; the order is methyl > primary > secondary.

mcqs.why: Methyl bromide has only one carbon and no beta-carbon at all, so beta-elimination to form an alkene is impossible for CH3Br.

mcqs.q: In E2 elimination, the rate depends on:
mcqs.why: E2 is a single concerted step where base removes the beta-proton as halide leaves, so rate depends on both [RX] and [base].

mcqs.q: C2H5Br with aqueous KOH gives ethanol, but with alcoholic KOH gives ethene. This shows:
options: Aqueous alkali favours substitution; alcoholic alkali favours elimination
mcqs.why: Aqueous KOH favours substitution to ethanol, while alcoholic KOH, higher temperature and strong base favour elimination to ethene.

lessons.title: Grignard's Reagents (Organometallic Compounds)
lessons.notes_html:
Organometallic Compounds and Preparation

Organometallic compounds are organic compounds containing a direct carbon-metal bond, for example CH3MgBr and (C2H5)4Pb. A Grignard reagent is prepared by adding an alkyl halide to dry magnesium turnings in dry ether: R-X + Mg -> R-MgX (dry ether), the ether and apparatus being kept completely free of moisture.

Why the Alkyl Part is Nucleophilic

In a Grignard reagent, RMgX, magnesium is much less electronegative than carbon, so the C-Mg bond is polarised as C delta- and Mg delta+. The alkyl group therefore carries a partial negative charge and a pair of electrons it can donate, behaving like a carbanion. It attacks electron-deficient (electrophilic) centres such as the carbonyl carbon, so the alkyl part acts as a nucleophile and a strong base.

Reactions of Grignard Reagents

  • With water: RMgX + H2O -> R-H + Mg(OH)X. Water is the standard reagent used to hydrolyse a Grignard reagent: the alkyl group takes a proton from water and the corresponding alkane is formed. The alkane formed always has the same carbon skeleton as the Grignard alkyl group, so methyl magnesium iodide itself gives methane, CH3MgI + H2O -> CH4 + Mg(OH)I; propane is obtained by the same method from propyl magnesium halide, C3H7MgX + H2O -> C3H8.
  • With carbon dioxide: RMgX + CO2 -> R-COOH after hydrolysis, a carboxylic acid with one extra carbon. Ethyl magnesium bromide gives propanoic acid: C2H5MgBr + CO2 -> C2H5COOH.
  • With an ester: the reagent first displaces the alkoxy group of the ester to give a ketone, RCOOR + RMgX -> R-CO-R; with a second equivalent of Grignard reagent the ketone reacts further to give a tertiary alcohol.
  • With amines (or any compound with an acidic hydrogen): the reagent is simply protonated to the alkane, RMgX + H2N-R -> R-H + BrMg-NH-R.

Conversion: Methyl Magnesium Bromide into Acetone

Step 1: methyl magnesium bromide is treated with carbon dioxide and the adduct is hydrolysed to give ethanoic acid: CH3MgBr + CO2 -> CH3COOH (after hydrolysis). Step 2: the acid is neutralised with Ca(OH)2 to give calcium acetate, (CH3COO)2Ca. Step 3: dry distillation of calcium acetate gives acetone: (CH3COO)2Ca -> CH3-CO-CH3 + CaCO3 on strong heating.

mcqs.why: Organometallic compounds contain a direct carbon-metal bond, for example CH3MgBr and (C2H5)4Pb as given in the lesson.

Adding alkyl halide to dry magnesium turnings in dry ether

The alkyl group carries a positive charge
The C-Mg bond is polarised C delta- and Mg delta+, like a carbanion

mcqs.why: The reagent first displaces the alkoxy group to give a ketone R-CO-R, which with a second equivalent reacts further to a tertiary alcohol.

options: A new amine with longer chain
mcqs.why: Any compound with an acidic hydrogen simply protonates the Grignard reagent to the alkane, RMgX + H2N-R gives R-H.

options: Reaction with water to give methane
Reaction with CO2 then hydrolysis to ethanoic acid
mcqs.why: CH3MgBr + CO2 followed by hydrolysis gives ethanoic acid, CH3COOH, which is then converted via calcium acetate to acetone.

mcqs.why: Dry distillation of (CH3COO)2Ca on strong heating gives acetone, CH3-CO-CH3, plus CaCO3, completing the conversion from CH3MgBr.

lessons.title: Amines
lessons.notes_html:
Structure and Basic Character

Amines act as bases because the nitrogen atom has a lone pair of electrons which it donates to a proton, forming an alkylammonium ion: R-NH2 + H+ -> R-NH3+. Accepting a proton is the behaviour of a base. In a primary amine the nitrogen is bonded to three atoms (one C and two H) and carries one lone pair, giving a tetrahedral pyramidal structure similar to ammonia, with a bond angle of about 107 degrees, slightly less than the tetrahedral angle because the lone pair repels the bond pairs. In water: R-NH2 + H2O <-> R-NH3+ + OH-. Basic strength is expressed by Kb or by the pKa of the conjugate acid.

Basicity of Amines

Alkyl groups are electron-donating (+I effect), so they push electron density onto the nitrogen and make its lone pair more available for accepting a proton; they also stabilise the alkylammonium ion formed. A secondary amine has two alkyl groups and a tertiary amine has three, so the effect is greater than in a primary amine with only one alkyl group, which is why secondary and tertiary amines are more alkaline than primary amines. In aqueous solution the order is modified by solvation and steric effects, but the inductive effect explains why substituted amines are stronger bases than ammonia and, in the gas phase, tertiary > secondary > primary. Aromatic amines such as aniline are much weaker bases, because the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring and is less available for protonation.

Preparations

From nitriles: nitriles (alkyl cyanides) are reduced with hydrogen in the presence of a nickel catalyst, or with LiAlH4 or sodium and alcohol, to give primary amines having one carbon more than the original alkyl halide used to make the nitrile: R-C triple bond N + 4[H] -> R-CH2-NH2, for example CH3-CN + 4[H] -> CH3-CH2-NH2 (ethylamine). This is a useful method because the chain is lengthened by one carbon atom.

From alkyl halides (ammonolysis): ethyl chloride is heated with an excess of alcoholic ammonia under pressure, when the chlorine is replaced by the -NH2 group: C2H5Cl + NH3 (alc., excess, heat) -> C2H5NH2 + HCl, the amine being obtained as its salt and liberated by alkali. Excess ammonia is used to reduce further alkylation. On further alkylation a primary amine gives a secondary amine and then a tertiary amine: R-NH2 + R-X -> R2NH + HX, and R2NH + R-X -> R3N + HX; with excess RX the tertiary amine gives the quaternary salt [R4N]+ X-.

Reaction with Nitrous Acid

A primary aliphatic (alkyl) amine reacts with nitrous acid (NaNO2 + HCl) to form an unstable diazonium salt which immediately decomposes, giving the corresponding alcohol with evolution of nitrogen: R-NH2 + HNO2 -> R-OH + N2 + H2O. Stable diazonium salts are formed only by aromatic primary amines at low temperature.

Conversions

Ethyl chloride into ethyl alcohol: C2H5Cl + KOH (aq.) -> C2H5OH + KCl, by boiling with aqueous potassium hydroxide (or moist silver oxide); alcoholic KOH must be avoided because it gives ethene instead.

Ethylamine into imine: ethylamine is dehydrogenated (oxidised) to the imine ethanimine, in which the -NH2 group becomes a C=N double bond: CH3-CH2-NH2 -> CH3-CH=NH + H2. Imine formation by condensation of an amine with an aldehyde or ketone with loss of water gives substituted imines (Schiff bases) in the same family.

mcqs.q: Amines act as bases because the nitrogen atom:
options: Has a lone pair it donates to a proton, forming R-NH3+
mcqs.why: Amines are bases because nitrogen donates its lone pair to a proton, R-NH2 + H+ gives R-NH3+, forming an alkylammonium ion.

mcqs.q: The structure of a primary amine is:
options: Tetrahedral pyramidal with bond angle about 107 degrees
mcqs.why: A primary amine is tetrahedral pyramidal like ammonia, about 107 degrees, slightly less than tetrahedral because the lone pair repels bond pairs.

mcqs.q: Alkyl groups increase amine basicity by:
options: Delocalising the lone pair into a ring
+I effect pushing electrons onto nitrogen and stabilising R-NH3+
mcqs.why: Alkyl groups have a +I effect, pushing electron density onto nitrogen, making the lone pair more available and stabilising the alkylammonium ion.

mcqs.q: Why is aniline a much weaker base than aliphatic amines?
options: It has no lone pair at all
Its nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring
mcqs.why: In aniline the lone pair is delocalised into the benzene ring and is less available for protonation, so aromatic amines are much weaker bases.

mcqs.q: Reduction of a nitrile such as CH3-CN gives:
options: Ethylamine, CH3-CH2-NH2, with one carbon more than the original halide chain
mcqs.why: CH3-CN + 4[H] gives CH3-CH2-NH2; nitrile reduction lengthens the chain by one carbon and gives a primary amine.

mcqs.q: Ethylamine is prepared from ethyl chloride by heating with:
mcqs.why: Ammonolysis uses excess alcoholic ammonia under pressure, C2H5Cl + NH3 gives C2H5NH2, excess ammonia reducing further alkylation.

mcqs.q: On further alkylation with R-X, a primary amine gives successively:
options: Secondary amine, then tertiary amine, then quaternary salt [R4N]+ X- with excess RX
mcqs.why: R-NH2 + R-X gives R2NH, then R3N, and with excess RX the quaternary salt [R4N]+ X- is formed, as shown in the lesson.

mcqs.q: A primary aliphatic amine with nitrous acid (NaNO2 + HCl) gives:
options: A stable diazonium salt at room temperature
The corresponding alcohol with evolution of nitrogen
mcqs.why: R-NH2 + HNO2 gives R-OH + N2 + H2O because the aliphatic diazonium salt is unstable and decomposes at once; stable salts are aromatic only.

mcqs.q: Ethyl chloride is converted to ethyl alcohol by:
options: Boiling with aqueous KOH (or moist silver oxide)
mcqs.why: Aqueous KOH gives C2H5OH by substitution, C2H5Cl + KOH (aq.) gives C2H5OH + KCl; alcoholic KOH must be avoided as it gives ethene.

mcqs.q: Ethylamine is dehydrogenated to which imine?
mcqs.why: Ethanimine, CH3-CH=NH, is formed by dehydrogenation of ethylamine, converting the -NH2 group into a C=N double bond with loss of H2.

lessons.title: Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols are organic compounds containing one or more hydroxyl (-OH) groups attached to an aliphatic carbon atom, general formula R-OH or CnH2n+1OH. They are classified in two ways: by the number of -OH groups, as monohydric (one -OH, e.g. ethanol), dihydric (two -OH, e.g. ethylene glycol) and trihydric/polyhydric (three or more, e.g. glycerol); and by the carbon bearing the -OH group, as primary (1 degree), secondary (2 degree) and tertiary (3 degree) alcohols.

Physical Properties

The -OH group of an alcohol can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules, and this attraction compensates for breaking the hydrogen bonds in water itself, so lower alcohols such as methanol and ethanol are miscible with water in all proportions. Solubility decreases as the non-polar alkyl chain becomes longer, because the hydrocarbon part opposes dissolution. Ethanol is a liquid at room temperature (b.p. 78 C) because its molecules are held together by strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds and are associated into larger clusters, whereas ethyl chloride has no hydrogen bonding and only weak van der Waals forces, so it escapes easily as a gas (b.p. about 12 C). Boiling point increases with molecular mass and with chain straightness, because a straight chain has a larger surface area and stronger van der Waals forces: n-pentyl alcohol (pentan-1-ol, b.p. about 138 C) boils higher than its branched isomers isopentyl and neopentyl alcohol, and much higher than ethyl alcohol.

Preparation from Grignard Reagents

  • Primary alcohol: RMgX + HCHO -> R-CH2-OMgX -> R-CH2OH (with H2O), from formaldehyde, the alcohol having one carbon more than R.
  • Secondary alcohol: RMgX + R-CHO -> R2CH-OH after hydrolysis, from any other aldehyde.
  • Tertiary alcohol: RMgX + R-CO-R -> R3C-OH after hydrolysis, from a ketone, the carbonyl carbon ending up attached to three carbon groups and one -OH group.

Important Reactions

  • With PCl3: 3C2H5OH + PCl3 -> 3C2H5Cl + H3PO3. Phosphorus trichloride replaces the -OH group by chlorine, giving ethyl chloride, a gas used as a local anaesthetic spray.
  • Dehydration: at 170 C with concentrated H2SO4 ethanol gives ethene, C2H5OH -> CH2=CH2 + H2O (intramolecular dehydration); at about 140 C two molecules lose one molecule of water between them (intermolecular dehydration) giving diethyl ether: 2C2H5OH -> C2H5-O-C2H5 + H2O (conc. H2SO4, 140 C). Excess ethanol and the lower temperature favour ether formation.
  • Hydration of ethene (industrial ethanol): CH2=CH2 + H2SO4 -> CH3CH2OSO3H, and CH3CH2OSO3H + H2O -> C2H5OH + H2SO4 (boil). Ethene is absorbed in hot concentrated sulphuric acid to form ethyl hydrogen sulphate, which on hydrolysis with boiling water gives ethanol.
  • Oxidation: with acidified potassium dichromate, ethanol is oxidised first to ethanal and then to ethanoic (acetic) acid, the orange dichromate turning green: CH3CH2OH + 2[O] -> CH3COOH + H2O. If the ethanal is distilled off as it forms, it can be isolated instead. A secondary alcohol is first oxidised to a ketone, R2CH-OH -> R2C=O, which is the intermediate product, and only under vigorous conditions is the ketone further cleaved to carboxylic acids with fewer carbons (for example propan-2-ol -> propanone -> ethanoic acid).
  • Reduction of acetic acid: CH3COOH -> CH3CH2OH with LiAlH4 in dry ether followed by H2O work-up; the -COOH group is converted into -CH2OH.
  • Ethyl bromide to ethanol: C2H5Br + KOH (aq.) -> C2H5OH + KBr, by boiling with aqueous KOH or moist Ag2O; alcoholic KOH would give ethene by elimination.

Cleavage of 1,2-Diols

Oxidative cleavage of a 1,2-diol (vicinal diol) occurs in the presence of periodic acid, HIO4, which specifically cleaves the C-C bond, each -CH(OH)- group being converted into a carbonyl group. For example, ethylene glycol gives two molecules of formaldehyde: HOCH2-CH2OH + HIO4 -> 2HCHO + HIO3 + H2O.

Lucas Test

Lucas reagent is a mixture of anhydrous ZnCl2 and concentrated HCl, which converts alcohols into insoluble alkyl chlorides that make the solution turbid. A tertiary alcohol reacts immediately and the mixture becomes turbid at once. A secondary alcohol becomes turbid within about five minutes. A primary alcohol does not react at room temperature and the mixture stays clear, reacting only on heating. The test works because tertiary carbocations form most easily.

Identification Tests for an Alcohol

(1) Sodium metal test: an alcohol gives brisk effervescence of hydrogen with a small piece of sodium, 2R-OH + 2Na -> 2R-ONa + H2. (2) Ester test: warmed with acetic acid and a few drops of concentrated H2SO4 it gives a sweet, fruity smell of the ester formed. Ethanol also gives the iodoform test, a yellow precipitate of CHI3 with I2/NaOH.

Commercial Applications of Alcohols

Ethanol is used as a fuel and fuel additive, as a solvent for paints, varnishes, perfumes and medicines, in alcoholic drinks and as an antiseptic; methanol is used to make formaldehyde, plastics and as an industrial solvent, and ethylene glycol is used as antifreeze.

mcqs.q: The general formula of alcohols is:
mcqs.why: Alcohols contain -OH on an aliphatic carbon with general formula R-OH or CnH2n+1OH, as defined at the start of the lesson.

mcqs.q: Ethylene glycol and glycerol are respectively:
mcqs.why: Ethylene glycol has two -OH groups (dihydric) and glycerol has three or more in the polyhydric class, while ethanol is monohydric.

mcqs.q: Lower alcohols are miscible with water in all proportions because:
options: Their alkyl chains are non-polar and long
The -OH group forms hydrogen bonds with water, compensating for breaking water hydrogen bonds
mcqs.why: Hydrogen bonding between alcohol -OH and water compensates for breaking water-water hydrogen bonds, so methanol and ethanol are fully miscible.

mcqs.q: Ethanol is a liquid (b.p. 78 C) while ethyl chloride is a gas (b.p. about 12 C) because ethanol has:
options: Strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding and association into clusters
mcqs.why: Ethanol molecules are held by strong hydrogen bonds into clusters, whereas ethyl chloride has only weak van der Waals forces and escapes as a gas.

mcqs.q: Which alcohol has the highest boiling point among those compared in the lesson?
mcqs.why: n-Pentyl alcohol boils highest at about 138 C because straight chains have larger surface area and stronger van der Waals forces than branched isomers.

mcqs.q: A primary alcohol is obtained from a Grignard reagent by reaction with:
mcqs.why: RMgX + HCHO then hydrolysis gives R-CH2OH, a primary alcohol with one carbon more than the Grignard alkyl group R.

mcqs.q: A tertiary alcohol is obtained from a Grignard reagent by reaction with:
mcqs.why: A ketone with RMgX then hydrolysis gives R3C-OH, a tertiary alcohol where the carbonyl carbon ends up attached to three carbons and -OH.

mcqs.q: Ethanol reacts with PCl3 to give:
mcqs.why: PCl3 replaces -OH by chlorine: 3C2H5OH + PCl3 gives 3C2H5Cl + H3PO3, and ethyl chloride is used as a local anaesthetic spray.

mcqs.q: Dehydration of ethanol with conc. H2SO4 at 170 C gives ethene, while at about 140 C it mainly gives:
mcqs.why: At 140 C two ethanol molecules lose one water between them to give diethyl ether, while at 170 C intramolecular dehydration gives ethene.

mcqs.q: Industrial ethanol by hydration of ethene proceeds via which intermediate?
mcqs.why: Ethene absorbed in hot conc. H2SO4 forms ethyl hydrogen sulphate, which on boiling with water hydrolyses to ethanol and regenerates H2SO4.

mcqs.q: Oxidation of ethanol with acidified potassium dichromate gives finally:
options: Ethanal only, with no further oxidation possible
Ethanoic (acetic) acid, dichromate turning from orange to green
mcqs.why: Ethanol is oxidised first to ethanal then to ethanoic acid, CH3CH2OH + 2[O] gives CH3COOH + H2O, with orange dichromate turning green.

mcqs.q: A secondary alcohol is first oxidised to:
options: A ketone, which is the intermediate product
mcqs.why: A secondary alcohol gives a ketone first, R2CH-OH gives R2C=O, and only under vigorous conditions is the ketone cleaved to acids with fewer carbons.

mcqs.q: Reduction of acetic acid to ethanol requires:
options: LiAlH4 in dry ether followed by H2O work-up
mcqs.why: LiAlH4 in dry ether then water work-up reduces CH3COOH to CH3CH2OH, converting the -COOH group into -CH2OH.

mcqs.q: Oxidative cleavage of ethylene glycol with periodic acid, HIO4, gives:
mcqs.why: HIO4 specifically cleaves the C-C bond of a 1,2-diol, so HOCH2-CH2OH gives 2HCHO plus HIO3 and H2O.

mcqs.q: In the Lucas test, a tertiary alcohol with ZnCl2 and conc. HCl:
options: Becomes turbid within about five minutes
mcqs.why: A tertiary alcohol reacts immediately and the mixture becomes turbid at once because tertiary carbocations form most easily in the Lucas test.

lessons.title: Phenols
lessons.notes_html:
Phenol, C6H5OH, is the aromatic compound in which a hydroxyl group is attached directly to a benzene ring; it is also called carbolic acid because it is weakly acidic. All carbon atoms of the benzene ring in phenol, including the one bearing the -OH group, are sp2 hybridised and part of the flat aromatic ring, which allows the oxygen lone pair to conjugate with the ring pi system. Pyrogallol (benzene-1,2,3-triol) is a trihydric phenol with three -OH groups on the ring; resorcinol and catechol are dihydric and cresol is monohydric.

Preparation of Phenol

  • From chlorobenzene (Dow process): chlorobenzene is fused with aqueous NaOH at about 350 C and 150 atmospheres pressure to give sodium phenoxide, which on acidification gives phenol: C6H5Cl + 2NaOH -> C6H5ONa + NaCl + H2O, then C6H5ONa + HCl -> C6H5OH + NaCl.
  • From sodium benzene sulphonate: the salt is fused with NaOH at about 300 C to give sodium phenoxide and sodium sulphite: C6H5SO3Na + 2NaOH -> C6H5ONa + Na2SO3 + H2O, and the phenoxide is then acidified to phenol.
  • From diazonium salt: a benzene diazonium salt solution, prepared by diazotising aniline at 0-5 C, on warming with water hydrolyses to phenol with evolution of nitrogen: C6H5N2+ Cl- + H2O -> C6H5OH + N2 + HCl (warm).

Alcohol versus Phenol

  • Solubility: lower alcohols such as ethanol are completely miscible with water because the small alkyl group allows extensive hydrogen bonding with water. Phenol is only sparingly soluble in cold water (about 8 g per 100 mL) because its large non-polar benzene ring opposes dissolution, although it becomes fully miscible above about 66 C.
  • Boiling point: phenol boils at about 182 C, much higher than ethanol (78 C), partly because of its larger molecular mass and strong hydrogen bonding combined with ring interactions. Alcohols also boil high for their mass due to hydrogen bonding, increasing with chain length (methanol 65 C, ethanol 78 C, propan-1-ol 97 C).
  • Acidic character: phenol is measurably acidic (pKa about 10): it turns blue litmus red, reacts with NaOH to form sodium phenoxide and water, and its phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance delocalisation into the ring. Alcohols are essentially neutral (pKa about 16-18), do not affect litmus and do not react with NaOH, because the alkoxide ion gets no such resonance stabilisation and the alkyl group pushes electrons onto oxygen. Phenol is therefore a much stronger acid than an alcohol, though weaker than carboxylic acids and carbonic acid.

Reactions of Phenol

  • With hot concentrated nitric acid: phenol is both nitrated and oxidised, the main isolated product being 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, picric acid, a yellow crystalline explosive: C6H5OH + 3HNO3 (conc., heat) -> C6H2(NO2)3-OH + 3H2O. In practice picric acid is usually made via sulphonation first to reduce oxidation losses.
  • With concentrated sulphuric acid at 100 C: phenol is sulphonated mainly at the para position, giving p-phenol sulphonic acid (4-hydroxybenzene sulphonic acid): C6H5OH + H2SO4 -> p-HO-C6H4-SO3H + H2O. The ortho product predominates at room temperature.
  • With bromine water: phenol instantly decolourises bromine water and gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol, because the -OH group strongly activates the ring at both ortho positions and the para position: C6H5OH + 3Br2 -> C6H2Br3-OH + 3HBr. This reaction is a confirmatory test for phenol.
  • With sodium metal: 2C6H5OH + 2Na -> 2C6H5ONa (sodium phenoxide) + H2, less vigorously than sodium with water or with carboxylic acids, in keeping with the weak acidity of phenol.
  • Oxidation to benzoquinone: C6H5OH + [O] -> O=C6H4=O (p-benzoquinone) + H2O, with Na2Cr2O7/H2SO4; a second carbonyl appears at the para position of the ring.

Identification Tests for Phenol

(1) Ferric chloride test: phenol gives a violet (purple) colouration with neutral FeCl3 solution. (2) Bromine water test: phenol decolourises bromine water and gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol. It also turns blue litmus slightly red, showing its weak acidity.

Commercial Applications of Phenol

Phenol is used to make Bakelite and other phenol-formaldehyde resins, nylon intermediates, dyes, antiseptics such as TCP and Dettol-type products, aspirin and picric acid.

mcqs.q: Phenol, also called carbolic acid, is:
options: C6H5OH with -OH directly attached to a benzene ring and weakly acidic
C2H5OH with -OH on an aliphatic carbon
mcqs.why: Phenol is C6H5OH with -OH directly on the benzene ring; it is weakly acidic and therefore also called carbolic acid.

mcqs.q: The carbon bearing the -OH group in phenol is:
mcqs.why: All ring carbons in phenol, including the one bearing -OH, are sp2 hybridised and part of the flat aromatic ring.

mcqs.q: Pyrogallol is classified as:
mcqs.why: Pyrogallol is benzene-1,2,3-triol with three -OH groups, so it is trihydric; resorcinol and catechol are dihydric and cresol is monohydric.

mcqs.q: In the Dow process, phenol is prepared from chlorobenzene by:
options: Heating with dilute HCl at room temperature
Fusing with aqueous NaOH at about 350 C and 150 atm, then acidifying sodium phenoxide
mcqs.why: Chlorobenzene fused with aqueous NaOH at 350 C and 150 atm gives sodium phenoxide, which on acidification gives phenol.

mcqs.q: Fusion of sodium benzene sulphonate with NaOH at about 300 C gives:
