mcqs.why: C6H5SO3Na + 2NaOH gives C6H5ONa + Na2SO3 + H2O, and acidification of the phenoxide then gives phenol.

mcqs.q: Phenol from a diazonium salt is obtained by:
options: Warming benzene diazonium salt solution with water, evolving nitrogen
mcqs.why: Warming C6H5N2+ Cl- with water hydrolyses it to C6H5OH + N2 + HCl; the diazonium salt is prepared by diazotising aniline at 0-5 C.

mcqs.q: Phenol is only sparingly soluble in cold water (about 8 g per 100 mL) because:
options: Its large non-polar benzene ring opposes dissolution
mcqs.why: The large non-polar benzene ring opposes dissolution, though phenol becomes fully miscible above about 66 C, unlike ethanol which is fully miscible.

mcqs.q: The boiling point of phenol compared with ethanol is:
options: Much higher, about 182 C versus 78 C for ethanol
mcqs.why: Phenol boils at about 182 C, much higher than ethanol at 78 C, due to larger mass, hydrogen bonding and ring interactions.

mcqs.q: Phenol (pKa about 10) is a stronger acid than alcohols (pKa about 16-18) because:
options: Phenol reacts with NaOH but alcohols also do
Alkyl groups withdraw electrons from oxygen
The phenoxide ion is stabilised by resonance delocalisation into the ring
mcqs.why: Phenoxide is resonance-stabilised by delocalisation into the ring, while alkoxide gets no such stabilisation, so phenol turns litmus red and reacts with NaOH.

mcqs.q: Phenol with hot concentrated nitric acid gives mainly:
options: 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol, picric acid, a yellow crystalline explosive
mcqs.why: Hot conc. HNO3 both nitrates and oxidises phenol to 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, picric acid, C6H2(NO2)3-OH, a yellow crystalline explosive.

mcqs.q: Phenol with conc. H2SO4 at 100 C gives mainly:
mcqs.why: At 100 C sulphonation occurs mainly at para, giving p-HO-C6H4-SO3H; the ortho product predominates at room temperature instead.

mcqs.q: Phenol with bromine water gives:
options: A white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol and decolourises bromine water
mcqs.why: The -OH strongly activates ortho and para positions, so phenol instantly decolourises bromine water and precipitates white 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

mcqs.q: Phenol reacts with sodium metal to give:
options: Sodium phenoxide and hydrogen, less vigorously than sodium with water
mcqs.why: 2C6H5OH + 2Na gives 2C6H5ONa + H2, less vigorously than with water or carboxylic acids, in keeping with phenol weak acidity.

mcqs.q: Oxidation of phenol with Na2Cr2O7/H2SO4 gives:
options: p-Benzoquinone, with a second carbonyl at the para position
mcqs.why: Phenol is oxidised to p-benzoquinone, O=C6H4=O, where a second carbonyl appears at the para position of the ring.

mcqs.q: The ferric chloride test for phenol gives:
options: A violet (purple) colouration with neutral FeCl3
mcqs.why: Phenol gives a violet colouration with neutral FeCl3 solution, one of its confirmatory identification tests alongside the bromine water test.

lessons.title: Ethers
lessons.notes_html:
Physical Properties

Alcohol molecules are associated by strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding through their -OH groups, so much heat is needed to separate them. Ether molecules have no hydrogen attached to oxygen and cannot form hydrogen bonds among themselves; only weak dipole forces hold them together. Ethers therefore boil at much lower temperatures than alcohols of comparable molecular mass, and they cannot form hydrogen bonds with water through an -OH group, so compounds like ethyl chloride and the higher ethers are practically insoluble in water.

Oxonium Ion Formation

An oxonium ion is a positively charged oxygen species in which oxygen carries three bonds and one lone pair, for example H3O+ and R2OH+. An ether oxygen has two lone pairs; in strong acid it accepts a proton on one lone pair to form a dialkyloxonium ion: R-O-R + H+ -> [R-O(H)-R]+, for example (C2H5)2O + HCl -> [(C2H5)2OH]+ Cl-. Formation of oxonium salts in concentrated acids explains why ethers dissolve in concentrated H2SO4 and how ether linkages are cleaved by hot concentrated HX.

Ethers as Solvents

Ethers are good solvents because they dissolve a wide range of organic compounds, both polar and non-polar, yet they are chemically quite unreactive towards acids, bases, oxidising and reducing agents under normal conditions. They do not react with Grignard reagents and organometallic compounds, which is why reactions like the preparation of RMgX are carried out in dry ether. Their low boiling points also make them easy to remove after the reaction.

Diethyl Ether

Diethyl ether is formed by heating ethanol with concentrated H2SO4 at about 140 C: 2C2H5OH -> C2H5-O-C2H5 + H2O. It was the first widely used general anaesthetic and produces unconsciousness when its vapour is inhaled; it is highly volatile and inflammable, which is why safer anaesthetics have largely replaced it in modern surgery. Ethers in general serve as solvents for oils, fats and Grignard reactions and as starting materials in industry.

mcqs.q: Ethers boil at much lower temperatures than alcohols of comparable mass because ether molecules:
options: Have no hydrogen attached to oxygen and only weak dipole forces hold them together
Form strong hydrogen bonds among themselves
mcqs.why: Ether molecules cannot form hydrogen bonds among themselves as they have no H on oxygen, so only weak dipole forces hold them together.

mcqs.q: An oxonium ion is:
options: A positively charged oxygen with three bonds and one lone pair, e.g. H3O+
An oxygen atom with no bonds
mcqs.why: An oxonium ion carries positive charge on oxygen with three bonds and one lone pair, for example H3O+ and R2OH+ as given in the lesson.

mcqs.q: Diethyl ether in strong acid forms an oxonium salt by:
options: Breaking the C-O bond at room temperature
Accepting a proton on an oxygen lone pair to give [(C2H5)2OH]+
mcqs.why: Ether oxygen accepts H+ on a lone pair: (C2H5)2O + HCl gives [(C2H5)2OH]+ Cl-, a dialkyloxonium ion.

mcqs.q: Formation of oxonium salts explains why ethers:
options: Dissolve in concentrated H2SO4 and are cleaved by hot concentrated HX
mcqs.why: Oxonium salt formation in concentrated acids explains dissolution in conc. H2SO4 and cleavage of ether linkages by hot concentrated HX.

mcqs.q: Ethers are good solvents for Grignard reactions because they:
options: React with Grignard reagents to activate them
Dissolve many organic compounds yet do not react with Grignard reagents
mcqs.why: Ethers dissolve polar and non-polar organics yet are unreactive towards Grignard and organometallic reagents, so RMgX is prepared in dry ether.

mcqs.q: Another advantage of ethers as solvents mentioned in the lesson is:
options: Their high boiling points keep them in the mixture
They form hydrogen bonds with products
Their low boiling points make them easy to remove after reaction
mcqs.why: Their low boiling points make ethers easy to remove after the reaction, in addition to being chemically quite unreactive.

mcqs.q: Diethyl ether is formed by heating ethanol with conc. H2SO4 at:
mcqs.why: At about 140 C, 2C2H5OH gives C2H5-O-C2H5 + H2O; at 170 C the product would instead be ethene.

mcqs.q: Diethyl ether was historically important as:
options: The first widely used general anaesthetic
mcqs.why: Diethyl ether was the first widely used general anaesthetic, producing unconsciousness when its vapour is inhaled.

mcqs.q: Diethyl ether has largely been replaced in modern surgery because it is:
mcqs.why: Diethyl ether is highly volatile and inflammable, which is why safer anaesthetics have largely replaced it in modern surgery.

mcqs.q: Ethers in general serve in industry as:
options: Solvents for oils, fats and Grignard reactions and as starting materials
Only anaesthetics with no solvent use
mcqs.why: Ethers serve as solvents for oils, fats and Grignard reactions and as starting materials in industry, as stated in the lesson.

chapters.title: Carbonyl Compounds I - Aldehydes and Ketones

lessons.title: Physical Properties
lessons.notes_html:
Boiling Points

The boiling points of aldehydes and ketones are lower than those of alcohols. Alcohols have -OH groups and form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds, while aldehydes and ketones have no hydrogen attached to oxygen, so they are held only by weaker dipole-dipole forces and need less heat to boil.

Solubility in Water

Formaldehyde is the most soluble carbonyl compound in water: it is the smallest aldehyde, its carbonyl oxygen hydrogen-bonds strongly with water, and there is no large non-polar hydrocarbon part to oppose dissolving. As the size of the alkyl or aryl group increases, as in acetaldehyde, benzaldehyde and acetophenone, the molecule becomes less polar and solubility in water decreases, so formaldehyde is highly soluble compared with the other aldehydes.

mcqs.q: Why are the boiling points of aldehydes and ketones lower than those of alcohols?
options: They form stronger hydrogen bonds than alcohols
Alcohols form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds, while aldehydes and ketones have no hydrogen attached to oxygen
Aldehydes and ketones are held together by ionic bonds
Their molecules are always much heavier than alcohol molecules
mcqs.why: Alcohols form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds through their -OH groups, but aldehydes and ketones have no hydrogen on oxygen, so they are held only by weaker dipole-dipole forces and boil lower.

mcqs.q: Which forces mainly hold aldehyde and ketone molecules together in the liquid?
options: Hydrogen bonds between their own molecules
mcqs.why: Weaker dipole-dipole forces hold aldehydes and ketones together because they have no hydrogen attached to oxygen and cannot hydrogen-bond like alcohols.

mcqs.q: Which carbonyl compound is the most soluble in water?
mcqs.why: Formaldehyde is the most soluble because it is the smallest aldehyde, its carbonyl oxygen hydrogen-bonds strongly with water, and it has no large non-polar hydrocarbon part.

mcqs.q: What happens to the water solubility of an aldehyde as the size of its alkyl or aryl group increases?
options: It changes the aldehyde into a salt
It decreases because the molecule becomes less polar
mcqs.why: Solubility decreases as the alkyl or aryl group grows, because the larger non-polar hydrocarbon part makes the molecule less polar and opposes dissolving in water.

mcqs.q: Why is formaldehyde highly soluble in water compared with other aldehydes?
options: Its carbonyl oxygen hydrogen-bonds strongly with water and there is no large non-polar hydrocarbon part
It reacts with water to form a salt
It contains a large phenyl group that attracts water
mcqs.why: Formaldehyde dissolves well because its carbonyl oxygen forms strong hydrogen bonds with water and, being the smallest aldehyde, it has no large non-polar part to oppose dissolving.

mcqs.q: Which change would make a carbonyl compound less soluble in water?
options: Keeping only the smallest group on the carbonyl carbon
Increasing the size of its alkyl or aryl group
Adding more water to the mixture
mcqs.why: Increasing the size of the alkyl or aryl group makes the molecule less polar, so its solubility in water decreases, as seen going from formaldehyde to benzaldehyde and acetophenone.

mcqs.q: Which set of compounds is given in the notes as less soluble in water than formaldehyde because of their larger groups?
options: Formic acid, acetic acid and propanoic acid
mcqs.why: Acetaldehyde, benzaldehyde and acetophenone are less soluble than formaldehyde because their larger alkyl or aryl groups make them less polar.

mcqs.q: Why do aldehydes and ketones need less heat to boil than alcohols?
options: They contain an -OH group on every carbon
They are held by metallic bonds
They are held only by weaker dipole-dipole forces
mcqs.why: They need less heat to boil because they are held only by weaker dipole-dipole forces, unlike alcohols whose strong hydrogen bonds take more heat to break.

mcqs.q: Which feature of alcohols allows them to form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds?
options: The hydrogen attached to oxygen in their -OH group
mcqs.why: Alcohols have a hydrogen attached to oxygen in the -OH group, which allows strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding that aldehydes and ketones cannot form.

mcqs.q: Which statement about these compounds is correct?
options: Ketones boil higher than alcohols because their hydrogen bonding is stronger
Aldehydes and ketones boil lower than alcohols because their intermolecular forces are weaker
Formaldehyde is the least soluble carbonyl compound in water
A larger aryl group increases solubility in water
mcqs.why: Aldehydes and ketones boil lower than alcohols because dipole-dipole forces are weaker than the hydrogen bonds between alcohol molecules.

lessons.title: Structure
lessons.notes_html:
Aldehydes are organic compounds containing the -CHO group, in which the carbonyl carbon is attached to at least one hydrogen, general formula R-CHO, while ketones contain the C=O group between two carbon groups, general formula R-CO-R. Acetophenone, C6H5-CO-CH3, is a member of the ketone family containing one alkyl group and one aryl group on the carbonyl carbon; a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon would make it an aldehyde, not a ketone.

Hybridisation of the Carbonyl Carbon

In both aldehydes and ketones the carbonyl carbon is sp2 hybridised: it forms three sigma bonds (to oxygen and to two other atoms) in a trigonal planar arrangement with angles of about 120 degrees, and the fourth valence forms a pi bond with oxygen using the unhybridised p-orbital. The C=O bond is polar because oxygen is more electronegative, so carbon carries a partial positive charge and oxygen a partial negative charge, which explains their nucleophilic addition reactions.

mcqs.q: What is the general formula of an aldehyde?
mcqs.why: An aldehyde has the general formula R-CHO, because its carbonyl carbon carries at least one hydrogen in the -CHO group.

mcqs.q: What is the general formula of a ketone?
mcqs.why: A ketone has the general formula R-CO-R, with the C=O group placed between two carbon groups and no hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon.

mcqs.q: Which statement about acetophenone is correct?
options: Its formula is C6H5-CHO and it is an aldehyde
It contains two aryl groups on the carbonyl carbon
It contains two identical methyl groups
Its formula is C6H5-CO-CH3 and it is a ketone with one alkyl and one aryl group
mcqs.why: Acetophenone is C6H5-CO-CH3, so its carbonyl carbon carries one phenyl (aryl) group and one methyl (alkyl) group, which makes it a ketone.

mcqs.q: If the carbonyl carbon of a compound carries a hydrogen atom, the compound belongs to which family?
mcqs.why: A hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon gives the -CHO group, so the compound is an aldehyde; a ketone has two carbon groups instead.

mcqs.q: What is the hybridisation of the carbonyl carbon in aldehydes and ketones?
mcqs.why: The carbonyl carbon is sp2 hybridised because it forms three sigma bonds in a trigonal planar arrangement and one pi bond to oxygen.

mcqs.q: What is the geometry and approximate bond angle around the carbonyl carbon?
mcqs.why: The carbonyl carbon is trigonal planar with angles of about 120 degrees, because its three sigma bonds lie in one plane in an sp2 arrangement.

mcqs.q: How many sigma bonds does the carbonyl carbon form?
mcqs.why: The carbonyl carbon forms three sigma bonds: one to oxygen and two to the other atoms attached to it, while the fourth valence forms the pi bond.

mcqs.q: How is the pi bond of the C=O group formed?
options: By overlap of two sp3 orbitals
By a hydrogen bond to oxygen
By sharing a lone pair from oxygen
By the unhybridised p-orbital of carbon overlapping with oxygen
mcqs.why: The pi bond is formed by the unhybridised p-orbital left on the sp2 carbonyl carbon overlapping with oxygen, in addition to the three sigma bonds.

mcqs.q: Why is the C=O bond polar, and where do the partial charges lie?
options: Oxygen is more electronegative, so carbon carries a partial positive charge and oxygen a partial negative charge
Carbon is more electronegative, so oxygen carries the partial positive charge
Both atoms carry partial positive charges
The bond is non-polar because the charges are equal
mcqs.why: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, so it pulls the shared electrons towards itself, leaving carbon partially positive and oxygen partially negative.

mcqs.q: How does the polarity of the C=O bond explain the reactions of aldehydes and ketones?
options: It makes them form hydrogen bonds like alcohols
It makes the oxygen attract nucleophiles
The partially positive carbonyl carbon is attacked by nucleophiles, giving nucleophilic addition reactions
It prevents any reaction at the carbonyl carbon
mcqs.why: Because the carbonyl carbon carries a partial positive charge, nucleophiles attack that carbon, which is why aldehydes and ketones characteristically undergo nucleophilic addition.

lessons.title: Preparations of Aldehydes and Ketones
lessons.notes_html:
Formaldehyde by Ozonolysis

Formaldehyde is obtained by the ozonolysis of ethene. Ethene reacts with ozone to form an unstable ozonide, which on hydrolysis with zinc and water breaks at the double bond: CH2=CH2 + O3 -> ozonide -> (Zn/H2O) 2HCHO + H2O. Each CH2 end of the double bond becomes one molecule of formaldehyde, and zinc prevents its further oxidation to formic acid.

Acetone by Hydration of Propyne

Water adds to propyne CH3-C triple bond CH according to Markownikov rule in the presence of H2SO4/HgSO4, giving an unstable enol CH3-C(OH)=CH2. This enol tautomerises to the more stable ketone, acetone CH3-CO-CH3.

Acetaldehyde by Hydration of Ethyne

HC triple bond CH + H2O -> CH3CHO in the presence of H2SO4/HgSO4. The major product is acetaldehyde (ethanal), formed through the unstable vinyl alcohol enol.

mcqs.q: Formaldehyde is prepared by the ozonolysis of which compound?
mcqs.why: Formaldehyde is obtained by ozonolysis of ethene: ethene reacts with ozone to form an ozonide which breaks at the double bond to give formaldehyde.

mcqs.q: In the ozonolysis preparation of formaldehyde, the ozonide is hydrolysed with which reagents?
mcqs.why: The ozonide is hydrolysed with zinc and water (Zn/H2O), which cleaves it at the double bond to give two molecules of formaldehyde.

mcqs.q: What is the role of zinc in the ozonolysis of ethene?
options: It oxidises formaldehyde to carbon dioxide
It prevents further oxidation of formaldehyde to formic acid
It converts ethene into ethane first
It acts as the source of ozone
mcqs.why: Zinc prevents the further oxidation of the formaldehyde formed to formic acid, so the product of ozonolysis is collected as formaldehyde.

mcqs.q: How many molecules of formaldehyde are formed from one molecule of ethene by ozonolysis?
mcqs.why: Two molecules are formed because each CH2 end of the ethene double bond becomes one molecule of formaldehyde when the ozonide is hydrolysed.

mcqs.q: Acetone is prepared by the hydration of which compound?
mcqs.why: Acetone is prepared by hydration of propyne, CH3-C triple bond CH, in the presence of H2SO4/HgSO4, through an unstable enol that tautomerises to acetone.

mcqs.q: Which catalyst is used for the hydration of propyne and of ethyne?
options: H2SO4 in the presence of HgSO4
mcqs.why: Hydration of alkynes to carbonyl compounds is carried out with water in the presence of H2SO4/HgSO4, for both propyne to acetone and ethyne to acetaldehyde.

mcqs.q: By which rule does water add to propyne during its hydration?
mcqs.why: Water adds to propyne according to the Markownikov rule, placing the -OH on the middle carbon and giving the enol CH3-C(OH)=CH2, which becomes acetone.

mcqs.q: What is the unstable enol first formed when water adds to propyne?
mcqs.why: The first product is the unstable enol CH3-C(OH)=CH2, formed by Markownikov addition of water to propyne, and it then tautomerises to acetone.

mcqs.q: How does the enol from propyne hydration change into acetone?
options: It is oxidised by chromic acid
It tautomerises to the more stable ketone, acetone
It loses water to form propyne again
mcqs.why: The enol tautomerises, shifting the double bond and the hydrogen, to give the more stable ketone acetone, CH3-CO-CH3.

mcqs.q: What is the major product of the hydration of ethyne in the presence of H2SO4/HgSO4?
mcqs.why: Hydration of ethyne gives acetaldehyde (ethanal) as the major product, formed through the unstable vinyl alcohol enol: HC triple bond CH + H2O gives CH3CHO.

lessons.title: Reactivity
lessons.notes_html:
Order of Reactivity

Formaldehyde is the most reactive carbonyl compound towards nucleophilic addition. It has two small hydrogen atoms on the carbonyl carbon, so there is almost no steric hindrance and no electron-donating alkyl group to reduce the positive charge on carbon; a nucleophile can therefore attack its carbonyl carbon most easily. In ketones two bulky alkyl groups donate electrons towards the carbonyl carbon, reducing its positive charge, and they also block the approach of the nucleophile sterically. The order of reactivity is: formaldehyde > other aldehydes > ketones, diethyl ketone and acetophenone being the least reactive of the common examples.

Factors Influencing Reactivity

Reactivity depends mainly on the charge on the carbonyl carbon and on steric hindrance around it. Electron-donating alkyl groups reduce the partial positive charge on carbon and make attack harder, and bulky groups near the carbonyl carbon block the approach of the nucleophile, so larger alkyl or aryl groups lower the reactivity, as in acetophenone. Strong nucleophiles and base catalysis favour addition with weak carbonyl compounds, while acid catalysis, by protonating the oxygen, increases the positive charge on carbon and helps weak nucleophiles to attack.

Acid-Catalysed and Base-Catalysed Addition

In base-catalysed addition, used with strong nucleophiles, the nucleophile Nu- attacks the carbonyl carbon first, forming an alkoxide intermediate, which then takes a proton from water to give the addition product, e.g. HCHO + HCN -> HCH(OH)CN in basic medium. In acid-catalysed addition, used with weak nucleophiles like water, alcohols and ammonia, the acid first protonates the carbonyl oxygen, which increases the positive charge on carbon and makes it more attractive for the weak nucleophile. The nucleophile then attacks the carbon, and loss of a proton gives the final product such as a hemiacetal. Thus acid activates the carbonyl compound, while base activates or supplies a strong nucleophile.

mcqs.q: Which compound is the most reactive towards nucleophilic addition?
mcqs.why: Formaldehyde is the most reactive because its carbonyl carbon carries two small hydrogen atoms, giving almost no steric hindrance and no alkyl group to reduce its positive charge.

mcqs.q: Why can a nucleophile attack the carbonyl carbon of formaldehyde most easily?
options: Its carbonyl carbon carries a negative charge
Its two small hydrogen atoms cause almost no steric hindrance and do not reduce the positive charge on carbon
Its alkyl groups push the nucleophile towards the carbon
It contains a phenyl group that attracts nucleophiles
mcqs.why: Formaldehyde has two small hydrogens on the carbonyl carbon, so there is almost no steric hindrance and no electron-donating alkyl group, leaving carbon strongly positive and easy to attack.

mcqs.q: What is the correct order of reactivity towards nucleophilic addition?
mcqs.why: The order is formaldehyde > other aldehydes > ketones, because reactivity falls as alkyl or aryl groups donate electrons and block the approach of the nucleophile.

mcqs.q: Which compounds are the least reactive of the common examples towards nucleophilic addition?
mcqs.why: Diethyl ketone and acetophenone are the least reactive common examples because their bulky alkyl and aryl groups donate electrons and hinder the nucleophile sterically.

mcqs.q: How do electron-donating alkyl groups affect the reactivity of a ketone?
options: They increase the positive charge on the carbonyl carbon
They have no effect on reactivity
They reduce the partial positive charge on the carbonyl carbon, making nucleophilic attack harder
mcqs.why: Alkyl groups donate electrons towards the carbonyl carbon and reduce its partial positive charge, so a nucleophile is attracted less strongly and attack becomes harder.

mcqs.q: Apart from the charge on carbon, what other factor lowers reactivity when groups near the carbonyl carbon are bulky?
options: They increase the solubility in water
They form hydrogen bonds with the nucleophile
They block the approach of the nucleophile, which is steric hindrance
mcqs.why: Bulky alkyl or aryl groups cause steric hindrance by physically blocking the approach of the nucleophile to the carbonyl carbon, as in acetophenone, so reactivity falls.

mcqs.q: In acid-catalysed addition, how does the acid activate the carbonyl compound?
options: It protonates the carbonyl oxygen, increasing the positive charge on carbon
It reduces the carbonyl group to CH2
mcqs.why: The acid first protonates the carbonyl oxygen, which increases the positive charge on the carbon and makes it more attractive for a weak nucleophile to attack.

mcqs.q: What is the first step in base-catalysed nucleophilic addition?
options: The carbonyl oxygen is protonated by an acid
The nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon, forming an alkoxide intermediate
A proton is lost from the final product
mcqs.why: In base-catalysed addition the nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon first, forming an alkoxide intermediate, which then takes a proton from water to give the product.

mcqs.q: In base-catalysed addition, how is the final product obtained from the alkoxide intermediate?
options: It is oxidised by chromic acid
It reacts with another carbonyl molecule
It takes a proton from water to give the addition product
mcqs.why: The alkoxide intermediate takes a proton from water to give the neutral addition product, for example HCHO + HCN gives HCH(OH)CN in basic medium.

mcqs.q: Which pairing of catalysis with nucleophile type is correct?
options: Acid catalysis is used with strong nucleophiles only
Base catalysis is used with weak nucleophiles like water
Strong nucleophiles favour base catalysis, while acid catalysis helps weak nucleophiles such as water, alcohols and ammonia
Neither acid nor base affects nucleophilic addition
mcqs.why: Strong nucleophiles work under base catalysis, while weak nucleophiles like water, alcohols and ammonia need acid catalysis, because protonating the oxygen makes the carbon more positive.

lessons.title: Reactions of Aldehydes and Ketones
lessons.notes_html:
Reactions of Acetaldehyde

  • With chromic acid: CH3CHO + [O] -> CH3COOH (H2CrO4); acetaldehyde is oxidised to acetic acid.
  • With LiAlH4: CH3CHO + 2[H] -> CH3CH2OH; it is reduced to ethanol, a primary alcohol.
  • With Zn-Hg and conc. HCl (Clemmensen reduction): CH3CHO + 4[H] -> CH3CH3 + H2O; the C=O is reduced to CH2 and ethane is formed.
  • With NaBH4: CH3CHO + 2[H] -> CH3CH2OH; the major product is ethanol.

Reduction Reactions

Clemmensen reduction is the conversion of aldehydes and ketones into alkanes by zinc amalgam Zn-Hg and concentrated HCl under strongly acidic conditions; the carbonyl group C=O is completely reduced to a CH2 group, for example CH3CHO -> CH3CH3. Wolf-Kishner reduction also gives alkanes but uses hydrazine NH2NH2 and strong base KOH instead. With LiAlH4, ketones are reduced to secondary alcohols: the hydride adds to the carbonyl carbon and R-CO-R gives R-CHOH-R, in which the -OH is attached to a carbon bonded to two other carbons.

Oxidation: Aldehydes versus Ketones

An aldehyde has a hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon which is easily removed during oxidation to a carboxylic acid, but a ketone has no such hydrogen and oxidation requires breaking a strong C-C bond, so aldehydes oxidise much faster and even with mild oxidising agents. Aldehydes are oxidised by Tollens reagent, Fehling solution and Benedict solution to a carboxylic acid with the same number of carbon atoms, e.g. CH3CHO -> CH3COOH. Ketones do not react with these mild reagents and are oxidised only by strong oxidising agents like acidified K2Cr2O7 with C-C bond cleavage, giving carboxylic acids with fewer carbons: CH3COCH3 + 4[O] -> CH3COOH + HCOOH (formic acid further oxidises to CO2 and H2O), the major carboxylic acid product being acetic acid.

Tests that Distinguish Aldehydes from Ketones

Tollens reagent is ammoniacal silver nitrate [Ag(NH3)2]OH. On warming with an aldehyde it is reduced to metallic silver, which deposits as a bright silver mirror on the test tube: RCHO + 2[Ag(NH3)2]OH -> RCOOH + 2Ag + 4NH3 + H2O; ketones give no mirror. Formaldehyde, HCHO, gives the silver mirror test with Tollens reagent. Fehling solution is an alkaline solution of copper sulphate complexed with tartrate. On heating with an aldehyde the blue Cu2+ is reduced to a red precipitate of cuprous oxide Cu2O: RCHO + 2Cu(OH)2 + NaOH -> RCOONa + Cu2O + 3H2O; ketones give no red precipitate.

Nucleophilic Addition Reactions of Formaldehyde

  • With hydrogen cyanide: HCHO + HCN -> CH2(OH)CN, the cyanohydrin hydroxyacetonitrile (glycolonitrile), in the presence of a base catalyst.
  • With a primary alcohol: HCHO + 2ROH -> CH2(OR)2 + H2O under acid catalysis, first a hemiacetal and then an acetal.
  • With methyl magnesium bromide: HCHO + CH3MgBr -> CH3CH2OMgBr -> (H2O/H+) CH3CH2OH, ethanol, a primary alcohol with one extra carbon.
  • With ammonia: formaldehyde does not give a simple imine; six molecules condense with four of ammonia to form hexamethylenetetramine (urotropine): 6HCHO + 4NH3 -> (CH2)6N4 + 6H2O.

Four Differences between Aldehydes and Ketones

  • An aldehyde has the carbonyl group at the end of the chain with at least one hydrogen attached (R-CHO), while a ketone has it in the middle, attached to two carbon groups (R-CO-R).
  • Aldehydes are easily oxidised to carboxylic acids by mild oxidising agents, while ketones resist mild oxidising agents and need strong ones.
  • Aldehydes give the Tollens silver mirror test and the Fehling red precipitate test, while ketones give neither test.
  • Aldehydes are more reactive towards nucleophilic addition than ketones because they have less steric hindrance and a more positively charged carbonyl carbon.

mcqs.q: What is formed when acetaldehyde is treated with chromic acid, H2CrO4?
mcqs.why: Chromic acid oxidises acetaldehyde to acetic acid: CH3CHO + [O] gives CH3COOH, keeping the same number of carbon atoms.

mcqs.q: What is the major product when acetaldehyde is reduced with LiAlH4?
mcqs.why: LiAlH4 reduces acetaldehyde to ethanol, a primary alcohol: CH3CHO + 2[H] gives CH3CH2OH, because the -OH ends up on a carbon bonded to only one other carbon.

mcqs.q: What is formed when acetaldehyde undergoes Clemmensen reduction with Zn-Hg and concentrated HCl?
mcqs.why: Clemmensen reduction completely reduces the C=O of acetaldehyde to CH2, giving ethane: CH3CHO + 4[H] gives CH3CH3 + H2O.

mcqs.q: Which reagents are used in Wolf-Kishner reduction of a carbonyl compound to an alkane?
options: Hydrazine, NH2NH2, and strong base KOH
mcqs.why: Wolf-Kishner reduction also converts aldehydes and ketones to alkanes, but it uses hydrazine NH2NH2 with strong base KOH instead of the acidic Zn-Hg/HCl of Clemmensen reduction.

mcqs.q: Ketones are reduced by LiAlH4 to which type of alcohol?
mcqs.why: LiAlH4 reduces a ketone R-CO-R to R-CHOH-R, a secondary alcohol, because the -OH is attached to a carbon bonded to two other carbons.

mcqs.q: What is the major carboxylic acid product when acetone is oxidised with acidified K2Cr2O7?
mcqs.why: Strong oxidation cleaves acetone with C-C bond breaking: CH3COCH3 + 4[O] gives CH3COOH + HCOOH, so the major carboxylic acid product is acetic acid.

mcqs.q: What is Tollens reagent, and what does it give with an aldehyde?
options: Fehling solution, giving a red precipitate
Ammoniacal silver nitrate, giving a bright silver mirror
Benedict solution, giving a blue precipitate
Chromic acid, giving a green colour
mcqs.why: Tollens reagent is ammoniacal silver nitrate [Ag(NH3)2]OH; an aldehyde reduces it to metallic silver, which deposits as a bright silver mirror, while ketones give no mirror.

mcqs.q: What is observed when an aldehyde is heated with Fehling solution?
options: A red precipitate of cuprous oxide, Cu2O, forms
mcqs.why: With Fehling solution the blue Cu2+ is reduced by the aldehyde to a red precipitate of cuprous oxide Cu2O; ketones give no red precipitate, so the test distinguishes aldehydes from ketones.

mcqs.q: What does formaldehyde form when it reacts with hydrogen cyanide in the presence of a base catalyst?
mcqs.why: Formaldehyde adds HCN to form its cyanohydrin, hydroxyacetonitrile (glycolonitrile): HCHO + HCN gives CH2(OH)CN, a nucleophilic addition product.

mcqs.q: What is obtained, after hydrolysis, when formaldehyde reacts with methyl magnesium bromide?
options: Ethanol, a primary alcohol with one extra carbon
mcqs.why: Formaldehyde with CH3MgBr gives CH3CH2OMgBr, which on hydrolysis with H2O/H+ gives ethanol, a primary alcohol containing one carbon more than formaldehyde.

chapters.title: Carbonyl Compounds II - Carboxylic Acid and Functional Derivatives

lessons.title: Physical Properties
lessons.notes_html:
Boiling Point

Carboxylic acids have unusually high boiling points, higher than alcohols of similar mass, because their molecules associate into cyclic dimers through two strong hydrogen bonds. The acids are more polar than alcohols and form very strong hydrogen bonds between two molecules, so a large amount of heat energy is needed to break these bonds and boil the acid. Acetic acid (boiling point 118 C) therefore boils higher than ethanol (78 C), acetaldehyde (20 C) and ethyl chloride (12 C). Alcohols form weaker, single hydrogen-bonded associations, hence acids of comparable mass boil higher than alcohols.

Solubility

The lower carboxylic acids up to four carbons are miscible or highly soluble in water because the -COOH group forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules. As the alkyl chain grows, the non-polar hydrocarbon part dominates, hydrogen bonding becomes less effective, and solubility falls rapidly, so higher fatty acids are practically insoluble in water though soluble in organic solvents.

mcqs.q: Why do carboxylic acids have unusually high boiling points?
options: Their molecules associate into cyclic dimers through two strong hydrogen bonds
They react with water on heating
mcqs.why: Carboxylic acids form cyclic dimers held by two strong hydrogen bonds between two molecules, so a large amount of heat is needed to break these bonds before the acid can boil.

mcqs.q: What is the boiling point of acetic acid?
mcqs.why: Acetic acid boils at 118 C, higher than ethanol at 78 C, acetaldehyde at 20 C and ethyl chloride at 12 C, because of its strong hydrogen-bonded dimers.

mcqs.q: Which of the following has the highest boiling point?
mcqs.why: Acetic acid has the highest boiling point, 118 C, compared with ethanol 78 C, acetaldehyde 20 C and ethyl chloride 12 C, because its molecules pair into strongly hydrogen-bonded dimers.

mcqs.q: Ethanol boils at 78 C. Which compound in the notes boils at only 12 C?
mcqs.why: Ethyl chloride boils at 12 C, the lowest of the compared compounds, while acetaldehyde boils at 20 C, ethanol at 78 C and acetic acid at 118 C.

mcqs.q: Which pair of boiling points from the notes is correct?
options: Acetaldehyde 78 C and ethyl chloride 118 C
Acetaldehyde 12 C and ethyl chloride 20 C
Acetaldehyde 20 C and ethyl chloride 12 C
Acetaldehyde 118 C and ethyl chloride 78 C
mcqs.why: The correct pair is acetaldehyde at 20 C and ethyl chloride at 12 C; ethanol is 78 C and acetic acid, held in dimers, is much higher at 118 C.

mcqs.q: The lower carboxylic acids are miscible or highly soluble in water up to how many carbon atoms?
mcqs.why: Lower carboxylic acids up to four carbons are miscible or highly soluble in water because the -COOH group forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules.

mcqs.q: Why are the lower carboxylic acids soluble in water?
options: The -COOH group forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules
mcqs.why: The lower acids dissolve because the -COOH group hydrogen-bonds with water, and in the lower members this polar group dominates over the small hydrocarbon part.

mcqs.q: What happens to the solubility of a carboxylic acid as its alkyl chain grows?
options: It stays the same at all chain lengths
It turns the acid into an alcohol
It falls rapidly as the non-polar hydrocarbon part dominates
mcqs.why: As the alkyl chain grows, the non-polar hydrocarbon part dominates and hydrogen bonding becomes less effective, so solubility in water falls rapidly.

mcqs.q: How do higher fatty acids behave in water?
options: They are practically insoluble in water
They are completely miscible with water
They dissolve better than formic acid
mcqs.why: Higher fatty acids are practically insoluble in water because their long non-polar chains dominate, although they are soluble in organic solvents.

mcqs.q: In which solvent do higher fatty acids dissolve, even though they do not dissolve in water?
mcqs.why: Higher fatty acids dissolve in organic solvents, which suit their dominant non-polar hydrocarbon chains, even though they are practically insoluble in water.

lessons.title: Structure
lessons.notes_html: A carboxylic acid contains the carboxyl group -COOH, which is a combination of a carbonyl group C=O and a hydroxyl group -OH on the same carbon. This carbon is sp2 hybridised and forms three sigma bonds - to R, to =O oxygen and to -OH oxygen - which arrange themselves in one plane at about 120 degrees to each other, so the -COOH structure is trigonal planar. The lone pairs on oxygen conjugate with the carbonyl pi bond, giving resonance in the group. Because of the polar C=O and the -OH, two molecules join by two hydrogen bonds into a cyclic dimer, which explains the high boiling points and association of carboxylic acids.

mcqs.q: The carboxyl group -COOH is a combination of which two groups on the same carbon?
options: A carbonyl group C=O and a hydroxyl group -OH
A carbonyl group and an amino group
An ether group and a hydroxyl group
mcqs.why: The carboxyl group combines a carbonyl group C=O and a hydroxyl group -OH on the same carbon, giving the -COOH group of a carboxylic acid.

mcqs.q: What is the hybridisation of the carboxyl carbon?
mcqs.why: The carboxyl carbon is sp2 hybridised, forming three sigma bonds in one plane at about 120 degrees to each other, so the group is trigonal planar.

mcqs.q: The carboxyl carbon forms three sigma bonds. To which atoms or groups are they made?
options: To R and two hydrogen atoms
To two carbons and one hydrogen
To R, to the =O oxygen and to the -OH oxygen
mcqs.why: The three sigma bonds of the carboxyl carbon go to R, to the double-bonded =O oxygen and to the -OH oxygen, all arranged in one plane at about 120 degrees.

mcqs.q: What are the approximate bond angles in the -COOH group?
mcqs.why: The three groups around the sp2 carboxyl carbon arrange themselves in one plane at about 120 degrees to each other, giving a trigonal planar structure.

mcqs.q: What is the shape of the -COOH structure?
mcqs.why: The -COOH structure is trigonal planar because the sp2 carboxyl carbon has its three sigma-bonded groups in one plane at about 120 degrees.

mcqs.q: Resonance in the carboxyl group arises because of which effect?
options: The alkyl group donates electrons into the ring
Two hydrogen bonds join the molecules
The carbon forms four sigma bonds
The lone pairs on oxygen conjugate with the carbonyl pi bond
mcqs.why: Resonance occurs in the carboxyl group because the lone pairs on oxygen conjugate with the carbonyl pi bond, spreading the electron density over the group.

mcqs.q: How do two carboxylic acid molecules join to form a dimer?
options: By one weak van der Waals force
By two hydrogen bonds, forming a cyclic dimer
mcqs.why: Two acid molecules join by two hydrogen bonds into a cyclic dimer, which explains the high boiling points and association of carboxylic acids.

mcqs.q: What type of dimer do carboxylic acid molecules form?
mcqs.why: The dimer is cyclic: the polar C=O and -OH groups of two molecules are linked by two hydrogen bonds in a ring-like arrangement.

mcqs.q: Which properties of carboxylic acids are explained by their dimer formation?
options: Their fruity smell and sweet taste
Their high boiling points and association
mcqs.why: Dimer formation explains the high boiling points and association of carboxylic acids, because extra energy is needed to break the two hydrogen bonds holding each pair together.

mcqs.q: Which set correctly lists the groups attached to the carboxyl carbon?
mcqs.why: The carboxyl carbon is attached to R, to the =O oxygen and to the -OH oxygen, which is exactly the combination that makes the -COOH group.

lessons.title: Acidity
lessons.notes_html: Carboxylic acids turn blue litmus red, react with metals, carbonates and alkalis, and lose the hydroxyl proton in water: RCOOH + H2O -> RCOO- + H3O+. They are stronger acids than alcohols and phenols because the carboxylate ion RCOO- is stabilised by resonance, the negative charge being shared equally by both oxygens, so the proton is lost easily. They are much stronger acids than ethanol, but weak acids compared with mineral acids like HCl, HNO3 and H2SO4, because their ionisation is only partial (acetic acid is only a few percent ionised) - the equilibrium lies to the left, whereas mineral acids ionise almost completely in water.

mcqs.q: What do carboxylic acids do to blue litmus?
mcqs.why: Carboxylic acids turn blue litmus red, showing their acidic nature, and they also react with metals, carbonates and alkalis.

mcqs.q: When a carboxylic acid dissolves in water, which ions are formed?
mcqs.why: The acid loses its hydroxyl proton to water: RCOOH + H2O gives RCOO- + H3O+, so the carboxylate ion and hydronium ion are formed.

mcqs.q: Which proton does a carboxylic acid lose when it ionises in water?
options: The hydroxyl proton of the -COOH group
A proton from the alkyl chain
A proton from the carbonyl oxygen
mcqs.why: The proton lost is the hydroxyl proton of the -COOH group, leaving the resonance-stabilised carboxylate ion RCOO-.

mcqs.q: Why are carboxylic acids stronger acids than alcohols and phenols?
options: They are completely ionised in water
The carboxylate ion RCOO- is stabilised by resonance, with the negative charge shared equally by both oxygens
mcqs.why: The carboxylate ion is stabilised by resonance, its negative charge being shared equally by both oxygens, so the proton is lost easily and the acid is stronger than alcohols and phenols.

mcqs.q: Why is a carboxylic acid a much stronger acid than ethanol?
options: Ethanol has a longer carbon chain
The carboxylate ion formed is resonance-stabilised, while the ethoxide ion from ethanol is not
Carboxylic acids ionise completely like HCl
mcqs.why: A carboxylic acid is stronger than ethanol because the RCOO- ion left after losing H+ is stabilised by resonance, whereas the ethoxide ion from ethanol has no such stabilisation.

mcqs.q: How do carboxylic acids compare in strength with mineral acids such as HCl, HNO3 and H2SO4?
options: They are weak acids compared with mineral acids, because their ionisation is only partial
They are stronger than all mineral acids
They are exactly equal in strength
They are not acids at all in water
mcqs.why: Carboxylic acids are weak compared with mineral acids: they ionise only partially in water, whereas HCl, HNO3 and H2SO4 ionise almost completely.

mcqs.q: How much is acetic acid ionised in water?
options: It does not ionise at all
It is only a few percent ionised
mcqs.why: Acetic acid is only a few percent ionised in water, so its ionisation equilibrium lies to the left and it behaves as a weak acid.

mcqs.q: For the ionisation of acetic acid in water, where does the equilibrium lie?
options: It changes into an esterification equilibrium
mcqs.why: The equilibrium lies to the left because acetic acid ionises only partially, with only a few percent of its molecules forming ions in water.

mcqs.q: How do mineral acids such as HCl and H2SO4 behave in water?
options: They ionise almost completely in water
They do not ionise at all
They ionise less than acetic acid
They form dimers and do not release protons
mcqs.why: Mineral acids ionise almost completely in water, which is why they are much stronger acids than carboxylic acids, whose ionisation is only partial.

mcqs.q: Which reactions show the acidic behaviour of carboxylic acids?
options: They react only with other acids
They react with metals, carbonates and alkalis
They do not react with bases
mcqs.why: Carboxylic acids show acidic behaviour by turning blue litmus red and by reacting with metals, carbonates and alkalis, as typical acids do.

lessons.title: Preparations of Carboxylic Acids and their Derivatives
lessons.notes_html:
Preparation of Carboxylic Acids

  • Carbonation of Grignard reagent: a Grignard reagent RMgX is treated with dry carbon dioxide (dry ice); the reagent adds to CO2 and the adduct on hydrolysis with dilute acid gives a carboxylic acid with one carbon more than R: RMgX + CO2 -> RCOOMgX -> (H3O+) RCOOH. For example, ethyl magnesium bromide gives propanoic acid: C2H5MgBr + CO2 -> C2H5COOMgBr -> (H3O+) C2H5COOH.
  • Hydrolysis of alkyl nitriles: an alkyl nitrile RCN is heated with dilute acid or alkali; it hydrolyses first to an amide and then to the acid: RCN + 2H2O -> (H+/heat) RCOOH + NH3.
  • Oxidation of primary alcohols: a primary alcohol is oxidised with a strong oxidising agent like acidified K2Cr2O7 or KMnO4, passing through the aldehyde stage to the acid with the same number of carbons: RCH2OH -> [O] RCHO -> [O] RCOOH; for example ethanol gives acetic acid.
  • Oxidation of alkyl benzenes: alkyl benzenes with a benzylic carbon are oxidised by strong oxidising agents like alkaline KMnO4 or acidified K2Cr2O7 to benzoic acid, whatever the length of the side chain: C6H5CH2CH3 -> [O] C6H5COOH, and toluene likewise gives benzoic acid: C6H5CH3 -> [O] C6H5COOH.

Formation of the Functional Derivatives

All functional derivatives of carboxylic acids are formed by replacing the -OH group of -COOH by another group: replacement by Cl gives an acyl halide RCOCl, by NH2 gives an amide RCONH2, by OR gives an ester and by OCOR gives an anhydride. Acyl halides are prepared using PCl3, PCl5 or thionyl chloride SOCl2, for example RCOOH + SOCl2 -> RCOCl + SO2 + HCl. Hydrochloric acid HCl alone cannot do this replacement, because it is not a chlorinating agent for the hydroxyl group.

mcqs.q: In the carbonation of a Grignard reagent, the carboxylic acid obtained has how many carbons compared with R?
mcqs.why: Carbonation adds the CO2 carbon to R, so the acid formed, RCOOH, has one carbon more than the R group of the Grignard reagent RMgX.

mcqs.q: Ethyl magnesium bromide is treated with dry CO2 and the adduct is hydrolysed with dilute acid. What acid is formed?
mcqs.why: Ethyl magnesium bromide gives propanoic acid: C2H5MgBr + CO2 gives C2H5COOMgBr, which on hydrolysis gives C2H5COOH, one carbon more than ethyl.

mcqs.q: An alkyl nitrile RCN is heated with dilute acid or alkali. Through which intermediate does it hydrolyse to the acid?
mcqs.why: Nitrile hydrolysis passes first through an amide stage and then gives the acid: RCN + 2H2O under H+/heat gives RCOOH + NH3.

mcqs.q: What are the products of the complete hydrolysis of an alkyl nitrile RCN with water under acid and heat?
mcqs.why: Complete hydrolysis of RCN with 2H2O under H+/heat gives the carboxylic acid RCOOH and ammonia NH3, passing through the amide on the way.

mcqs.q: Oxidation of a primary alcohol to a carboxylic acid passes through which stage, and how does the carbon count change?
options: Through a ketone stage, gaining one carbon
Through an ether stage, losing one carbon
Directly to the acid with no intermediate
Through the aldehyde stage, keeping the same number of carbons
mcqs.why: A primary alcohol is oxidised through the aldehyde stage to the acid with the same number of carbons: RCH2OH gives RCHO and then RCOOH, for example ethanol gives acetic acid.

mcqs.q: Which acid is obtained when ethanol is oxidised with a strong oxidising agent such as acidified K2Cr2O7?
mcqs.why: Ethanol is a primary alcohol, so strong oxidation takes it through acetaldehyde to acetic acid, keeping the same two carbon atoms.

mcqs.q: What is formed when ethylbenzene is oxidised with a strong oxidising agent such as alkaline KMnO4?
mcqs.why: Alkyl benzenes with a benzylic carbon are oxidised to benzoic acid whatever the length of the side chain: C6H5CH2CH3 gives C6H5COOH.

mcqs.q: Which replacement in the -COOH group gives an amide, an ester and an anhydride respectively?
options: NH2 replaces -OH for an ester, OR for an amide
NH2 gives an amide, OR gives an ester and OCOR gives an anhydride
OR gives an anhydride and OCOR gives an ester
mcqs.why: All derivatives come from replacing the -OH of -COOH: NH2 gives an amide RCONH2, OR gives an ester, and OCOR gives an anhydride.

mcqs.q: Which derivative is formed when the -OH group of a carboxylic acid is replaced by Cl?
mcqs.why: Replacing the -OH of -COOH by Cl gives an acyl halide RCOCl, for example RCOOH + SOCl2 gives RCOCl + SO2 + HCl.

mcqs.q: Which reagent cannot be used to prepare an acyl halide from a carboxylic acid?
mcqs.why: HCl alone cannot prepare an acyl halide because it is not a chlorinating agent for the hydroxyl group; PCl3, PCl5 and thionyl chloride SOCl2 are used instead.

lessons.title: Reactions of Carboxylic Acids and their Derivatives
lessons.notes_html:
The Four Derivatives from Acetic Acid

  • Acetyl chloride (acyl halide): CH3COOH + SOCl2 -> CH3COCl + SO2 + HCl
  • Acetic anhydride (acid anhydride): 2CH3COOH -> (P2O5/heat) (CH3CO)2O + H2O. On strong heating, or with a dehydrating agent like P2O5, two molecules of acetic acid lose one molecule of water and join through an oxygen atom.
  • Ethyl acetate (ester): CH3COOH + C2H5OH -> (conc. H2SO4) CH3COOC2H5 + H2O. This is esterification; the ester formed has a sweet fruity smell.
  • Acetamide (amide): CH3COOH + NH3 -> CH3COONH4 -> (heat) CH3CONH2 + H2O. The acid first forms an ammonium salt, which on heating loses water to give the amide.

Reactions of the Derivatives

An ester is converted back into a carboxylic acid by hydrolysis: heating with dilute acid or alkali; with alkali the salt is formed, which on acidification gives the acid: CH3COOC2H5 + H2O -> (H+/heat) CH3COOH + C2H5OH. Esters give fruits their pleasant odours: the characteristic fruity smell and flavour of pineapple is due to the ester ethyl butanoate, and many fruits get their odours from such low molar mass esters.

Formation of Formic Acid by Oxidation

Formaldehyde is fully oxidised by a mixture of potassium dichromate and sulphuric acid, first to formic acid and then to carbon dioxide and water: HCHO -> (K2Cr2O7/H2SO4) HCOOH -> CO2 + H2O, and the orange dichromate turns green.

Natural Sources of Carboxylic Acids

  • Formic acid (methanoic acid, HCOOH): occurs in the sting of bees, from where it enters the skin and causes pain and irritation (according to the book), and is also associated with ant venom.
  • Acetic acid: present in vinegar, formed by the fermentation of ethanol in air.
  • Valeric acid (pentanoic acid): occurs in the valerian plant root, from which it takes its name.
  • Caproic acid (hexanoic acid): occurs in goat milk and goat fat (capra means goat) and in small amounts in other animal fats. Counting the carboxyl carbon, its formula is C5H11COOH, that is C6H12O2 in total.

Commercial Applications

Carboxylic acids are used as preservatives, flavouring agents and acidity regulators in the food industry, for example acetic acid as vinegar and benzoic acid as a preservative. They are starting materials for making soaps (salts of long-chain fatty acids), detergents, perfumes and esters used as solvents and flavours. They are also used in making medicines such as aspirin, in the manufacture of polymers like nylon and polyester, and in the rubber, textile dyeing and leather industries.

mcqs.q: What are the products when acetic acid reacts with thionyl chloride, SOCl2?
mcqs.why: Acetic acid with SOCl2 gives acetyl chloride: CH3COOH + SOCl2 gives CH3COCl + SO2 + HCl, the -OH being replaced by Cl.

mcqs.q: How is acetic anhydride formed from acetic acid?
options: One molecule of acetic acid reacts with ethanol
Acetic acid reacts with ammonia and is heated
Two molecules of acetic acid lose one molecule of water on strong heating or with P2O5
mcqs.why: Two molecules of acetic acid lose one water molecule on strong heating or with the dehydrating agent P2O5, joining through oxygen to give acetic anhydride, (CH3CO)2O.

mcqs.q: Acetic acid reacts with ethanol in the presence of concentrated H2SO4. What is this reaction and its product?
mcqs.why: This is esterification: CH3COOH + C2H5OH under conc. H2SO4 gives CH3COOC2H5 (ethyl acetate) + H2O, and the ester has a sweet fruity smell.

mcqs.q: How is acetamide prepared from acetic acid and ammonia?
options: The acid first forms ammonium acetate, which on heating loses water to give acetamide
The acid reacts directly to give ethyl acetate
Ammonia reduces the acid to ethanol
Ammonia converts the acid into acetic anhydride
mcqs.why: Acetic acid first forms the ammonium salt CH3COONH4 with ammonia, and this salt on heating loses water to give acetamide, CH3CONH2.

mcqs.q: An ester such as ethyl acetate is heated with dilute acid. What does hydrolysis give?
mcqs.why: Ester hydrolysis reverses esterification: CH3COOC2H5 + H2O under H+/heat gives CH3COOH + C2H5OH; with alkali the salt forms first and acidification then gives the acid.

mcqs.q: The characteristic fruity smell and flavour of pineapple is due to which compound?
mcqs.why: Pineapple owes its characteristic fruity smell and flavour to the ester ethyl butanoate; many fruits get their pleasant odours from such low molar mass esters.

mcqs.q: What happens when formaldehyde is treated with a mixture of potassium dichromate and sulphuric acid?
options: It is oxidised first to formic acid and then to carbon dioxide and water
mcqs.why: Formaldehyde is fully oxidised by K2Cr2O7/H2SO4, first to formic acid HCOOH and then to CO2 + H2O, and the orange dichromate turns green.

mcqs.q: According to the book, formic acid occurs naturally in which source?
options: The sting of bees, and it is also associated with ant venom
mcqs.why: Formic acid (methanoic acid, HCOOH) occurs in the sting of bees, from where it enters the skin and causes pain and irritation, and it is also associated with ant venom.

mcqs.q: Valeric acid (pentanoic acid) takes its name from, and occurs in, which source?
options: Goat milk, because capra means goat
mcqs.why: Valeric acid occurs in the valerian plant root, from which it takes its name; caproic acid is the one linked with goats, and acetic acid with vinegar.

mcqs.q: What is the formula of caproic acid, counting the carboxyl carbon?
options: C4H9COOH, that is C5H10O2 in total
C6H13COOH, that is C7H14O2 in total
C5H11COOH, that is C6H12O2 in total
C7H15COOH, that is C8H16O2 in total
mcqs.why: Caproic acid is hexanoic acid: counting the carboxyl carbon its formula is C5H11COOH, which is C6H12O2 in total, and it occurs in goat milk and goat fat.

lessons.title: Carbohydrates
lessons.notes_html:
Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes and ketones, or substances that yield such compounds on hydrolysis; sugars such as glucose, fructose and sucrose belong to this class. They are the main source of energy for the body, with sources like rice, potato, wheat and barley.

Classification on the Basis of Structure

  • Monosaccharides: a single sugar unit, cannot be hydrolysed further, e.g. glucose, fructose and galactose.
  • Disaccharides: two units, e.g. sucrose, lactose and maltose. Sucrose (table sugar) is made of glucose and fructose.
  • Oligosaccharides: 3 to 10 units, e.g. kestose and melezitose.
  • Polysaccharides: more than 10 units, e.g. starch, cellulose and glycogen. Starch is made of very many glucose units joined together and is used as energy storage in plants.

Role of the Common Sugars in Health

  • Glucose: the immediate source of energy for cells and the normal sugar of blood; its level is controlled by insulin, and its failure leads to diabetes while its shortage causes weakness.
  • Fructose: the sweetest natural sugar, taken from sweet fruits such as grapes, apples, mangoes and dates and from honey; it is metabolised in the liver and provides energy, but excess intake burdens the liver. Table sugar sucrose also gives fructose on hydrolysis.
  • Sucrose: the common table sugar from sugarcane and beet, hydrolysed to glucose and fructose and supplying quick energy, though excess causes obesity and tooth decay.
  • Lactose: the milk sugar, obtained only from milk and milk products such as curd and cheese; it provides energy to infants and helps absorption of calcium, but people lacking the enzyme lactase cannot digest it properly (lactose intolerance). On digestion it is hydrolysed to glucose and galactose.

Dietary Importance

Carbohydrates are the main and quickest source of energy for our tissues and organs; glucose is the immediate fuel, especially for the brain, and 1 g gives about 4 kcal. They spare proteins from being used as fuel, store extra energy as glycogen in liver and muscles and as starch-rich foods, and provide dietary fibre (cellulose) that aids digestion and bowel movement.

mcqs.q: Carbohydrates are best defined as which type of compounds?
options: Esters of fatty acids and alcohols
Polyhydroxy aldehydes and ketones, or substances yielding them on hydrolysis
Inorganic elements needed in small amounts
mcqs.why: Carbohydrates are polyhydroxy aldehydes and ketones, or substances that yield such compounds on hydrolysis, as with glucose, fructose and sucrose.

mcqs.q: Which sugar is a monosaccharide that cannot be hydrolysed further?
mcqs.why: Glucose is a single sugar unit, so it is a monosaccharide and cannot be hydrolysed into a simpler sugar.

mcqs.q: Sucrose, the common table sugar, is made up of which two units?
mcqs.why: Sucrose is a disaccharide made of glucose and fructose, and on hydrolysis it gives these two monosaccharides.

mcqs.q: Oligosaccharides contain how many sugar units?
mcqs.why: Oligosaccharides contain 3 to 10 sugar units, as in kestose and melezitose, between disaccharides and polysaccharides.

mcqs.q: Starch is classified as a polysaccharide because it is:
options: Made of two glucose units only
Made of very many glucose units joined together
mcqs.why: Starch consists of very many glucose units joined together, more than ten, so it is a polysaccharide used for energy storage in plants.

mcqs.q: The level of glucose in the blood is normally controlled by which hormone?
mcqs.why: Insulin controls the blood glucose level; failure of this control leads to diabetes, while shortage of glucose causes weakness.

mcqs.q: Which sugar is described as the sweetest natural sugar and is metabolised in the liver?
mcqs.why: Fructose is the sweetest natural sugar, obtained from fruits and honey, and it is metabolised in the liver to provide energy.

mcqs.q: On digestion, lactose is hydrolysed into which pair of sugars?
mcqs.why: Lactose, the milk sugar, is hydrolysed on digestion to glucose and galactose; people lacking lactase cannot digest it properly.

mcqs.q: How much energy is obtained from 1 g of carbohydrate?
mcqs.why: 1 g of carbohydrate gives about 4 kcal, making carbohydrates the main and quickest source of energy for tissues and organs.

mcqs.q: Dietary fibre that aids digestion and bowel movement is provided by:
mcqs.why: Cellulose acts as dietary fibre; it aids digestion and bowel movement even though carbohydrates mainly supply energy.

lessons.title: Proteins
lessons.notes_html:
Proteins are natural condensation polymers whose building blocks are alpha amino acids. According to the book, there are 22 alpha amino acids in total that take part in making proteins in living organisms; some can be made by the body itself while the essential ones must be supplied through diet. In a protein, the -COOH group of one amino acid joins with the -NH2 group of the next amino acid with loss of a water molecule, forming a -CO-NH- bond called the peptide linkage, and long chains of such linkages make the protein. On hydrolysis proteins give back these amino acids.

Classification on the Basis of Function

  • Structural proteins (collagen, keratin) that build tissues.
  • Enzymes (amylase, pepsin) that catalyse body reactions.
  • Hormones (insulin) that regulate processes.
  • Transport proteins (haemoglobin) that carry substances.
  • Protective proteins (antibodies) that fight infection.
  • Contractile proteins (actin, myosin) that cause muscle movement.
  • Storage proteins (casein of milk) that store amino acids and nutrients.

Structure of Proteins

The primary structure is the specific sequence in which amino acids are joined by peptide bonds in the polypeptide chain; it decides all higher structures of the protein. The secondary structure is the regular folding of this chain into an alpha-helix or a beta-pleated sheet, held by hydrogen bonds between C=O and N-H groups of nearby peptide bonds. The tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional folding of the whole chain upon itself, stabilised by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulphide bonds and hydrophobic interactions, and it is this final shape that gives the protein its biological activity.

Physical Properties of Proteins

Proteins are colourless, mostly tasteless, high molar mass macromolecular solids; some are crystalline while most are amorphous. Some proteins like albumin of egg are soluble in water forming colloidal solutions, while fibrous proteins like keratin are insoluble in water and common solvents. They are denatured (their structure is destroyed) by heat, strong acids, alkalis, alcohol and heavy metal salts, as seen when egg white sets on heating. Proteins also show optical activity, can be precipitated from solution, and on strong heating they char and give a characteristic burnt-hair smell.

Essential Functions in the Body

Proteins are the body-building material: they build and repair muscles, skin and other tissues and are essential for growth. Many proteins act as enzymes and hormones that control and speed up the chemical reactions and processes of the body, such as insulin and digestive enzymes. Proteins like antibodies defend the body against disease, haemoglobin carries oxygen, and in need proteins can also be oxidised to provide energy.

mcqs.q: The bond formed between two amino acids in a protein is called a:
mcqs.why: A peptide linkage is the -CO-NH- bond formed when the -COOH group of one amino acid joins the -NH2 group of the next with loss of water.

mcqs.q: According to the book, how many alpha amino acids take part in making proteins in living organisms?
mcqs.why: The book gives 22 alpha amino acids in total that take part in making proteins in living organisms.

mcqs.q: Essential amino acids are those which must be:
mcqs.why: Essential amino acids cannot be made adequately by the body itself, so they must be supplied through the diet.

mcqs.q: Which pair is an example of structural proteins?
mcqs.why: Collagen and keratin are structural proteins that build tissues, whereas amylase and pepsin are enzymes.

mcqs.q: Haemoglobin is classified on the basis of function as a:
mcqs.why: Haemoglobin is a transport protein because it carries oxygen and other substances in the blood.

mcqs.q: The primary structure of a protein is:
options: The specific sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain
mcqs.why: Primary structure is the specific sequence in which amino acids are joined by peptide bonds, and it decides all higher structures.

mcqs.q: The secondary structure of a protein is held together mainly by:
options: Hydrogen bonds between C=O and N-H groups
mcqs.why: Secondary structure, the alpha-helix or beta-pleated sheet, is held by hydrogen bonds between C=O and N-H groups of nearby peptide bonds.

mcqs.q: Which interactions stabilise the tertiary structure of a protein?
options: Hydrogen, ionic and disulphide bonds and hydrophobic interactions
mcqs.why: Tertiary structure is stabilised by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulphide bonds and hydrophobic interactions, giving the protein its biological activity.

mcqs.q: Which protein is soluble in water and forms a colloidal solution?
mcqs.why: Albumin of egg is soluble in water forming a colloidal solution, while fibrous proteins like keratin are insoluble in water and common solvents.

mcqs.q: Proteins are denatured by which set of agents?
options: Heat, strong acids, alkalis, alcohol and heavy metal salts
mcqs.why: Heat, strong acids, alkalis, alcohol and heavy metal salts denature proteins, destroying their structure, as when egg white sets on heating.

lessons.title: Lipids
lessons.notes_html:
Lipids are water-insoluble, heterogeneous organic compounds which are chemically esters of fatty acids and alcohols, soluble in organic solvents like ether and chloroform. They are classified into simple lipids (fats, oils and waxes), compound lipids (phospholipids and glycolipids) and derived lipids (steroids, fatty acids, glycerol). Cell membranes are built mainly of a double layer of phospholipids, whose hydrophilic phosphate heads face the water on both sides and whose hydrophobic fatty acid tails face inwards; triglycerides are storage fats, while glycolipids and steroids are present in membranes only in smaller amounts.

Properties and Biological Significance

Their properties include insolubility in water, greasy feel, lower density than water, hydrolysis by alkali (saponification) and becoming rancid on oxidation. The three main functions of lipids are: first, they act as a concentrated store of energy and provide about twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates; second, they form the structural material of cell membranes, especially phospholipids, and protect delicate internal organs as a cushion; third, they act as thermal insulators under the skin, prevent water loss, and serve as solvents and carriers for the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.

Why Lipids are a Better Source of Energy

Lipids contain a much higher proportion of carbon and hydrogen and very little oxygen compared with carbohydrates and proteins, so they can be oxidised more completely. On complete oxidation 1 g of lipid gives about 9 kcal (about 38 kJ) of energy, while 1 g of carbohydrate or protein gives only about 4 kcal. Lipids are also stored in the body in nearly water-free form, so more energy is stored per unit weight, making them the better energy source.

Saponification

Saponification is the hydrolysis of a fat or oil with an alkali to form glycerol and soap, which is the sodium or potassium salt of a long-chain fatty acid: triglyceride (fat/oil) + 3NaOH -> (heat) glycerol + 3RCOONa (soap). For example, glyceryl stearate boiled with NaOH gives glycerol and sodium stearate, a common soap.

Rancidity

Rancidity is the spoiling of fats and oils on standing in air, in which they develop a bad taste and unpleasant smell and become unfit to eat. It involves two simultaneous reactions: oxidation of the unsaturated fatty acid parts by atmospheric oxygen, and hydrolysis of the ester bonds by moisture, helped by enzymes and micro-organisms. The products include volatile short-chain fatty acids and aldehydes that cause the bad odour.

mcqs.q: Lipids are chemically described as:
options: Esters of fatty acids and alcohols
mcqs.why: Lipids are esters of fatty acids and alcohols; they are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents like ether and chloroform.

mcqs.q: Phospholipids and glycolipids belong to which class of lipids?
mcqs.why: Phospholipids and glycolipids are compound lipids, while fats, oils and waxes are simple lipids and steroids are derived lipids.

mcqs.q: The major lipid component of the cell membrane is the:
mcqs.why: Cell membranes are built mainly of a double layer of phospholipids, with hydrophilic heads facing water and hydrophobic tails facing inwards.

mcqs.q: In the phospholipid double layer of a membrane, the hydrophobic tails face:
mcqs.why: The hydrophobic fatty acid tails face inwards, away from water, while the hydrophilic phosphate heads face the water on both sides.

mcqs.q: Saponification is the hydrolysis of a fat or oil with:
mcqs.why: Saponification is alkaline hydrolysis: a fat or oil boiled with an alkali such as NaOH gives glycerol and soap, the salt of a fatty acid.

mcqs.q: Glyceryl stearate boiled with NaOH gives glycerol and which soap?
mcqs.why: Glyceryl stearate with NaOH gives glycerol and sodium stearate, a common soap, according to the saponification reaction in the book.

mcqs.q: How much energy is obtained from 1 g of lipid on complete oxidation?
mcqs.why: 1 g of lipid gives about 9 kcal, about 38 kJ, roughly twice the energy from 1 g of carbohydrate or protein, because lipids contain little oxygen.

mcqs.q: Rancidity of fats and oils involves which two simultaneous reactions?
mcqs.why: Rancidity involves oxidation of unsaturated fatty acid parts by air and hydrolysis of ester bonds by moisture, producing bad-smelling acids and aldehydes.

mcqs.q: Lipids serve as solvents and carriers for which vitamins?
options: Vitamins A, D, E and K
mcqs.why: Lipids carry the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K, besides storing energy, building membranes and insulating the body.

mcqs.q: Why are lipids stored in a nearly water-free form an advantage?
options: Less energy is stored per gram
More energy is stored per unit weight
mcqs.why: Because lipids are stored nearly water-free, more energy is stored per unit weight, making them a better, concentrated energy source.

lessons.title: Minerals of Biological Significance
lessons.notes_html:
Minerals are inorganic elements needed in small amounts for building body structures and for regulating enzymes, fluids, nerves and energy processes, and their deficiency causes specific diseases.

  • Calcium: builds bones and teeth, helps blood clotting and muscle contraction; its deficiency causes weak bones.
  • Iron: is the central part of haemoglobin and carries oxygen in blood; its deficiency causes anaemia.
  • Zinc: is essential for the normal development and working of immune cells, for enzyme activity, growth and wound healing; its deficiency weakens immunity and makes a person more prone to infections.
  • Phosphorus: with calcium, forms bones and teeth, and as part of ATP it stores and transfers energy, besides being a component of DNA, RNA and cell membranes.

mcqs.q: Minerals are needed by the body in what amounts?
mcqs.why: Minerals are inorganic elements needed in small amounts for building body structures and regulating enzymes, fluids, nerves and energy processes.

mcqs.q: Calcium is essential mainly for:
options: Building bones and teeth and helping blood clotting
mcqs.why: Calcium builds bones and teeth and helps blood clotting and muscle contraction; its deficiency causes weak bones.

mcqs.q: Deficiency of calcium in the body causes:
mcqs.why: Calcium deficiency causes weak bones because calcium is a main building material of bones and teeth.

mcqs.q: Iron performs its oxygen-carrying role as the central part of:
mcqs.why: Iron is the central part of haemoglobin, the protein in blood that carries oxygen to the tissues.

mcqs.q: Deficiency of iron causes which disease?
mcqs.why: Iron deficiency causes anaemia because without enough iron, haemoglobin cannot carry sufficient oxygen in the blood.

mcqs.q: Zinc is essential for the normal development and working of:
mcqs.why: Zinc is essential for immune cells, enzyme activity, growth and wound healing; its deficiency weakens immunity and increases infections.

mcqs.q: A person deficient in zinc is likely to show:
mcqs.why: Zinc deficiency weakens immunity and makes a person more prone to infections, and it also impairs growth and wound healing.

mcqs.q: Phosphorus stores and transfers energy in the body as part of:
mcqs.why: Phosphorus, as part of ATP, stores and transfers energy, and with calcium it forms bones and teeth.

mcqs.q: Phosphorus is also a component of which structures?
mcqs.why: Phosphorus is a component of DNA, RNA and cell membranes, in addition to bones, teeth and ATP.

mcqs.q: Which mineral helps both blood clotting and muscle contraction?
mcqs.why: Calcium helps blood clotting and muscle contraction, besides building bones and teeth, as stated in the lesson.

lessons.title: Introduction to the Chemical Industry
lessons.notes_html:
Industrial chemistry is the branch of chemistry which deals with the conversion of raw materials into useful products through chemical processes. Its primary objective is to investigate new ways and technologies to enhance the efficiency of chemical processes, reduce expenses and increase product yields. An industrial chemist plays a crucial role in enhancing productivity through the exploration of novel catalysts and optimising reaction conditions, while also aiming to reduce production costs by utilising economical raw materials. Industrial chemists also ensure safety standards, risk assessment and proper storage protocols. This multi-disciplinary field intersects with other scientific branches, including agriculture, engineering and pharmaceuticals.

Chemical Industries

The term chemical industries refers to all those companies that manufacture chemicals. These industries involve a broad range of activities including production of chemicals, quality assurance, packaging and distribution. Several chemical industries are involved in the manufacturing of basic chemicals, including acids, alkalis, salts, gases and more. Chemicals play an important role in the production of a wide range of products such as dyes, cosmetics, synthetic polymers, pesticides, cement, detergents, fertilisers, fibres, glasses, agrochemicals, etc. These industries encompass a wide range of sectors, generate substantial revenue and create employment opportunities. In Pakistan, the control and regulation of chemical industries involves government agencies such as the Pakistan Standards and Quality Control Authority (PSQCA) and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

Main Types of Chemical Industries

  • Petrochemical industries: primarily focused on the extraction, refining and processing of petroleum and natural gases. Crude oil on refining is used as fuel for transportation and power supply, and petrochemical feedstock or basic petrochemicals (methane, ethane, ethene, propene, butene, benzene, etc.) are converted into alcohols, carboxylic acids, amines, ethers, aldehydes and halogen derivatives, and then into final products such as solvents, polymers, fertilisers, pesticides, detergents, dyes and cosmetics, which meet the basic needs of clothing, shelter, food, health, transportation and communication. They also produce many other chemicals as by-products, which are then sold as raw materials for several useful substances.
  • Fertiliser industries: responsible for the production of fertilisers, substances used to improve soil fertility and promote plant growth. Fertilisers provide essential nutrients to plants, enhancing crop yields and agricultural productivity. There are two main types: organic fertilisers, derived from natural sources, and synthetic fertilisers, manufactured chemically.
  • Textile industries: sectors that involve the production of fabrics and textiles, including natural fibres like cotton and wool as well as synthetic materials like polyester and nylon, providing products from clothing and household items to industrial materials.
  • Paint industries: produce liquid or powdered substances used for coating surfaces, providing protection, decoration and other functional purposes in construction, automotive and industrial sectors.

lessons.title: Pharmaceutical Industry
lessons.notes_html:
Scope of the Pharmaceutical Industry in Pakistan

The pharmaceutical industry of Pakistan manufactures a large share of the medicines used in the country, including tablets, syrups, injections, antibiotics, painkillers and life-saving drugs, and it also exports medicines to many countries. It provides employment to a large number of chemists, pharmacists and workers and saves foreign exchange by reducing imports of finished drugs. Its scope is growing with increasing population and health needs, although it still depends largely on imported raw materials (active ingredients).

Important Drug Types

  • Antimalarial drugs: chloroquine is the well-known drug used for the prevention and treatment of malaria caused by the Plasmodium parasite.
  • Analgesics and antipyretics: aspirin is acetylsalicylic acid, prepared by acetylating salicylic acid with acetic anhydride; it acts as an analgesic (pain reliever), antipyretic (fever reducer) and anti-inflammatory drug. (Ascorbic acid is vitamin C.) Drugs that bring a raised body temperature (fever) back to normal are called antipyretics, common examples being paracetamol and aspirin.
  • Antihistamines: an antihistamine is a drug that blocks the action of histamine, a chemical released in the body during allergic reactions. It is used for symptoms such as sneezing, running nose, itching, skin rashes and hives (urticaria), watery eyes and hay fever. Common examples are diphenhydramine and cetirizine; some older antihistamines also cause drowsiness and are used in cough and cold medicines. Ibuprofen and paracetamol are pain relievers and fever reducers, and diphenhydramine is an antihistamine used for allergy.

lessons.title: Pesticides
lessons.notes_html:
Pesticides are chemicals used to kill or control pests that damage crops, stored food and health. Pesticides increase crop yield but must be used carefully because many are poisonous and persist in the environment.

Types of Pesticides

  • Insecticides: kill insects, e.g. DDT (dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane), widely used commercially to kill insects, especially mosquitoes spreading malaria.
  • Herbicides (weedicides): kill unwanted weeds in fields, e.g. 2,4-D.
  • Fungicides: kill fungi attacking crops, e.g. Bordeaux mixture.
  • Rodenticides: kill rats and mice damaging stored grain.
