lessons.title: Synthetic Polymers (PVC and Nylon)
lessons.notes_html:
Natural and Synthetic Polymers

Two synthetic polymers are polyethene (used for bags and bottles) and nylon (used for fibres and ropes), both manufactured in industry from petrochemical monomers. Two natural polymers are cellulose (the structural material of plant cell walls, in wood and cotton) and starch (the energy-storage polymer of plants); cellulose is a natural polymer obtained from plants and is not a synthetic plastic, whereas nylon, Teflon and polyethene are synthetic polymers. Natural rubber and proteins are other examples of natural polymers.

Nylon 6,6

Nylon 6,6 is prepared by the condensation polymerisation of hexamethylene diamine (6 carbons) with adipic acid (6 carbons), with loss of water molecules and formation of amide links; the two 6-carbon monomers give it the name nylon 6,6. Nylon is a strong, elastic, abrasion-resistant polyamide fibre used for ropes, fabrics, carpets, brushes and machine parts.

Polyvinyl Chloride (PVC)

PVC is prepared by addition polymerisation of vinyl chloride CH2=CHCl: nCH2=CHCl -> -[CH2-CHCl]n-. PVC is hard, tough, chemically resistant, non-flammable and a good electrical insulator; it is used for water and drainage pipes, electric cable insulation, floor tiles, raincoats, bottles and plastic sheets.

Thermosetting Plastics

Bakelite, made from phenol and formaldehyde, is an example of a thermosetting plastic: it forms a hard cross-linked network on heating and cannot be softened or remoulded again. Polyethene, PVC and nylon are thermoplastics that soften on heating and can be remoulded.

lessons.title: Cosmetics: Lipsticks, Nail Polish and Remover, Perfumes
lessons.notes_html:
Cosmetics are substances applied to the body, especially the face, skin, hair and nails, to clean, protect, beautify and improve appearance.

Commonly Used Cosmetics

  • Nail polish: a coloured lacquer of nitrocellulose, resin, plasticiser and solvent applied on nails. Its four main components are: (1) a film-forming polymer, usually nitrocellulose, which forms the hard glossy film on the nail; (2) a resin, which improves adhesion and gloss; (3) a plasticiser such as camphor or dibutyl phthalate, which keeps the film flexible and prevents cracking; and (4) solvents such as ethyl acetate or butyl acetate, plus pigments and colours that give the polish its shade.
  • Nail polish remover: consists mainly of acetone, a powerful solvent that quickly dissolves the film-forming polymer and pigments of dried nail polish.
  • Lipstick: a mixture of waxes, oils and pigments applied to the lips.
  • Perfumes: solutions of fragrant oils in alcohol that give a pleasant smell.
  • Hair dyes: colour the hair; permanent dyes use hydrogen peroxide H2O2 as the oxidising agent (developer), which oxidises the dye precursors so that large coloured molecules form inside the hair, and also lightens the natural pigment. Resorcinol is a dye coupler used in them, not the oxidiser.

Other common cosmetics include face creams, lotions and powders.

lessons.title: Adhesives
lessons.notes_html:
Adhesives are substances used to join two surfaces together by bonding, for example glues, gums and resins used in woodwork, packaging and industry.

Super Glue

Super glue is chemically based on cyanoacrylate (methyl or ethyl cyanoacrylate), which polymerises within seconds on contact with the moisture present on surfaces. It therefore forms an extremely strong bond between almost any materials, even skin, almost instantly, so it is used for quick repairs and even in surgery, unlike the slower-setting epoxy resins or polyvinyl acetate adhesives.

Silicone Resins

Silicone resins (the book writes silicon resins) are heat-resistant, water-repellent adhesives and sealants that remain flexible over a wide temperature range, used for sealing joints, in electronics and in high-temperature applications.

lessons.title: Chemistry of the Troposphere
lessons.notes_html:
The atmosphere is divided into layers: the troposphere extends from the surface to about 11 km, the stratosphere from 11 km to 50 km, the mesosphere from 50 to 85 km and the thermosphere from 85 to 500 km. We live in the lowest layer, the troposphere, which contains the air we breathe and where weather phenomena like rain, clouds and storms occur.

Chemistry of Nitrogen and Sulphur Oxides in the Troposphere

Nitrogen and its oxides react as: N2 + O2 -> (lightning/engine heat) 2NO, and 2NO + O2 -> 2NO2; NO2 with water and sunlight forms nitric acid and ozone, contributing to acid rain and photochemical smog, e.g. 4NO2 + 2H2O + O2 -> 4HNO3. Sulphur in coal and oil burns to SO2: S + O2 -> SO2, which oxidises further: 2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3, and SO3 + H2O -> H2SO4 (sulphuric acid), or SO2 + H2O -> H2SO3. These acids return as acid rain, while NOx with hydrocarbons and ozone together produce smog that harms lungs, crops and materials.

Smog

The word smog is made from smoke + fog. Industrial smog is the grey, harmful smog found over industrial cities, formed mainly from the burning of coal and fossil fuels. It is a mixture of fog, smoke particles, ash and sulphur dioxide; the SO2 oxidises and combines with water droplets to form sulphuric acid aerosol: 2SO2 + O2 -> 2SO3, SO3 + H2O -> H2SO4. It forms especially in cold, damp, still weather under temperature inversion, reduces visibility and causes respiratory diseases and damage to buildings.

Acid Rain

Normal rain is slightly acidic (pH about 5.6) because of dissolved CO2, but acid rain contains sulphuric acid and nitric acid formed from SOx and NOx pollutants, which lowers its pH further, typically below 5 and often near 4. Acid rain harms human health mainly indirectly: it dissolves toxic metals like aluminium, lead and mercury from soil into drinking water, irritates the eyes, skin and respiratory system through its precursor gases SO2 and NOx, and damages crops and water supplies on which people depend. It also corrodes buildings, monuments and metal structures. Prevention measures include reducing SO2 and NOx emissions by using low-sulphur fuels, fitting scrubbers in factory chimneys and catalytic converters in vehicles, shifting to cleaner and renewable energy sources, and enforcing environmental laws through agencies like the EPA.

Greenhouse Effect and Global Warming

The greenhouse effect is the warming of the Earth's atmosphere by gases that allow sunlight to reach the surface but absorb the infrared (heat) radiation re-emitted by the Earth, like the glass of a greenhouse; in natural amounts it keeps the Earth warm enough for life. The main greenhouse gases are carbon dioxide CO2 (from burning fossil fuels and deforestation), methane CH4 (from decaying matter, livestock and rice fields), nitrous oxide N2O (from fertilisers), water vapours, ozone O3 and chlorofluorocarbons CFCs. Oxygen, nitrogen and argon, the main components of air, do not absorb infrared radiation in this way. Human activities enhance the effect: burning fossil fuels in industries, vehicles and power plants releases huge amounts of CO2, deforestation reduces CO2 absorption, agriculture and livestock release methane and nitrous oxide, and industries release CFCs. The main cause of the rise in global average temperature (global warming) is this increased emission of greenhouse gases, chiefly carbon dioxide. The trapped heat disturbs weather patterns: heatwaves become more frequent, rainfall becomes irregular with more floods and droughts, glaciers and polar ice melt raising sea level, and storms and extreme weather events become stronger and less predictable.

Catalytic Converters

A catalytic converter is a device fitted in the exhaust system of automobiles, containing a honeycomb coated with platinum, palladium and rhodium catalysts (mainly Pt and Pd), which converts harmful exhaust gases into harmless ones at high temperature. The main pollutants it targets are carbon monoxide CO (converted to CO2: 2CO + O2 -> 2CO2), unburnt hydrocarbons (converted to CO2 and H2O) and nitrogen oxides NOx (converted to N2 and O2: 2NO -> N2 + O2). It requires unleaded petrol, because lead poisons the catalyst.

mcqs.q: Up to what height does the troposphere extend from the surface of the Earth?
mcqs.why: The troposphere extends from the surface to about 11 km. Above it lie the stratosphere (11-50 km), mesosphere (50-85 km) and thermosphere (85-500 km).

mcqs.q: In which layer of the atmosphere do we live, and where do rain, clouds and storms occur?
mcqs.why: We live in the troposphere, the lowest layer, which contains the air we breathe and where weather phenomena like rain, clouds and storms occur.

mcqs.q: Nitric oxide is formed in the troposphere during lightning and in hot engines by which reaction?
mcqs.why: At the high temperature of lightning or an engine, nitrogen and oxygen combine as N2 + O2 -> 2NO. The NO then oxidises further to NO2.

mcqs.q: Sulphur trioxide reacts with water in the atmosphere to form which acid, a component of acid rain?
mcqs.why: SO3 + H2O -> H2SO4, sulphuric acid. Sulphur in coal and oil burns to SO2, which oxidises to SO3 and then forms this acid.

mcqs.q: The word smog is made by combining which two words?
mcqs.why: Smog is made from smoke + fog. It is a harmful mixture of fog with smoke particles and pollutant gases that hangs over industrial cities.

mcqs.q: Industrial smog forms especially under which weather conditions?
options: Cold, damp, still weather under temperature inversion
mcqs.why: Industrial smog forms especially in cold, damp, still weather under temperature inversion, when fog, smoke, ash and SO2 are trapped near the ground.

mcqs.q: Normal rain has a pH of about 5.6 mainly because of which dissolved gas?
mcqs.why: Normal rain is slightly acidic, pH about 5.6, because of dissolved CO2. Acid rain is much more acidic because it also contains H2SO4 and HNO3 from pollutants.

mcqs.q: The pH of acid rain is typically:
mcqs.why: Acid rain typically has a pH below 5 and often near 4, because sulphuric acid and nitric acid formed from SOx and NOx pollutants lower the pH of normal rain.

mcqs.q: Acid rain harms human health indirectly because it dissolves which toxic metals from soil into drinking water?
mcqs.why: Acid rain dissolves toxic metals like aluminium, lead and mercury from the soil into drinking water, and its precursor gases SO2 and NOx irritate the eyes, skin and respiratory system.

mcqs.q: Which measure helps prevent acid rain by removing sulphur gases from factory chimney gases?
mcqs.why: Fitting scrubbers in factory chimneys removes SO2 from chimney gases. Using low-sulphur fuels and catalytic converters in vehicles also reduce acid rain.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a greenhouse gas?
mcqs.why: Oxygen is not a greenhouse gas: oxygen, nitrogen and argon, the main components of air, do not absorb infrared radiation, whereas CO2, CH4 and CFCs do.

mcqs.q: In the greenhouse effect, greenhouse gases warm the Earth because they:
options: Block all sunlight from reaching the Earth
Absorb the infrared heat radiation re-emitted by the Earth
mcqs.why: Greenhouse gases allow sunlight to reach the surface but absorb the infrared (heat) radiation re-emitted by the Earth, like the glass of a greenhouse, warming the atmosphere.

mcqs.q: The main cause of the rise in global average temperature (global warming) is:
options: Increased emission of greenhouse gases, chiefly carbon dioxide
The natural greenhouse effect at its normal level
Melting of polar ice by itself
mcqs.why: Global warming is mainly caused by the increased emission of greenhouse gases, chiefly CO2 from burning fossil fuels, increased by deforestation which reduces CO2 absorption.

mcqs.q: Which is one effect of global warming on weather patterns described in the book?
options: Storms become weaker and fully predictable
Sea level falls as glaciers grow
Glaciers and polar ice melt, raising sea level, with more floods and droughts
mcqs.why: The trapped heat makes heatwaves more frequent, rainfall irregular with more floods and droughts, melts glaciers and polar ice raising sea level, and makes storms stronger.

mcqs.q: A catalytic converter in a vehicle uses which catalysts, coated on a honeycomb, to clean exhaust gases?
mcqs.why: Catalytic converters contain a honeycomb coated with platinum, palladium and rhodium (mainly Pt and Pd), converting CO to CO2, hydrocarbons to CO2 and H2O, and NOx to N2 and O2. Lead poisons the catalyst, so unleaded petrol is required.

lessons.title: Chemistry of the Stratosphere
lessons.notes_html:
The stratosphere extends from 11 km to about 50 km above the Earth. The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere, about 15 to 35 km above the Earth, where ozone O3 is formed from oxygen by ultraviolet radiation. This layer absorbs most of the harmful UV radiation of the Sun and protects life on Earth from it.

Causes of Ozone Depletion

Ozone depletion in the upper atmosphere is mainly caused by chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs). The main cause is the release of ozone-depleting substances, especially CFCs from refrigerators, air conditioners, aerosol sprays and foam making, and also halons and nitrogen oxides. In the stratosphere, UV radiation breaks CFCs and releases chlorine atoms: CFCl3 -> (UV) CFCl2 + Cl. The chlorine atom destroys ozone in a repeating chain: Cl + O3 -> ClO + O2 and ClO + O -> Cl + O2, so one chlorine atom can destroy about 100,000 ozone molecules, thinning the ozone layer.

Ozone-Depleting Substances (ODS)

Ozone-depleting substances are man-made chemicals that release chlorine or bromine in the stratosphere and destroy ozone, mainly chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), halons, carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform and HCFCs. Human activities that contributed include the wide use of CFCs as refrigerants in refrigerators and air conditioners, as propellants in aerosol sprays and in foam blowing, halons in fire extinguishers, and nitrogen oxides from jet aircraft and fertilisers. Because of the resulting ozone hole and increased UV radiation, the Montreal Protocol has phased out most ODS and replaced them with safer alternatives like HFCs and hydrocarbons.

mcqs.q: The stratosphere extends over which range of height above the Earth?
options: From the surface to about 11 km
mcqs.why: The stratosphere extends from 11 km to about 50 km above the Earth, lying above the troposphere and below the mesosphere.

mcqs.q: The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere at about which height above the Earth?
mcqs.why: The ozone layer lies in the stratosphere, about 15 to 35 km above the Earth, where ozone O3 is formed from oxygen by ultraviolet radiation.

mcqs.q: Ozone in the stratosphere is formed when ultraviolet radiation acts on which gas?
mcqs.why: Ozone O3 is formed from oxygen by ultraviolet radiation in the stratosphere. The resulting layer absorbs most of the harmful UV radiation of the Sun.

mcqs.q: Ozone depletion in the upper atmosphere is mainly caused by:
mcqs.why: Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) are the main cause of ozone depletion: in the stratosphere UV radiation breaks them and releases chlorine atoms that destroy ozone in a chain reaction.

mcqs.q: When CFCl3 is broken by UV radiation in the stratosphere, which atom is released that attacks ozone?
mcqs.why: UV radiation breaks CFCl3 as CFCl3 -> CFCl2 + Cl. The free chlorine atom released then reacts with ozone: Cl + O3 -> ClO + O2.

mcqs.q: In the ozone-destroying chain, the chlorine atom first reacts with ozone to give:
mcqs.why: The chain runs Cl + O3 -> ClO + O2, then ClO + O -> Cl + O2. The chlorine atom is regenerated, so the destruction repeats many times.

mcqs.q: About how many ozone molecules can a single chlorine atom destroy?
mcqs.why: One chlorine atom can destroy about 100,000 ozone molecules, because it is regenerated in each cycle of the chain Cl + O3 -> ClO + O2 and ClO + O -> Cl + O2.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an ozone-depleting substance (ODS)?
mcqs.why: Halons are ozone-depleting substances, along with CFCs, carbon tetrachloride, methyl chloroform and HCFCs; they release chlorine or bromine in the stratosphere and destroy ozone.

mcqs.q: CFCs were widely used by humans in which of the following?
options: Refrigerators, air conditioners, aerosol sprays and foam making
mcqs.why: CFCs were widely used as refrigerants in refrigerators and air conditioners, as propellants in aerosol sprays and in foam blowing, which released them into the atmosphere.

mcqs.q: Under the Montreal Protocol, ozone-depleting substances have largely been replaced by safer alternatives such as:
mcqs.why: The Montreal Protocol has phased out most ODS and replaced them with safer alternatives like HFCs and hydrocarbons, to protect the ozone layer.

lessons.title: Water Pollution and Water Analysis
lessons.notes_html:
Sources of Water Pollution

The major source of water pollution is industrial activities: industries discharge untreated effluents containing toxic chemicals, heavy metals, dyes, acids and oils into rivers and groundwater. Domestic sewage and agricultural run-off of fertilisers and pesticides are the other major sources.

Testing of Waste Water

  • pH measurement: shows whether the water is acidic or alkaline compared with safe limits.
  • BOD (biochemical oxygen demand): the oxygen used by micro-organisms to decompose organic matter in a fixed time; higher BOD means more organic pollution.
  • COD (chemical oxygen demand): the oxygen needed to chemically oxidise the pollutants with a strong oxidising agent.
  • Dissolved solids and specific pollutants: determination of dissolved solids and pollutants such as heavy metals, oil and grease, so the water can be compared with WHO and environmental standards before discharge.

mcqs.q: The major source of water pollution is:
mcqs.why: Industrial activities are the major source of water pollution, because industries discharge untreated effluents containing toxic chemicals, heavy metals, dyes, acids and oils into rivers and groundwater.

mcqs.q: Untreated industrial effluents discharged into rivers typically contain:
options: Toxic chemicals, heavy metals, dyes, acids and oils
mcqs.why: Industrial effluents contain toxic chemicals, heavy metals, dyes, acids and oils, which is why industry is the major source of water pollution.

mcqs.q: Apart from industry, which are the other major sources of water pollution named in the book?
options: Domestic sewage and agricultural run-off of fertilisers and pesticides
mcqs.why: Besides industrial activities, the other major sources are domestic sewage and agricultural run-off carrying fertilisers and pesticides into rivers and groundwater.

mcqs.q: In waste water testing, pH measurement shows:
options: Whether the water is acidic or alkaline compared with safe limits
The amount of dissolved solids present
The concentration of heavy metals only
mcqs.why: pH measurement shows whether the water is acidic or alkaline compared with safe limits; it is one of the four fundamental tests of waste water.

mcqs.q: BOD (biochemical oxygen demand) of waste water is:
options: The oxygen needed to chemically oxidise pollutants with a strong oxidising agent
The oxygen dissolved naturally in clean water
The oxygen used by micro-organisms to decompose organic matter in a fixed time
The oxygen released by plants in the water
mcqs.why: BOD is the oxygen used by micro-organisms to decompose organic matter in a fixed time. It measures the organic pollution load of the waste water.

mcqs.q: A higher BOD value of a water sample means:
options: More organic pollution in the water
The water contains more dissolved oxygen for fish
mcqs.why: Higher BOD means more organic pollution, because more oxygen is used by micro-organisms to decompose the larger amount of organic matter present.

mcqs.q: COD (chemical oxygen demand) is the oxygen needed to:
options: Support fish and other water life
Chemically oxidise the pollutants with a strong oxidising agent
Neutralise the acidity of the water
mcqs.why: COD is the oxygen needed to chemically oxidise the pollutants with a strong oxidising agent, unlike BOD which depends on micro-organisms decomposing organic matter.

mcqs.q: How does COD differ from BOD in waste water testing?
options: COD uses micro-organisms, BOD uses chemicals
They are exactly the same test
COD measures pH, BOD measures temperature
COD uses a strong oxidising agent chemically, while BOD uses micro-organisms
mcqs.why: COD measures the oxygen needed to chemically oxidise pollutants with a strong oxidising agent, whereas BOD measures oxygen used by micro-organisms to decompose organic matter in a fixed time.

mcqs.q: Determination of dissolved solids and specific pollutants in waste water includes checking for:
options: Only the colour of the water
mcqs.why: This test determines dissolved solids and specific pollutants such as heavy metals, oil and grease, so the water can be compared with WHO and environmental standards.

mcqs.q: Before waste water is discharged, its test results are compared with:
options: The results of neighbouring factories only
The pH of pure distilled water only
mcqs.why: Test results for pH, BOD, COD, dissolved solids and specific pollutants are compared with WHO and environmental standards before the water is discharged.

lessons.title: Green Chemistry
lessons.notes_html: The primary goal of green chemistry is to design chemical products and processes that are safe for human health and the environment, preventing pollution at its source - that is, developing environmentally friendly chemicals. Its goals include developing environmentally friendly chemicals, minimising waste generation and hazards, reducing energy consumption, and using renewable raw materials and safer solvents. Green chemistry is applied in industry together with measures such as fitting catalytic converters in vehicles, using low-sulphur fuels, scrubbing factory chimney gases and shifting to cleaner and renewable energy sources, so that harmful emissions of SOx, NOx, CO and unburnt hydrocarbons are prevented rather than treated afterwards.

mcqs.q: The primary goal of green chemistry is to:
options: Design chemical products and processes that are safe for human health and the environment
Maximise industrial production at any cost
Increase the use of hazardous solvents
Treat pollution only after it is produced
mcqs.why: The primary goal of green chemistry is to design chemical products and processes that are safe for human health and the environment, preventing pollution at its source.

mcqs.q: Green chemistry prevents pollution mainly by:
options: Preventing pollution at its source rather than treating it afterwards
Exporting hazardous waste to other countries
mcqs.why: Green chemistry prevents pollution at its source by developing environmentally friendly chemicals and processes, instead of treating harmful emissions after they are produced.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a goal of green chemistry?
mcqs.why: Minimising waste generation and hazards is a stated goal of green chemistry, along with developing environmentally friendly chemicals, reducing energy use and using renewable raw materials.

mcqs.q: Which raw materials does green chemistry prefer to use?
mcqs.why: Green chemistry aims to use renewable raw materials and safer solvents, while minimising waste and hazards and reducing energy consumption.

mcqs.q: In green chemistry, which type of solvents should be preferred?
options: No solvents can ever be used
mcqs.why: Green chemistry promotes safer solvents as part of designing products and processes that are safe for human health and the environment.

mcqs.q: Reducing energy consumption in chemical processes is:
options: Against the aims of green chemistry
One of the goals of green chemistry
Only a goal of the Montreal Protocol
Relevant only to transport, not industry
mcqs.why: Reducing energy consumption is one of the goals of green chemistry, together with minimising waste and hazards and using renewable raw materials and safer solvents.

mcqs.q: Which vehicle device is used together with green chemistry measures to cut harmful exhaust emissions?
mcqs.why: Fitting catalytic converters in vehicles is applied together with green chemistry measures; they convert CO, unburnt hydrocarbons and NOx into harmless gases.

mcqs.q: Using low-sulphur fuels and scrubbing factory chimney gases are examples of:
options: Measures applied with green chemistry to prevent harmful emissions
mcqs.why: Using low-sulphur fuels and scrubbing factory chimney gases are measures applied in industry together with green chemistry so that harmful emissions are prevented rather than treated afterwards.

mcqs.q: Shifting to cleaner and renewable energy sources helps green chemistry by:
options: Increasing emissions of SOx and NOx
Reducing harmful emissions of SOx, NOx, CO and unburnt hydrocarbons
Removing the need for catalytic converters everywhere
mcqs.why: Cleaner and renewable energy sources reduce the harmful emissions of SOx, NOx, CO and unburnt hydrocarbons that green chemistry aims to prevent at the source.

mcqs.q: Developing environmentally friendly chemicals is described in the book as:
options: The primary aim of green chemistry
The function of a catalytic converter
mcqs.why: Developing environmentally friendly chemicals is the primary aim of green chemistry: designing chemical products and processes safe for human health and the environment.

lessons.title: Methods of Spectroscopy
lessons.notes_html:
The Electromagnetic Spectrum

In the electromagnetic spectrum, energy increases in the order radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible, UV, X-rays, gamma rays (E = hv, so higher frequency means higher energy). IR radiation therefore has energy higher than radio waves and microwaves, but lower than UV waves and X-rays. Each region causes a different change in a molecule: UV-visible radiations have enough energy to raise electrons from a lower energy level to a higher one (electronic excitation or electronic transition); IR radiation only increases bond vibrations; and radio waves only change nuclear spin.

UV-Visible Spectroscopy

The purpose of UV-visible spectroscopy is to study molecules that absorb UV or visible light through electronic transitions, and thereby to identify conjugated systems and measure the concentration of a substance from its absorbance. The transitions, in decreasing order of energy required, are: sigma to sigma* (highest energy, because sigma bonds are very strong and their electrons are held tightly, absorbing at the shortest wavelength in the far UV), then n to sigma*, then pi to pi*, and n to pi* (lowest). In chemistry the technique is used for structure determination, studying reaction kinetics, detecting impurities and in quantitative analysis and quality control of drugs. In biology it is used to measure proteins and nucleic acids (DNA absorbs at 260 nm and proteins at 280 nm), to study enzymes and to estimate the concentration of biological samples.

Lambda max: lambda max is the wavelength at which a substance shows the maximum absorption of UV-visible radiation in its spectrum; it is a characteristic property of the compound and the transition involved. In the UV-visible spectrum of ethanol shown in the book (absorbance plotted against wavelength in nm, 200-500 nm), the curve rises to a single strong peak with maximum absorbance of about 1.5 at about 270-280 nm and then falls to nearly zero above 300 nm. The wavelength at the top of this peak is the lambda max of ethanol, arising from the n to sigma* transition of the lone-pair electrons of the -OH oxygen, and ethanol shows no significant absorption in the visible region.

Infrared (IR) Spectroscopy

IR spectroscopy is the technique used to determine the functional groups in a given organic molecule: each functional group absorbs IR radiation at a characteristic wavenumber (for example C=O at about 1680-1740 cm-1 and O-H at about 3600-3650 cm-1). By noting which absorptions are present, IR spectroscopy identifies the bonds and functional groups present. In the IR spectrum frequency is expressed as wavenumber, the number of waves per centimetre, whose unit is reciprocal centimetre, cm-1; the useful IR range is about 4000-670 cm-1, while nanometre and angstrom are units of wavelength used in UV-visible spectroscopy. The fingerprint region, typically 1500-500 cm-1, contains many bending and skeletal vibrations and gives a complex pattern that is unique for each molecule, like a fingerprint of a person; it is used to identify a compound by comparing its spectrum with that of a known sample.

Proton NMR Spectroscopy

Proton NMR (1H NMR) spectroscopy is the study of the absorption of radio waves by hydrogen nuclei of a molecule placed in a strong magnetic field. It detects nuclei that have spin, principally the hydrogen nucleus 1H (a single proton) present in the sample. Only nuclei with an odd number of protons or neutrons, such as 1H and 13C, have a magnetic spin and can absorb radio waves in a magnetic field and be detected. The protons act like tiny magnets and align with or against the field; when they absorb radiofrequency energy of the right frequency they flip to the higher energy state (resonance). Protons in different environments absorb at slightly different frequencies (chemical shift, in ppm, with TMS as reference at 0 ppm), and the number of signals, their splitting and their areas reveal the structure of the molecule. In a proton NMR spectrum the x-axis represents the chemical shift, delta, in ppm, increasing from right (0 ppm, the TMS reference) to left (downfield, up to about 10-12 ppm), and the y-axis represents the intensity or strength of absorption (signal height/area), which is proportional to the number of equivalent protons producing that signal. D2O (heavy water) is used as a solvent in NMR spectroscopy because deuterium does not give a proton NMR signal, so it does not hide the signals of the sample; it is also used to identify -OH and -NH protons, which exchange with deuterium and their peaks disappear from the spectrum. NMR is applied in determining the structure of organic compounds, identifying ethanol and other substances, studying proteins, medical imaging (MRI) and quality control.

NMR spectrum of ethanol: the proton NMR graph of ethanol shows three signals because ethanol has three kinds of protons: CH3, CH2 and OH, in the ratio 3:2:1. Peak a at about 1.2 ppm is the CH3 group, split into a triplet by the two neighbouring CH2 protons, with the largest area (3 protons). Peak c at about 3.7 ppm is the CH2 group, split into a quartet by the three CH3 protons, with area for 2 protons; it is further downfield because it is directly attached to oxygen. Peak b at about 4.6 ppm is the single OH proton, appearing as a broad singlet with the smallest area (1 proton), most deshielded because it is bonded to electronegative oxygen. In the book, the hydroxyl proton of C2H5OH appears as a broad singlet around 4-5 ppm; its exact position varies with concentration and solvent because of exchange of the OH proton. Together the positions, splitting and areas of a, b and c confirm the structure CH3-CH2-OH.

Mass Spectroscopy

Mass spectroscopy gives the accurate relative molecular mass of a compound from its molecular ion peak (M+), from which its molecular formula can be worked out. The fragmentation pattern - the smaller peaks at different mass-to-charge (m/z) values - shows how the molecule breaks up, which reveals the groups and arrangement of atoms present and can distinguish between isomers. Its applications include identification of unknown compounds, structure determination, purity checking, detection of drugs and forensic materials, isotope abundance measurement, and quality control in the pharmaceutical and food industries.

Atomic Absorption and Emission Spectroscopy

In atomic emission spectroscopy the sample is heated or excited so that its atoms emit light of characteristic wavelengths on returning to lower energy levels, giving bright lines on a dark background. In atomic absorption spectroscopy light from a lamp is passed through the vapour of the sample and the atoms absorb their characteristic wavelengths, giving dark lines against a bright background. Emission measures the light given out and is used mostly for qualitative detection, while absorption measures the light absorbed and is widely used for quantitative determination of metals.

mcqs.q: In the electromagnetic spectrum, the energy of the radiations increases in which order?
options: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible, UV, X-rays, gamma rays
Gamma rays, X-rays, UV, visible, infrared
mcqs.why: Energy increases in the order radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible, UV, X-rays, gamma rays, because E = hv and higher frequency means higher energy.

mcqs.q: An infrared wave has a wavelength of 10 micrometres. What is its wavenumber? (1 micrometre = 1 x 10-4 cm)
mcqs.why: Wavenumber = 1 / wavelength in cm. Wavelength = 10 x 10-4 cm = 1 x 10-3 cm, so wavenumber = 1 / (1 x 10-3) = 1000 cm-1, which lies in the useful IR range.

mcqs.q: What is the frequency of light of wavelength 500 nm? (c = 3.0 x 10^8 m/s, 500 nm = 5.0 x 10-7 m)
mcqs.why: Frequency v = c / wavelength = (3.0 x 10^8) / (5.0 x 10-7) = 6.0 x 10^14 Hz. This is visible light, energetic enough for electronic transitions.

mcqs.q: Electronic excitation (electronic transition) in a molecule occurs when it absorbs:
mcqs.why: UV-visible radiations have enough energy to raise electrons from a lower energy level to a higher one. IR radiation only increases bond vibrations and radio waves only change nuclear spin.

mcqs.q: Which UV-visible transition requires the highest energy?
mcqs.why: The sigma to sigma* transition requires the highest energy because sigma bonds are very strong and their electrons are held tightly; the order is sigma to sigma* > n to sigma* > pi to pi* > n to pi*.

mcqs.q: Lambda max of a substance is:
options: The shortest wavelength it can absorb
The wavelength at which it shows maximum absorption of UV-visible radiation
The wavelength of visible light it reflects
The wavenumber of its strongest IR band
mcqs.why: Lambda max is the wavelength at which a substance shows the maximum absorption of UV-visible radiation; it is a characteristic property of the compound and the transition involved.

mcqs.q: In the UV-visible spectrum of ethanol in the book, the lambda max is at about:
options: 270-280 nm, from the n to sigma* transition of the -OH oxygen lone pair
500 nm, in the middle of the visible region
Above 300 nm, where absorbance is maximum
mcqs.why: Ethanol's curve rises to a single strong peak with maximum absorbance of about 1.5 at about 270-280 nm, its lambda max, arising from the n to sigma* transition of the lone-pair electrons of the -OH oxygen; it falls to nearly zero above 300 nm.

mcqs.q: Infrared (IR) spectroscopy is the technique used to determine which feature of an organic molecule?
mcqs.why: Each functional group absorbs IR radiation at a characteristic wavenumber (for example C=O at about 1680-1740 cm-1 and O-H at about 3600-3650 cm-1), so IR spectroscopy identifies the functional groups present.

mcqs.q: The fingerprint region of an IR spectrum typically lies in the range:
mcqs.why: The fingerprint region, typically 1500-500 cm-1, contains many bending and skeletal vibrations and gives a complex pattern unique for each molecule, used to identify a compound by comparison with a known sample.

mcqs.q: NMR spectroscopy is carried out using which radiations interacting with molecules in a strong magnetic field?
mcqs.why: NMR spectroscopy uses low-energy radiofrequency (radio) radiations. In a strong magnetic field, nuclei such as 1H absorb radio waves at a characteristic resonance frequency.

mcqs.q: In a proton NMR spectrum, the x-axis represents:
options: Chemical shift, delta, in ppm, with TMS as reference at 0 ppm
mcqs.why: The x-axis represents the chemical shift, delta, in ppm, increasing from right (0 ppm, the TMS reference) to left (downfield, up to about 10-12 ppm); the y-axis is intensity, proportional to the number of equivalent protons.

mcqs.q: D2O (heavy water) is used as a solvent in NMR spectroscopy because:
options: It increases the magnetic field strength
It gives a very strong proton signal itself
Deuterium does not give a proton NMR signal, so it does not hide the sample signals
mcqs.why: D2O is used in NMR spectroscopy because deuterium does not give a proton NMR signal, so it does not hide the signals of the sample; -OH and -NH protons exchange with deuterium and their peaks disappear.

mcqs.q: The proton NMR spectrum of ethanol shows three signals with area ratio:
mcqs.why: Ethanol has three kinds of protons, CH3, CH2 and OH, giving three signals in the ratio 3:2:1. The CH3 peak at about 1.2 ppm is a triplet, the CH2 peak at about 3.7 ppm is a quartet, and the OH peak at about 4.6 ppm is a broad singlet.

mcqs.q: In mass spectroscopy, the accurate relative molecular mass of a compound is obtained from:
mcqs.why: Mass spectroscopy gives the accurate relative molecular mass from the molecular ion peak (M+), from which the molecular formula can be worked out; the fragmentation pattern at different m/z values shows how the molecule breaks up.

mcqs.q: An atomic absorption spectrum is represented by:
options: Dark lines against a bright background
Bright lines against a dark background
Bright lines against a bright background
Dark lines against a dark background
mcqs.why: In atomic absorption spectroscopy, atoms absorb their characteristic wavelengths from light passed through the sample vapour, giving dark lines against a bright background; bright lines on a dark background belong to an emission spectrum.
